data.description: An indolent lymphoma, formerly called nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, featuring scattered large lymphocyte-predominant cells within nodules of small lymphocytes. These cells usually express B-cell markers and lack CD15 and CD30.
symptoms_not_in_common: Apparent CD15 and CD30 positivity in atypical cells argues against the usual phenotype
Isolated nasopharyngeal disease without peripheral lymphadenopathy is unusual
Parotid swelling is not a typical presenting feature

data.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma associated with Epstein–Barr virus that can involve extranodal sites and contain Hodgkin-like large cells. Confirmation requires B-cell immunostains and EBV testing.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent nasopharyngeal mass causing nasal obstruction
Failure to resolve with antibiotics or steroids
Possible CD30 expression in atypical cells
symptoms_not_in_common: A predominantly nodular small-lymphocyte infiltrate is less typical than a diffuse large-cell proliferation
No clonal B-cell population was detected, although sampling can limit flow cytometry
CD15 positivity is less characteristic than in classical Hodgkin lymphoma

data.diagnosis: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue
data.description: An indolent small B-cell lymphoma that can involve upper-airway mucosal tissue or salivary glands. Diagnosis requires demonstration of a characteristic B-cell infiltrate and supporting immunophenotypic or molecular findings.
symptoms_in_common: Right parotid swelling, which could reflect salivary-gland involvement
Absence of distant lymphadenopathy and negative bone marrow biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Scattered CD15-positive and CD30-positive large atypical cells are not characteristic
Flow cytometry did not identify a clonal B-cell population
No associated autoimmune disease or chronic inflammatory disorder was reported

data.diagnosis: Reactive adenoid lymphoid hyperplasia with atypical immunoblasts
data.description: A nonmalignant enlargement of nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue that may contain activated atypical lymphocytes and mimic lymphoma. Persistent recurrence and the illustrated atypical-cell staining warrant careful exclusion of malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: Adenoid pad enlargement causing nasal congestion
Initial biopsy interpreted as atypical lymphoid hyperplasia
No clonal B cells detected by flow cytometry
No distant lymphadenopathy or bone marrow involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: A recurrent 4.1 cm mass in a 50-year-old adult is concerning for more than routine reactive enlargement
Failure to improve with antibiotics and steroids
Large atypical cells with apparent combined CD15 and CD30 expression favor consideration of Hodgkin lymphoma

data.diagnosis: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma of the nasopharynx (extranodal, stage IE; likely lymphocyte-rich or mixed cellularity subtype)
data.description: B-cell derived lymphoma characterized by scarce Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells (CD30+, CD15+) in a reactive background of small lymphocytes, eosinophils and histiocytes. Primary involvement of Waldeyer's ring/nasopharynx is rare but well described.
symptoms_in_common: Nasopharyngeal mass with unilateral nasal congestion
No response to antibiotics and steroids
Scattered large atypical cells in atypical lymphoid background
Binucleated Reed-Sternberg-like cell with prominent nucleoli on H&E
Large cells positive for CD30 and CD15 (membranous and Golgi pattern)
Nodular infiltrate of small lymphocytes with eosinophils
Flow cytometry without clonal B cells (typical because neoplastic cells are scarce)
symptoms_not_in_common: Extranodal nasopharyngeal primary without any lymphadenopathy is unusual
No B symptoms reported
Parotid swelling is atypical
Absence of cervical or mediastinal nodal disease

data.description: Indolent B-cell lymphoma with scattered large LP ('popcorn') cells within nodules of small B lymphocytes; LP cells are CD20+, CD45+ and usually CD30-/CD15-.
symptoms_in_common: Negative flow cytometry for clonal B cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Large cells are CD30 and CD15 positive
Classic binucleated Reed-Sternberg morphology rather than popcorn cells
Eosinophil-rich background is uncommon
Usually presents with peripheral lymphadenopathy rather than a nasopharyngeal mass

data.description: EBV-associated epithelial malignancy of the nasopharynx with a dense lymphoid stroma that can mimic lymphoma; tumor cells are cytokeratin positive.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral nasopharyngeal mass with nasal obstruction
Large atypical cells in a lymphoid background
No response to antibiotics and steroids
symptoms_not_in_common: No cervical lymphadenopathy (usually present early)
Large cells express CD30 and CD15 rather than forming cohesive epithelial syncytia
Reed-Sternberg-like morphology with eosinophils
No epistaxis, otitis media or cranial nerve deficits reported

data.description: Aggressive EBV-driven lymphoma of the nasal cavity/nasopharynx with angiocentric, angiodestructive growth and necrosis; cells are CD56+, cytoplasmic CD3+, cytotoxic marker and EBER positive.
symptoms_in_common: No clonal B cells on flow cytometry
Disease confined to the upper aerodigestive tract
Mixed inflammatory infiltrate with atypical cells
symptoms_not_in_common: No necrosis, ulceration or angioinvasion described
No epistaxis or midline destruction
CD15-positive Reed-Sternberg-like cells are not expected
Predominantly small bland lymphocytes in a nodular pattern
More common in Asian and Latin American populations

data.diagnosis: Reactive/atypical lymphoid hyperplasia of the adenoids (including EBV-related or EBV-positive mucocutaneous lymphoproliferation)
data.description: Benign or self-limited lymphoid proliferation of Waldeyer's ring caused by infection (e.g., EBV), irritation such as smoking, or immune dysregulation; may contain scattered CD30+ immunoblasts that mimic Hodgkin cells.
symptoms_in_common: Adenoid pad swelling with nasal congestion
Initial biopsy read as atypical lymphoid hyperplasia
No lymphadenopathy and negative bone marrow
Scattered CD30-positive large cells can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: 4.1 cm mass that recurred within 3 months of adenoidectomy
No response to antibiotics and steroids
CD15 co-expression on large binucleated cells
Adenoid hypertrophy is unusual at age 50
No immunosuppression reported
Persistent FDG-avid mass

data.description: 52-year-old woman with exertional right buttock and thigh pain that resolves within 2 minutes of rest. Exercise tolerance worsened over past year, now limited to several blocks. Previously able to run 5-6 miles per day. Recently diagnosed hypertension controlled with lisinopril (5 mg daily). No other cardiovascular risk factors. Physical exam shows blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg bilaterally, high-pitched systolic bruit over right subcostal region and umbilicus, normal peripheral pulses. Ankle brachial index (ABI) at rest borderline normal (0.91) on right and normal (1.03) on left. Remainder of examination normal.

data.diagnosis: Multivessel fibromuscular dysplasia involving the right renal and iliac arteries
data.description: A nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory arterial disorder causing alternating stenoses and dilatations. The renal angiogram shows a string-of-beads appearance strongly suggestive of fibromuscular dysplasia; iliac involvement can explain exertional claudication.
symptoms_in_common: Recently diagnosed hypertension, potentially related to renal artery involvement
High-pitched right subcostal and umbilical systolic bruits
Exertional right buttock and thigh pain relieved promptly by rest
Progressive reduction in walking and running tolerance
Borderline right resting ABI despite normal peripheral pulses
Absence of conventional atherosclerotic risk factors
Angiographic arterial beading and iliac narrowing
symptoms_not_in_common: Lower-extremity claudication is a less common presentation than renal or cerebrovascular manifestations

data.description: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the aorta or iliac arteries can reduce blood flow during exercise, causing buttock and thigh claudication.
symptoms_in_common: Pain resolves within 2 minutes of rest
symptoms_not_in_common: No cardiovascular risk factors other than recently diagnosed hypertension
Renal arterial string-of-beads appearance rather than typical atherosclerotic plaque
Normal peripheral pulses are less typical of advanced flow-limiting aortoiliac disease

data.description: Nonatherosclerotic thickening of the iliac artery lining, usually associated with endurance athletics, can cause exercise-induced lower-limb ischemia with relatively normal resting vascular findings.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral exertional thigh and buttock pain
Normal peripheral pulses and near-normal resting ABI
symptoms_not_in_common: Renal arterial beading is not explained by isolated iliac endofibrosis
Recently diagnosed hypertension and right subcostal bruit suggest additional renal vascular disease
Age 52 is older than the usual presentation

data.description: A systemic inflammatory disease of medium-sized arteries that can cause renal vascular hypertension, arterial stenoses, aneurysms, and limb ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Hypertension potentially associated with renal arterial disease
Exertional limb pain compatible with arterial ischemia
symptoms_not_in_common: Regular renal arterial beading favors fibromuscular dysplasia rather than vasculitic branch-vessel microaneurysms
Otherwise normal examination without reported systemic inflammatory, skin, or neuropathic manifestations
Isolated, reproducible exertional pain with prompt relief is less typical of systemic vasculitis

data.diagnosis: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
data.description: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal can compress nerve roots and cause buttock or thigh pain during standing or walking, typically relieved by sitting or bending forward.
symptoms_in_common: Buttock and thigh pain during walking
symptoms_not_in_common: Rapid relief with rest alone rather than documented sitting or lumbar flexion
Abdominal systolic bruits
Borderline right ABI
Renal and iliac angiographic abnormalities
No reported back pain, sensory changes, or other neurologic findings

diagnoses.name: External iliac artery dissection
diagnoses.title: Aneurysm or dissection of iliac artery[External iliac artery]

data.diagnosis: Fibromuscular dysplasia (multifocal, renal and external iliac arteries)
data.description: Non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory arteriopathy of medium-sized arteries, most common in middle-aged women, producing a 'string of beads' appearance on angiography; commonly affects renal, carotid, and iliac arteries.
symptoms_in_common: Exertional buttock and thigh claudication relieved quickly by rest
High-pitched systolic bruit over right subcostal region and umbilicus
Beaded appearance of the right renal artery on angiography
Irregular beaded stenoses/dilatations of the right iliac artery
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal peripheral pulses at rest (may be seen, however, in mild disease)
No headache, pulsatile tinnitus or other cervical artery symptoms

data.diagnosis: Atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease (iliac) with renal artery stenosis
data.description: Plaque-related narrowing of the aorto-iliac and renal arteries causing claudication and renovascular hypertension, usually in older patients with cardiovascular risk factors.
symptoms_in_common: Exertional buttock and thigh pain relieved by rest
symptoms_not_in_common: No smoking, diabetes, or hyperlipidemia
Previously very athletic
Beaded mid-vessel angiographic pattern rather than ostial/proximal plaque
Normal peripheral pulses
Relatively young woman

data.description: Chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its main branches, causing stenoses, bruits, hypertension and limb claudication, typically in women under 40.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age over 40 at onset
No constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss, malaise)
Equal blood pressure in both arms and normal pulses
Beaded pattern rather than long smooth tapered stenoses
No aortic or subclavian involvement described

data.description: Intimal fibrotic thickening of the external iliac artery seen in endurance athletes (cyclists, runners), causing exertional thigh/buttock pain with normal resting examination.
symptoms_in_common: Exertional unilateral thigh and buttock pain relieved by rest
Normal resting pulses and near-normal resting ABI
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypertension
Renal (subcostal) bruit
Renal artery beading on angiography
Beaded rather than smooth, lengthened narrowing of the iliac artery
Typically affects younger competitive athletes, mostly cyclists

data.description: Rare non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic arteriopathy with lysis of the arterial media causing dissections, aneurysms and beaded stenoses, mainly of visceral and renal arteries in middle-aged and older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries on angiography
Absence of atherosclerotic risk factors and inflammatory symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic progressive claudication rather than acute presentation
No abdominal or flank pain, haemorrhage or dissection
Iliac artery involvement is uncommon
No visceral (coeliac/mesenteric) aneurysms described

data.description: 15-year-old boy with congenital neutropenia due to an ELA2 mutation and refractory anemia with excess blasts 2, referred for bone marrow transplantation. He had a long history of low absolute neutrophil counts (200–1,000/μL) since infancy, requiring granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and treatment for recurrent bacterial skin and lung infections. For several weeks, he had multiple nonpruritic skin ulcerations on the right abdomen, scalp, and left ankle.

Infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei, most strongly supported here by a mite visible within the stratum corneum. Immunocompromised patients can develop atypical, nonpruritic lesions, sometimes complicated by bacterial infection.
symptoms_in_common: Mite visible within the stratum corneum on the supplied histology
Multiple skin lesions involving the abdomen, scalp, and ankle
Severe neutropenia, which can predispose to atypical presentations
Absence of itching can occur in immunocompromised patients

Scalp involvement is uncommon in otherwise healthy adolescents

data.description: 78-year-old woman with 2 months of lethargy and easy fatigue, referred for anemia and elevated ESR. Past history: hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, treated with perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination showed normal cardiac, respiratory, and neurologic findings, with no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy; ECOG performance status 1. Labs revealed anemia (Hb 99 g/L), elevated ESR (120 mm/h), mild creatinine elevation (110 mmol/L), hypercalcemia (2.81 mmol/L), and mildly elevated LDH (333 U/L). Further studies showed IgG kappa paraprotein 32 g/L, elevated β₂-microglobulin (6.3 mg/L), markedly increased free kappa light chains (1,400 mg/L) with kappa/lambda ratio 280, and urinary kappa Bence-Jones protein. 24-hour urine protein was normal. Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, and alkaline phosphatase were normal. Bone densitometry showed elevated bone mineral density at the lumbar spine and femoral neck.

A rare form of plasma-cell malignancy associated with increased bone density rather than typical osteolytic lesions. This is the leading possibility given the IgG kappa paraprotein, markedly abnormal free light chains, anemia, hypercalcemia, and apparent osteosclerosis. Bone marrow immunophenotyping is needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Free kappa light chains of 1,400 mg/L and kappa/lambda ratio of 280
Increased bone mineral density and apparent diffuse skeletal sclerosis
Biopsy images suggest thickened bone trabeculae with an intervening cellular infiltrate
symptoms_not_in_common: Diffuse osteosclerosis is rare in multiple myeloma overall, although characteristic of this uncommon variant
Normal total urinary protein despite substantial circulating free light chains is less typical of significant myeloma-associated kidney injury

data.description: A multisystem syndrome associated with a monoclonal plasma-cell disorder and sclerotic bone lesions. Polyneuropathy is a mandatory diagnostic feature, and the monoclonal protein is usually lambda-restricted; the available findings therefore do not establish this diagnosis.

symptoms_not_in_common: Normal neurologic examination without reported polyneuropathy

Markedly elevated free light chains and substantial paraprotein concentration
Anemia rather than the thrombocytosis or polycythemia often seen

data.diagnosis: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with an IgG paraprotein

data.description: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and fed breast milk and formula, presented with 2 days of worsening fussiness, pallor, fever, vomiting, tachycardia, mottled skin, and respiratory distress. On admission he was pale, listless, and fussy with temperature 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, and oxygen saturation 97% on 1 L/min nasal cannula. Exam showed a grade 2/6 holosystolic-flow murmur, splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin, and cool mottled extremities. Urinalysis revealed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts. Labs showed severe anemia, marked thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH and AST, and blood smear with numerous intracellular ring forms; CSF also showed intraerythrocytic ring forms.

Babesia infection of red blood cells causes hemolysis and can produce life-threatening illness in young infants. The apparent four-organism Maltese-cross formation in the provided smear strongly favors babesiosis; congenital transmission is possible but requires confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Severe anemia with pallor and elevated LDH
Dark red urine consistent with hemoglobinuria during hemolysis
Tachycardia, respiratory distress, and cool mottled extremities
Intraerythrocytic ring forms and an apparent Maltese-cross tetrad on the blood smear
symptoms_not_in_common: Parasite-containing erythrocytes in CSF are unusual and may reflect blood contamination rather than direct central nervous system infection
Proteinuria and granular casts suggest renal involvement, which is a complication rather than a defining feature

data.description: Transplacentally acquired Plasmodium infection can present during the first weeks of life with fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and splenomegaly. Ring forms can resemble Babesia, although a true Maltese-cross tetrad favors babesiosis.
symptoms_in_common: Dark urine and respiratory distress in severe infection
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent Maltese-cross tetrad on the smear is characteristic of Babesia rather than Plasmodium
Parasite-containing erythrocytes in CSF are not a typical diagnostic finding of malaria

data.diagnosis: Late-onset bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation

Splenomegaly is less typical of an acute two-day bacterial illness
Parasite-containing erythrocytes in CSF are not explained by bacterial meningitis

Dark red urine from acute intravascular hemolysis is not a defining HLH feature
Parasite-containing erythrocytes in CSF are not a typical HLH finding

data.description: Infection of red blood cells by Babesia microti, usually tick-borne but occasionally acquired transplacentally or by transfusion; causes fever, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly, with pleomorphic intraerythrocytic ring forms and occasional tetrads (Maltese cross) on smear.

dark red urine with blood and protein (hemoglobinuria)
numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms with multiple parasites per cell and tetrad-like forms
no pigment or gametocytes seen on smear
onset at about 5 weeks of age consistent with vertical transmission
tachycardia, flow murmur, mottled skin and respiratory distress from severe anemia and shock

severity is unusual in an immunocompetent host, though it is recognised in neonates

data.description: A 21-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with intermittent left-sided pain in the anterior chest wall associated with neck discomfort. The pain was described as 'stabbing' in nature and had arisen suddenly while watching television, with no history of trauma before onset. The pain was not exacerbated by inspiration or effort. His medical history and physical examination were initially unremarkable. Several days later, he attended the emergency department with worsening chest pain and dyspnea. On examination, chest expansion was equal and breath sounds were normal, although there was crepitus on auscultation of the precordium. Palpation of the neck and supraclavicular fossae detected subcutaneous emphysema. His respiratory rate was 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturations were 100%. His full blood count and inflammatory markers were within normal limits.

Air leaks from ruptured alveoli into the mediastinum without trauma, sometimes extending into the neck. This is the most likely diagnosis: the images show mediastinal air, and precordial crepitus is consistent with Hamman's sign.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden stabbing chest pain in a young adult
Preserved oxygen saturation and normal breath sounds
Normal blood count and inflammatory markers
symptoms_not_in_common: No major discordant findings; absence of an obvious precipitating event does not exclude this diagnosis

data.description: A tear in the esophagus can release air and digestive contents into the mediastinum. It is an important dangerous alternative, although the history and absence of systemic inflammation make it less likely here.

Normal blood count and inflammatory markers several days after onset
No reported fever or systemic toxicity

Normal breath sounds and equal chest expansion
Preserved oxygen saturation
No reported hemoptysis

data.description: 27-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis presented with 2 weeks of fatigue and about 11 days of persistent nonbloody loose diarrhea with bloating, decreased exercise tolerance, and ~4.5 kg weight loss. He had recently traveled to rural India and moved from Indonesia to the United States 11 days before presentation. He had no fever, chills, vomiting, cramping, or abdominal pain. Past ulcerative colitis had been diagnosed 2 years earlier by colonoscopy and biopsy and improved with mesalamine; current medications included mesalamine and acetaminophen. On examination, vital signs were normal, with a palpable spleen tip and an erythematous papular rash on the anterior thorax. Laboratory testing showed marked leukocytosis with severe eosinophilia.

A group of disorders characterized by marked eosinophilia with eosinophil-related organ injury. Gastrointestinal and skin involvement can cause diarrhea and rash. The images appear to show extensive blood and marrow eosinophilia and an eosinophil-rich intestinal infiltrate; secondary and clonal causes require investigation.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent eosinophilic infiltration of intestinal tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported finding clearly excludes this diagnosis

data.diagnosis: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and a tyrosine kinase gene fusion

data.description: 14-year-old boy presented to trauma unit with gunshot wound to left eye. Alert and hemodynamically stable, blind in left eye, no CSF rhinorrhea. Pubertal status: Tanner stage S3, height: 1.7m (75th percentile). Laboratory findings: 8am serum cortisol 28 nmol/L (normal 171-536), thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.63 mIU/L (normal 0.27-4.20), free thyroxine 13.5 pmol/L (normal 13.6-23.2), luteinising hormone 0.7 IU/L (normal 1.3-9.8), insulin-like growth factor 1 19.4 nmol/L (normal 28.8-127.3), prolactin 13.04 pmol/L (normal 174-660.9), testosterone undetectable <0.1 nmol/L (normal 1-38.5).

data.description: Inadequate pituitary stimulation of the thyroid produces low free thyroxine without an appropriately elevated TSH. The minimally low free thyroxine supports this possibility, but acute illness can also affect thyroid tests.
symptoms_in_common: Free thyroxine of 13.5 pmol/L, slightly below the supplied reference range
TSH of 0.63 mIU/L, inappropriately non-elevated for a low free thyroxine
Other biochemical evidence of anterior pituitary dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Left-eye blindness is not a manifestation of thyroid hormone deficiency
Profound cortisol deficiency and undetectable testosterone are not explained by isolated central hypothyroidism
Normal-to-tall stature is not typical of longstanding untreated childhood hypothyroidism

data.diagnosis: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to traumatic gonadotropin deficiency
data.description: Deficient hypothalamic or pituitary stimulation of the testes causes low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins. Following acute pituitary injury, this may interrupt previously established pubertal progression.
symptoms_in_common: Very low testosterone despite Tanner stage 3 pubertal development
symptoms_not_in_common: Tanner stage 3 development argues against complete longstanding prepubertal gonadotropin deficiency, but not an acquired deficiency
Low cortisol, free thyroxine, and prolactin are not explained by isolated gonadotropin deficiency
Left-eye blindness is unrelated to testosterone deficiency

data.diagnosis: Possible growth hormone deficiency due to traumatic pituitary injury
data.description: Damage to pituitary growth hormone secretion can reduce insulin-like growth factor 1 and impair subsequent growth. Low IGF-1 supports suspicion but does not establish the diagnosis, particularly during acute illness; age- and pubertal-stage interpretation and appropriate follow-up testing are needed.
symptoms_in_common: Insulin-like growth factor 1 of 19.4 nmol/L, below the supplied reference range
Penetrating injury near the sellar region
Multiple accompanying anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies
symptoms_not_in_common: Height of 1.7 m at the 75th percentile is not typical of longstanding childhood growth hormone deficiency
Left-eye blindness is not caused by growth hormone deficiency
Profoundly low cortisol and undetectable testosterone are not explained by isolated growth hormone deficiency

data.diagnosis: Traumatic panhypopituitarism from bullet lodged in the sella turcica (penetrating pituitary injury)
data.description: Direct destruction of the pituitary gland by a projectile that traversed the orbit and came to rest in the sella/sphenoid region, causing acute deficiency of multiple anterior pituitary hormones.
symptoms_in_common: Metallic foreign body in the sella turcica on skull X-ray and CT
Low free T4 with inappropriately normal TSH
Very low prolactin (indicating direct pituitary destruction rather than stalk lesion)
Left eye blindness from orbital/optic nerve trajectory
Normal height and prior pubertal progression indicating acute onset
symptoms_not_in_common: Hemodynamically stable despite severe cortisol deficiency
No CSF rhinorrhea despite skull base penetration
No reported polyuria/diabetes insipidus

data.diagnosis: Pituitary stalk transection / hypothalamic injury (post-traumatic hypopituitarism)
data.description: Traumatic brain injury may shear the pituitary stalk or damage the hypothalamus, interrupting releasing-hormone delivery and causing anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies, often with diabetes insipidus.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prolactin is very low (stalk lesions usually raise prolactin by loss of dopamine inhibition)
No diabetes insipidus reported
Bullet located within the sella itself rather than suprasellar region

data.diagnosis: Critical illness-related endocrine suppression (non-thyroidal illness / stress-induced functional hypogonadism)
data.description: Acute severe illness or trauma can transiently suppress the thyroid, gonadal and somatotropic axes without structural pituitary damage.
symptoms_in_common: Low-normal TSH with marginally low free T4
symptoms_not_in_common: Cortisol should be elevated in stress, not profoundly low
Prolactin is usually normal or raised in acute stress, not very low
Patient is alert and stable rather than critically ill
Bullet in the sella provides a structural explanation

data.diagnosis: Pre-existing sellar/suprasellar tumour (e.g., craniopharyngioma) with hypopituitarism
data.description: Sellar-region tumours in children compress the pituitary and optic pathways, causing multiple hormone deficiencies, visual loss, growth failure and delayed puberty.
symptoms_not_in_common: Height at 75th percentile (no growth failure)
Puberty already progressed to Tanner stage 3
Low prolactin (usually normal or raised from stalk effect)
No mass or calcification on imaging, only a metallic bullet
Visual loss explained by gunshot to the eye
No history of headaches or chronic symptoms

data.diagnosis: Congenital/idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or combined pituitary hormone deficiency
data.description: Genetic or developmental disorders of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis leading to deficient gonadotropins (with or without other pituitary hormones), presenting with absent or delayed puberty and often poor growth.
symptoms_in_common: Low cortisol and low free T4 (if combined deficiency)
Low prolactin (can occur in POU1F1/PROP1 defects)
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal stature at 75th percentile
Tanner stage 3 puberty already achieved, indicating previously functioning axis
Acute presentation after gunshot wound
Bullet in the sella on imaging
Left eye blindness

data.description: A 67-year-old man with advanced alcoholic cirrhosis presented with progressive dyspnea. Physical examination after thoracentesis revealed right lung crackles, and the patient developed coughing, tachypnea, and tachycardia. His oxygen saturation was 82% while breathing ambient air.

Acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema after rapid re-expansion of a previously compressed lung, typically following drainage of a large pleural effusion. This is the leading diagnosis given the post-thoracentesis deterioration and extensive right-sided airspace opacities.
symptoms_in_common: Acute worsening of dyspnea after thoracentesis
Severe hypoxemia with oxygen saturation of 82% on ambient air
Extensive unilateral right lung airspace opacities on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive dyspnea before thoracentesis is better explained by the underlying pleural effusion than by re-expansion pulmonary edema

data.description: A usually right-sided pleural effusion caused by passage of ascitic fluid through diaphragmatic defects in patients with cirrhosis. It likely explains the initial large effusion but not the entire post-drainage deterioration.
symptoms_in_common: Extensive right hemithorax opacification consistent with a large pleural effusion
symptoms_not_in_common: New cough, tachypnea, and tachycardia after pleural drainage
Right lung crackles after thoracentesis
Diffuse right lung airspace opacities after drainage rather than pleural fluid alone

data.description: Chemical lung injury caused by aspiration of gastric contents, producing acute hypoxemia and pulmonary infiltrates, sometimes predominantly in the right lung.
symptoms_not_in_common: Deterioration specifically following thoracentesis favors re-expansion injury
Initial large right pleural effusion is not a typical manifestation of acute aspiration pneumonitis
Progressive dyspnea before the procedure is not explained by an acute aspiration event

data.description: Infection of the right lung that can cause consolidation, cough, crackles, hypoxemia, and an associated parapneumonic effusion.
symptoms_in_common: Right lung consolidation or airspace opacities
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt symptom development immediately after thoracentesis is less typical of pneumonia
The marked clearing of right-sided opacities between the supplied CT panels, if obtained over a short interval, would be less typical of infection

data.description: Air entering the pleural space after thoracentesis can cause sudden respiratory deterioration. It is an important procedural complication to consider, although the supplied imaging favors pulmonary edema instead.
symptoms_not_in_common: Right lung crackles are less typical than diminished breath sounds
Extensive right lung airspace opacities rather than a visible pleural air collection
Progressive dyspnea preceding thoracentesis cannot be attributed to an iatrogenic pneumothorax

data.description: Noncardiogenic, usually unilateral pulmonary edema that develops shortly after rapid reexpansion of a collapsed lung following drainage of a large pleural effusion or pneumothorax.
symptoms_in_common: Large right pleural effusion with whiteout of the right hemithorax (hepatic hydrothorax in cirrhosis)
Unilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation in the reexpanded right lung on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive dyspnea before the procedure (explained by the effusion itself rather than this complication)

data.description: Air entering the pleural space as a complication of thoracentesis, causing lung collapse and respiratory compromise.
symptoms_not_in_common: Crackles rather than diminished breath sounds
CT shows a reexpanded lung with parenchymal opacities rather than pleural air with collapsed lung

data.description: Fluid accumulation in the alveoli due to elevated left heart filling pressures, as in heart failure or cirrhotic cardiomyopathy with volume overload.
symptoms_not_in_common: Strictly unilateral involvement of the right lung
Clear left lung
Acute onset immediately after thoracentesis
No described cardiac history or other signs of heart failure

data.description: Infection of the lung parenchyma causing consolidation; patients with alcoholic cirrhosis are at increased risk of both infection and aspiration.
symptoms_in_common: Right lung consolidation and ground-glass opacities
Risk factors of alcohol use and cirrhosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt onset immediately after thoracentesis
No fever or purulent sputum described
Diffuse involvement of the whole reexpanded lung rather than a lobar or dependent distribution

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary hemorrhage or hemothorax from procedural injury
data.description: Bleeding into the lung parenchyma or pleural space from needle injury to the lung or an intercostal vessel during thoracentesis, more likely in cirrhotic patients with coagulopathy.
symptoms_not_in_common: No hemoptysis reported
No hypotension or drop in hemoglobin described
Diffuse opacities throughout the reexpanded lung rather than focal opacity around the puncture site
No reaccumulating high-density pleural collection described

data.description: 45-year-old man with acute onset of nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting beginning the day before admission. Three days earlier he sustained dog bites to the hands and forearms; he also had recent head trauma from a rusty nail and dental extractions 1–2 weeks earlier. Past history includes asthma, mild COPD, anxiety, depression, chronic back pain, and alcohol abuse with heavy recent intake. On examination he was ill-appearing, anxious, and diaphoretic, with hypothermia (35.6°C), tachycardia (110 bpm), tachypnea (28/min), hypertension (154/102 mmHg), and delayed capillary refill (5 seconds). He had numerous lacerations and scratch marks with necrotic edges on the hands and forearms, including a 3–4 cm right forearm lesion with a 5–7 cm purplish surrounding border.

data.diagnosis: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with purpura fulminans
data.description: A potentially fatal infection transmitted through dog saliva, especially in people with heavy alcohol use. It can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation and ischemic skin necrosis. This is the leading possibility; the slender, fusiform organisms in the microscopy image are compatible but require laboratory confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Dog bites three days before illness
Acute nausea, epigastric pain, and vomiting
Purplish skin lesions and widespread mottling visible in the photographs
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypertension rather than hypotension, although this does not exclude early sepsis

data.diagnosis: Pasteurella multocida wound infection with sepsis
data.description: A bacterial infection commonly acquired from dog or cat bites that can cause rapidly developing cellulitis and occasionally bloodstream infection.
symptoms_in_common: Recent dog bites to the hands and forearms
Tachycardia, tachypnea, and delayed capillary refill
symptoms_not_in_common: Widespread purpuric skin changes are uncommon unless severe sepsis causes coagulopathy
Prominent epigastric pain is not a characteristic presenting feature
The long, slender organisms shown are less typical than the small coccobacilli expected for Pasteurella

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection of the forearm
data.description: A rapidly progressive infection of deep soft tissues, potentially caused by mixed bacteria introduced through bite wounds. It is a surgical emergency, and absence of visible gas on radiographs does not exclude it.
symptoms_in_common: A forearm lesion with a broad purplish border
Severe systemic illness with hypothermia, tachycardia, and tachypnea
symptoms_not_in_common: Epigastric pain and vomiting as the dominant initial symptoms
Widespread skin discoloration away from the forearm is not typical of an isolated local infection

data.description: An invasive infection caused by anaerobic, fusiform gram-negative bacteria from the mouth or contaminated wounds. Recent dental procedures provide a possible entry site, though the dog-bite history favors Capnocytophaga.
symptoms_in_common: Dental extractions one to two weeks earlier
Acute systemic illness with hypothermia, tachycardia, and tachypnea
Slender, fusiform organisms in the microscopy image
Purpuric lesions, if complicated by sepsis-associated coagulopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Necrotic lesions centered on recent dog bites favor a bite-associated pathogen
Prominent nausea and epigastric pain are not characteristic
Diffuse acral discoloration is not typical without severe systemic complications

data.description: A fulminant bloodstream infection caused by Neisseria meningitidis that can produce disseminated intravascular coagulation, purpuric skin lesions, and rapidly impaired circulation, sometimes without meningitis.
symptoms_in_common: Widespread purplish skin changes and peripheral discoloration
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent dog bites with necrotic wound edges suggest a different infectious source
Prominent epigastric pain is less characteristic
The microscopy image shows slender rods rather than the diplococci expected for meningococci
Hypertension is less typical of advanced meningococcal circulatory failure

data.diagnosis: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with purpura fulminans/DIC
data.description: Fulminant sepsis caused by a fastidious, thin, fusiform gram-negative rod from dog oral flora, transmitted by dog bites; particularly severe in people with alcohol abuse or asplenia. Causes septic shock, DIC, and purpura fulminans.
symptoms_in_common: Dog bites to hands and forearms 3 days before onset
Heavy alcohol use as risk factor
Acute nausea, vomiting, and epigastric pain
Necrotic edges of bite wounds with purplish border
Widespread mottled purpuric/livedoid rash on back, hands, and legs
Long, thin, fusiform gram-negative rods on Gram stain
No gas or bony injury on forearm radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypertension rather than hypotension at presentation
No documented asplenia
Prominent gastrointestinal symptoms are nonspecific

data.diagnosis: Pasteurella multocida wound infection with sepsis
data.description: Gram-negative coccobacillus that is a common cause of dog and cat bite infections, typically producing rapid-onset cellulitis within 24 hours and occasionally bacteremia in patients with liver disease or immunocompromise.
symptoms_in_common: Dog bites to hands and forearms
Alcohol abuse as risk factor for bacteremia
symptoms_not_in_common: Organisms are long, thin fusiform rods rather than small coccobacilli
Diffuse purpura fulminans is uncommon
No prominent purulent cellulitis or lymphangitis described
Onset of illness delayed 2 days after the bite rather than within 24 hours
Hypothermia

data.diagnosis: Necrotizing soft tissue infection / streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
data.description: Rapidly progressive infection of fascia and subcutaneous tissue (often group A Streptococcus or polymicrobial) with systemic toxicity, shock, and multiorgan failure.
symptoms_in_common: Skin wounds as portal of entry
Necrotic wound edges with purplish discoloration
Systemic toxicity with tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis
symptoms_not_in_common: No soft tissue gas on forearm radiograph
No severe pain out of proportion, bullae, or crepitus described
Gram stain shows gram-negative rods rather than gram-positive cocci in chains
Diffuse, distant mottled purpura rather than localized spreading necrosis
Hypertension rather than hypotension

data.diagnosis: Meningococcemia (Neisseria meningitidis sepsis) with purpura fulminans
data.description: Fulminant bloodstream infection with gram-negative diplococci causing septic shock, DIC, and petechial/purpuric rash, sometimes with adrenal hemorrhage.
symptoms_in_common: Acute onset of nausea and vomiting
symptoms_not_in_common: Gram stain shows long thin rods rather than diplococci
Recent dog bites with necrotic wounds point to a zoonotic source
No headache, neck stiffness, or meningeal signs described
Hypothermia rather than high fever
No known exposure or outbreak

data.description: Inflammation of the pancreas, commonly triggered by heavy alcohol intake, presenting with epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting; may cause a systemic inflammatory response. Concurrent alcohol withdrawal causes autonomic hyperactivity.
symptoms_in_common: Anxiety, diaphoresis, and hypertension (consistent with withdrawal)
symptoms_not_in_common: Necrotic bite wounds with purplish border
Widespread purpuric/mottled rash
Gram-negative rods on Gram stain
Hypothermia
Delayed capillary refill out of proportion to the abdominal findings

data.description: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and adalimumab. Four months before admission, she developed pain and stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission, she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli. On admission, she had fever (38.7°C) and pancytopenia, without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. She had traveled to Athens 7 months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

data.diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis with secondary cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
data.description: Systemic infection, likely due to Leishmania infantum, transmitted by sand flies in Mediterranean regions where dogs are important reservoirs. Immunosuppression increases susceptibility. The smear appears to contain numerous amastigote-like organisms, and the serum image suggests precipitation consistent with cryoglobulins, although laboratory confirmation is required.
symptoms_in_common: Purpura and livedo reticularis potentially caused by secondary cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
Methotrexate and adalimumab treatment increasing susceptibility to infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of hepatosplenomegaly is atypical for classic visceral leishmaniasis
Prominent inflammatory joint symptoms and vasculitic skin lesions are uncommon unless secondary immune complications develop

data.description: Small-vessel inflammation caused by circulating immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold. It can accompany infections, autoimmune diseases, or lymphoproliferative disorders. The serum photograph suggests a precipitate but does not alone establish its composition.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia is not typical of uncomplicated cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
The apparent organisms in the smear require an underlying infectious explanation

data.description: An uncommon systemic complication of rheumatoid arthritis involving small and medium-sized vessels, often producing lower-extremity purpura, ulcers, or ischemic lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Pain and stiffness in multiple joints
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia is not a usual direct manifestation
The apparent organisms in the smear are not explained by rheumatoid vasculitis
The Mediterranean travel history suggests an alternative infectious cause

data.description: An invasive fungal infection that can involve bone marrow and cause fever and cytopenias, particularly during TNF-inhibitor treatment. Small intracellular yeast forms can resemble Leishmania on microscopy, although budding rather than kinetoplasts supports Histoplasma.
symptoms_in_common: Possible small organisms on the smear
symptoms_not_in_common: Athens travel and contact with dogs are more suggestive of Mediterranean leishmaniasis
Livedo reticularis and ankle purpura are not characteristic manifestations
Prominent inflammatory polyarthralgia is not a typical dominant feature

data.description: An autoimmune adverse effect of TNF inhibitors that may cause fever, inflammatory joint symptoms, skin manifestations, and occasionally cytopenias. Diagnosis requires compatible serology and exclusion of infection.
symptoms_in_common: Skin lesions potentially associated with immune-mediated vascular inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked pancytopenia is less typical than isolated cytopenias
Livedo reticularis and malleolar purpura are less typical than photosensitive or lupus-like rashes
The apparent organisms in the smear are not explained by a drug-induced autoimmune syndrome
Mediterranean travel provides an infectious exposure not explained by this diagnosis

data.diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania infantum) with secondary cryoglobulinemia
data.description: Protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies, endemic in the Mediterranean basin with dogs as reservoir; infects macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system, causing fever, pancytopenia and polyclonal B-cell activation that can produce mixed cryoglobulinemia and vasculitis-like features. Risk is increased by anti-TNF therapy.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to Athens (endemic area) 7 months earlier with exposure to dogs
Bone marrow smear showing macrophages filled with numerous small intracellular and extracellular bodies consistent with amastigotes
Purpura and livedo reticularis from secondary cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of hepatosplenomegaly
Absence of lymphadenopathy
Prominent joint and cutaneous vasculitic presentation is atypical

data.diagnosis: Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (e.g., hepatitis C–related or essential)
data.description: Immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by cold-precipitating immunoglobulins, classically presenting with purpura, arthralgia and weakness; often secondary to HCV, autoimmune disease or lymphoproliferative disorders.
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever of 38.7°C
Pancytopenia
Intracellular organisms in bone marrow macrophages
Travel and dog exposure history points to an infectious trigger

data.diagnosis: Rheumatoid arthritis flare with rheumatoid vasculitis
data.description: Exacerbation of RA with systemic small- and medium-vessel vasculitis occurring in long-standing seropositive disease, causing skin lesions, constitutional symptoms and sometimes neuropathy.
symptoms_in_common: Pain and stiffness of MCP and interphalangeal joints, knees and ankle
symptoms_not_in_common: Pancytopenia
High fever
Parasite-laden macrophages in bone marrow
Occurrence despite methotrexate and anti-TNF therapy

data.description: Systemic fungal infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, seen in immunosuppressed patients including those on TNF inhibitors; yeasts multiply inside macrophages and can mimic Leishmania amastigotes on marrow smears.
symptoms_in_common: Small intracellular organisms within bone marrow macrophages
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel to a histoplasmosis-endemic area (Greece is not endemic)
Dog exposure in the Mediterranean is not a risk factor
Organisms appear to have nucleus and kinetoplast without a clear halo, favouring amastigotes
Cryoglobulinemia, purpura and livedo reticularis
No hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or pulmonary symptoms

data.diagnosis: Drug-induced lupus / anti-TNF–induced autoimmune syndrome (with methotrexate myelotoxicity)
data.description: Adalimumab can induce a lupus-like syndrome or vasculitis with arthritis, rash, fever and cytopenias; methotrexate can independently cause bone marrow suppression.
symptoms_in_common: Livedo reticularis and purpuric skin lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Intracellular organisms in bone marrow macrophages
Marked cryoprecipitate in serum
Epidemiological exposure in an endemic area with dogs
Pancytopenia of this degree is uncommon in drug-induced lupus

data.description: A 22-year-old African American/Asian college-age woman presented with a 3-month history of mild exertional dyspnea that progressively worsened despite treatment with inhalers for suspected reactive airway disease. She reported shortness of breath with mild exertion, nonproductive cough for several weeks, and a 5-lb weight loss. She denied fever, chills, headaches, syncope, dizziness, bone pain, nausea, or vomiting. Physical examination was unremarkable except for decreased breath sounds and slight dullness to percussion on the left. Routine laboratory work-up was unremarkable. Initially, chest x-ray showed mediastinal widening, which led to further imaging and biopsy. An open mediastinal biopsy was performed after CT-guided biopsy failed, revealing a poorly differentiated carcinoma initially thought to be thymic carcinoma. Flow cytometry from tissue showed T cells and polyclonal B cells with no immunophenotypic evidence of malignancy.

A rare, aggressive carcinoma defined by a NUTM1 rearrangement, often arising in the thorax of young patients. It can resemble poorly differentiated thymic carcinoma; confirmation requires NUT immunohistochemistry or molecular testing.
symptoms_in_common: Lack of a malignant lymphoid population on flow cytometry
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported symptoms or findings clearly exclude this diagnosis
The initially mild, three-month course is less characteristic of its often rapidly aggressive presentation

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor arising in the thymus that can invade surrounding thoracic structures and cause respiratory symptoms. The initial biopsy interpretation supports this possibility, but specialist pathology review is needed.
symptoms_in_common: Biopsy interpreted initially as poorly differentiated thymic carcinoma
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 is younger than the usual presentation
No other reported symptoms are distinctly atypical

data.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that commonly presents as a bulky mediastinal mass in young women. Negative flow cytometry does not completely exclude it, but a confirmed epithelial carcinoma on biopsy would argue strongly against it.
symptoms_in_common: Decreased left-sided breath sounds and dullness to percussion
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy reported as poorly differentiated carcinoma rather than lymphoma
Flow cytometry showed polyclonal B cells without evidence of a malignant population

data.diagnosis: Primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumor
data.description: An extragonadal malignancy that may produce a large mediastinal mass. Some components can resemble poorly differentiated carcinoma; tissue markers and serum AFP and beta-hCG help distinguish it.
symptoms_in_common: Poorly differentiated malignant tissue on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Female sex is very uncommon for primary mediastinal nonseminomatous germ cell tumors
The initial pathology favored thymic carcinoma rather than a germ cell tumor

data.diagnosis: Poorly differentiated primary lung carcinoma with mediastinal involvement
data.description: A pulmonary epithelial malignancy that can involve the mediastinum and obstruct airways, causing lung collapse or pleural changes. It is uncommon at this age and would require confirmation of pulmonary origin.
symptoms_in_common: Decreased breath sounds and dullness on the left
Substantial left-sided thoracic opacity on the supplied CT image
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 is highly unusual for conventional primary lung carcinoma
The reported lesion was mediastinal, and the initial pathology favored thymic origin

data.description: Rare, highly aggressive poorly differentiated carcinoma defined by NUTM1 gene rearrangement (commonly BRD4-NUT), arising in midline structures such as the mediastinum, typically in adolescents and young adults; often misdiagnosed initially as thymic carcinoma or other poorly differentiated tumors.
symptoms_in_common: Flow cytometry negative for hematologic malignancy
Large mass with left hemithorax involvement/lung collapse on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Relatively indolent 3-month course (often more rapid)
No bone pain or symptoms of distant metastasis
No reported lymphadenopathy

data.description: Malignant epithelial tumor of the thymus arising in the anterior mediastinum, with frequent local invasion of adjacent structures and pleura.
symptoms_in_common: Polyclonal lymphocytes without lymphoid malignancy on flow cytometry
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age (typically occurs in 5th-6th decade)
Mass extending into middle/posterior mediastinum and left hemithorax rather than confined to the anterior compartment
No chest pain or superior vena cava syndrome

data.description: Aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising from thymic B cells, classically presenting as a bulky mediastinal mass in young women.
symptoms_in_common: Decreased breath sounds and dullness (possible effusion or compression)
symptoms_not_in_common: Flow cytometry showing polyclonal B cells without evidence of malignancy
Histology showing carcinoma rather than lymphoma
No fever or night sweats
Unremarkable labs (LDH often elevated)

data.diagnosis: Primary mediastinal germ cell tumor (nonseminomatous or seminoma)
data.description: Extragonadal germ cell tumors arising in the mediastinum of young adults; can appear as poorly differentiated malignant neoplasms and may be associated with elevated AFP or beta-hCG.
symptoms_not_in_common: Female sex (malignant mediastinal germ cell tumors occur overwhelmingly in males)
Unremarkable laboratory work-up (no reported tumor marker elevation)
Histology interpreted as carcinoma rather than germ cell tumor

data.diagnosis: Poorly differentiated non-small cell lung carcinoma with mediastinal invasion
data.description: Primary lung carcinoma (e.g., poorly differentiated squamous cell or adenocarcinoma, including driver-mutated tumors in young non-smokers) that invades or metastasizes to the mediastinum and causes airway obstruction and lung collapse.
symptoms_in_common: Left-sided decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion
Mass involving left hemithorax on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age (22 years)
No reported smoking history or risk factors
Predominantly mediastinal-centered mass
No hemoptysis

data.description: 11-year-old boy who received his first black henna tattoo while on holiday in Portugal in August 2013. One week after getting the tattoo, the area became hot, red, raised and itchy. Physical exam showed bullae with clear yellow-orange discharge and golden crusting on a background of erythematous plaque.

data.diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine in black henna
data.description: A delayed hypersensitivity reaction to para-phenylenediamine, a dye commonly added to black henna. This is the leading diagnosis given the timing and tattoo-shaped eruption.
symptoms_in_common: Onset approximately one week after the first black henna tattoo
Eruption closely following the tattoo design
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent golden crusting may indicate secondary bacterial infection, although dried eczema exudate can also produce crusting

data.description: Direct skin injury caused by irritating chemicals in the tattoo mixture, rather than an allergic immune response.
symptoms_in_common: Inflammation confined to the tattooed skin
symptoms_not_in_common: A one-week delay is less typical than the earlier onset often seen with strong irritants
Prominent itching rather than burning or pain favors allergic contact dermatitis
Golden crusting may reflect secondary infection rather than irritation alone

data.description: A superficial bacterial infection, usually caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus, that produces fragile blisters and crusted erosions. It may occur secondarily on inflamed tattooed skin.
symptoms_not_in_common: Precise reproduction of the tattoo design favors contact dermatitis as the primary process
A prominently raised, intensely itchy plaque is more characteristic of eczema
Delayed onset after black henna exposure specifically favors an allergic reaction

data.description: A bacterial infection of the deeper skin that can develop when blistering dermatitis disrupts the skin barrier.
symptoms_in_common: Bullae can occur in severe infection
Weeping and crusting suggest a disrupted skin barrier
symptoms_not_in_common: Itching is less typical than pain or tenderness
Inflammation closely confined to the tattoo design is atypical for a spreading deeper infection
Golden surface crusting is more characteristic of impetigo or weeping eczema

data.description: A skin reaction caused by the combination of a photosensitizing substance and ultraviolet exposure, potentially relevant during a summer holiday.
symptoms_in_common: Recent topical exposure while on a summer holiday
A patterned eruption corresponding to the area of topical exposure
symptoms_not_in_common: A one-week delay is less typical than onset within hours to a few days after ultraviolet exposure
Marked itching is less typical than burning or pain
Golden crusting is not a defining feature
The history does not establish ultraviolet exposure of the tattooed area or a photosensitizing ingredient

data.description: 55-year-old man with a history of heart failure, obesity, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and HFpEF presented with 3 days of sudden-onset right foot and calf swelling and pain without trauma, progressively extending to the upper leg, with new dusky discoloration of the right toes on the day of presentation.
