data.description: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous rash followed 1 week later by progressive generalized muscle pain and weakness, with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Exam showed heliotrope rash, erythematous papules on the fingers/extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, periungual erythema/edema, pitting edema of the arms and legs, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, hypoactive bowel sounds, and severe proximal muscle weakness, including inability to lift the arms, legs, or head against gravity. Muscle bulk, tone, reflexes, and sensation were normal. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier; no smoking or illicit drug use.

An autoimmune inflammatory muscle disease characterized by proximal muscle weakness and distinctive skin findings. This is the strongest fit for the presentation; severe cases may include extensive edema and respiratory or gastrointestinal muscle involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Erythematous papules over the fingers and extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees, consistent with Gottron papules
Difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs
Limb edema, which can occur in severe edematous dermatomyositis
symptoms_not_in_common: Diminished breath sounds at both lung bases are not a defining feature and require evaluation for an associated pulmonary process
Hypoactive bowel sounds are not typical, although gastrointestinal involvement can occur

data.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing subacute, symmetric proximal muscle weakness without the characteristic skin manifestations of dermatomyositis. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive proximal muscle weakness over several weeks
Difficulty rising from a squat and climbing stairs
Severe weakness of the shoulder, hip, and neck muscles
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash
Papules over the fingers and extensor surfaces
Periungual erythema and edema
Prominent pitting edema of all limbs
Hypoactive bowel sounds
Diminished breath sounds at both lung bases

data.description: An autoimmune myopathy associated with muscle-fiber necrosis, often producing rapidly progressive, profound proximal weakness. It can occur without statin exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to lift the arms, legs, or head against gravity
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash
Papules over the fingers, elbows, and knees
Periungual erythema and edema
Extensive pitting limb edema
Hypoactive bowel sounds
Diminished breath sounds at both lung bases

data.description: An autoimmune syndrome involving inflammatory myopathy, often accompanied by interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, and rough, cracked skin called mechanic's hands. Some patients have dermatomyositis-type skin findings.
symptoms_in_common: Dermatomyositis-type rash, which may occur in this syndrome
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent pitting edema of the arms and legs
Hypoactive bowel sounds
Diminished basal breath sounds rather than the inspiratory crackles more characteristic of interstitial lung disease

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with inflammatory myositis
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause inflammatory muscle weakness, skin disease, and serosal inflammation. A lupus–dermatomyositis overlap is a consideration, but the characteristic rash here favors dermatomyositis.
symptoms_in_common: Limb edema, potentially associated with renal involvement
Diminished basal breath sounds, potentially associated with pleural effusions
symptoms_not_in_common: Heliotrope rash is more characteristic of dermatomyositis
Papules over the fingers and extensor surfaces are more characteristic of dermatomyositis
Profound proximal and neck weakness is uncommon in lupus unless there is significant associated myositis
Hypoactive bowel sounds

data.description: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules) and symmetric proximal muscle weakness; may be associated with interstitial lung disease, dysphagia/GI involvement, and malignancy.
symptoms_in_common: erythematous papules on fingers, elbows and knees (Gottron papules/sign)
difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a squat
subcutaneous limb edema (seen in severe edematous disease)
diminished basal breath sounds (possible interstitial lung disease or respiratory muscle weakness)
hypoactive bowel sounds (possible GI smooth muscle involvement)
symptoms_not_in_common: generalized pitting edema of arms and legs is uncommon
hypoactive bowel sounds are unusual
relatively young male (more common in women)

data.diagnosis: Anti-MDA5 or antisynthetase syndrome-associated dermatomyositis with interstitial lung disease
data.description: Subsets of inflammatory myopathy defined by myositis-specific autoantibodies (anti-MDA5, anti-Jo-1 and other antisynthetases) featuring skin rash, myositis, arthritis, mechanic's hands, and often rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease.
symptoms_in_common: papules on fingers and extensor surfaces
diminished breath sounds at both lung bases (possible interstitial lung disease)
symptoms_not_in_common: severe profound weakness (anti-MDA5 disease is often amyopathic or mildly myopathic)
no reported dyspnea, cough, fever, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, or mechanic's hands
no cutaneous ulcers or palmar papules reported
pitting limb edema
hypoactive bowel sounds

data.description: Dermatomyositis occurring in association with an underlying malignancy (often with anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 antibodies); tends to be severe, with prominent skin disease, edema, and dysphagia. In a young man, testicular germ cell tumor or lymphoma would be considerations.
symptoms_in_common: subcutaneous limb edema (associated with severe disease and anti-NXP2)
diminished breath sounds at bases (possible effusions or metastatic disease)
symptoms_not_in_common: young age (malignancy association is more common after age 40-50)
no reported weight loss, lymphadenopathy, masses, or other tumor-related symptoms
no smoking history

data.description: Multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive rashes, serositis, nephritis with edema, and occasionally inflammatory myositis.
symptoms_in_common: pitting edema of limbs (could reflect nephrotic syndrome)
diminished breath sounds at lung bases (possible pleural effusions/serositis)
hypoactive bowel sounds (possible serositis or enteritis)
symptoms_not_in_common: heliotrope rash is specific to dermatomyositis
papules over the knuckles (lupus rash typically spares the knuckles)
severe profound proximal weakness is unusual
male sex
no reported arthritis, oral ulcers, fever, or malar rash sparing nasolabial folds

data.diagnosis: Overlap myositis (mixed connective tissue disease or systemic sclerosis–myositis overlap)
data.description: Autoimmune overlap syndromes (e.g., anti-U1 RNP, anti-PM/Scl) combining features of myositis, scleroderma, and lupus, with swollen hands, Raynaud phenomenon, GI dysmotility, and interstitial lung disease.
symptoms_in_common: edema of the hands and limbs (puffy hands/edematous phase)
diminished basal breath sounds (possible interstitial lung disease or effusions)
symptoms_not_in_common: no reported Raynaud phenomenon
no skin thickening or sclerodactyly
no arthritis reported
classic heliotrope rash and this degree of severe weakness favor primary dermatomyositis
male sex

data.description: A 16-year-old girl presented with acute left shoulder pain, left-sided chest pain, and shortness of breath. She had a 4-month history of intermittent left shoulder and left-sided chest pain following a dance recital, which had been treated with analgesia and physiotherapy. She denied fever, cough, orthopnea, weight loss, and appetite change. Physical examination revealed tenderness at the location of the left fifth rib and reduced left chest expansion.

data.diagnosis: Primary osteosarcoma of the left fifth rib
data.description: A malignant bone tumor that produces osteoid. The rib-associated chest wall mass and apparent irregular osteoid-like material among atypical cells in the biopsy make this a leading possibility, although pathology confirmation is required.
symptoms_in_common: Four months of localized left chest and shoulder pain
Tenderness over the left fifth rib
Shortness of breath and reduced left chest expansion
Rib-associated chest wall mass with apparent mineralization and a left pleural effusion
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported symptoms clearly exclude this diagnosis; absence of fever or weight loss is compatible with localized disease

data.description: An aggressive bone or soft-tissue malignancy affecting children and adolescents. Rib tumors can produce a substantial chest wall mass and pleural effusion.
symptoms_in_common: Chest wall mass and ipsilateral pleural effusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Apparent mineralized tumor matrix is less typical
The biopsy appears more pleomorphic and matrix-producing than the usual uniform small round-cell pattern

data.description: A malignant cartilage-producing tumor that can arise in the chest wall and form a painful, mineralized mass. It is uncommon at this patient's age.
symptoms_in_common: Shortness of breath and reduced chest expansion from an intrathoracic mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation at age 16 is unusual for conventional chondrosarcoma
Acute symptom escalation with pleural effusion is less typical
The provided biopsy does not clearly demonstrate a characteristic cartilage matrix

data.diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the rib
data.description: A clonal disorder of Langerhans cells that can cause a painful destructive rib lesion in children and adolescents, sometimes with an adjacent soft-tissue component.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent symptoms without fever or weight loss
symptoms_not_in_common: A bulky, apparently mineralized chest wall mass is atypical
Pleural effusion and substantial shortness of breath are uncommon in isolated rib disease
The biopsy is not clearly characteristic of Langerhans cells with an eosinophil-rich infiltrate

data.diagnosis: Chronic osteomyelitis of the left fifth rib with adjacent inflammatory mass
data.description: An infection of the rib that may cause chronic focal pain, bone destruction, and an adjacent abscess or inflammatory mass. Pleural involvement can cause an effusion.
symptoms_in_common: Shortness of breath with a left pleural effusion
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of fever makes an active infection less typical, although it does not exclude chronic infection
The apparently mineralized solid mass is more suggestive of a bone-forming tumor
The biopsy appears to contain atypical matrix-associated cells rather than a predominantly suppurative inflammatory infiltrate

diagnoses.name: Rib osteosarcoma
diagnoses.title: Osteosarcoma of bone or articular cartilage of ribs, sternum or clavicle

data.diagnosis: Ewing sarcoma of the chest wall (Askin tumor)
data.description: Malignant small round blue cell tumor of the Ewing sarcoma family arising from rib or chest wall soft tissue in adolescents, often with pleural extension and effusion.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic intermittent chest wall and shoulder pain over 4 months
Localized tenderness over the left fifth rib
Shortness of breath and reduced chest expansion
Chest wall/pleural-based enhancing soft tissue mass with pleural involvement on imaging
Cellular lesion with small round cells on biopsy
Symptoms initially attributed to musculoskeletal injury
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No weight loss or appetite change
No palpable mass described

data.diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma of rib)
data.description: Clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells producing lytic bone lesions, commonly in ribs, skull and spine of children and adolescents, sometimes with an associated soft tissue mass.
symptoms_in_common: Pain noticed after minor trauma or activity
Mixed cellular infiltrate with histiocyte-like cells on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Large soft tissue mass with pleural involvement
Shortness of breath
Reduced chest expansion
Acute worsening of pain

data.diagnosis: Primary bone lymphoma / lymphoma involving the chest wall
data.description: Malignant lymphoid neoplasm (e.g., lymphoblastic or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) that may involve rib, chest wall and pleura, presenting as a soft tissue mass with small round blue cells.
symptoms_in_common: Small round cell infiltrate on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever, night sweats or weight loss
No lymphadenopathy reported
Focal rib tenderness with 4-month localized course
No obvious mediastinal mass

data.diagnosis: Rib osteomyelitis / chest wall infection (including tuberculosis with empyema necessitans)
data.description: Bacterial or mycobacterial infection of rib and adjacent soft tissue that can form an inflammatory mass or abscess and pleural collection.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic localized rib pain and tenderness
Chest wall soft tissue lesion with pleural involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No cough
No weight loss or appetite change
No reported exposure or immunocompromise
No skin erythema or draining sinus

data.diagnosis: Osteosarcoma or other primary chest wall sarcoma (e.g., rhabdomyosarcoma, chondrosarcoma)
data.description: Malignant mesenchymal tumors that can arise from rib or chest wall soft tissue in adolescents, causing a painful destructive mass with pleural extension.
symptoms_in_common: Chest wall mass with pleural extension
symptoms_not_in_common: Rib is an uncommon site for osteosarcoma
No osteoid or chondroid matrix evident on imaging
Histology showing small round cells rather than spindle or osteoid-producing cells
No systemic symptoms

data.description: 3-year-old boy, born at 41 weeks gestation without perinatal problems, birth weight 3.4kg. Parents were not consanguineous and had no medical history. History of 3 prior hospitalizations for viral pneumonia at 12, 18, and 27 months. Presented with recurrent and persistent pneumonia. Current symptoms included cough, sputum and fever. Physical exam showed: temperature 39.5°C, pulse 129/min, respiration 28/min, BP 95/55 mmHg. Weight 15.3kg (50-75th percentile), height 96.5cm (50-75th percentile). Two 3mm ulcers in uvula, fine crackles in both lung fields, palpable liver 1 finger-breadth below right costal margin, palpable spleen tip.

An inherited defect in phagocyte NADPH oxidase that impairs microbial killing. This is the leading diagnosis: the rhodamine flow-cytometry patterns appear consistent with absent oxidative burst in an affected individual, a mosaic carrier pattern, and a normal control. Genetic sequencing could confirm the subtype, but the gene and variant are not labeled.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent pneumonia with fever, cough, sputum, and bilateral crackles
Pulmonary consolidation and pleural fluid on imaging
Palpable liver edge and spleen tip, potentially reflecting infection or inflammation
Male sex and early childhood presentation
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior pneumonias described as viral are less characteristic than bacterial or fungal infections
Normal growth is less typical of severe longstanding disease, although it does not exclude the diagnosis

data.description: A neutrophil enzyme deficiency that can produce an abnormal dihydrorhodamine oxidative-burst assay and mimic chronic granulomatous disease. Most affected individuals are asymptomatic; additional functional testing distinguishes the disorders.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent respiratory infections can occur in symptomatic cases
Fever and pulmonary consolidation during infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Repeated severe pneumonia beginning in infancy is unusual
Oropharyngeal ulcers are not characteristic
Palpable liver and spleen are not characteristic
The apparent mosaic carrier pattern is less consistent with this usually autosomal recessive disorder

data.description: A BTK-related disorder causing markedly reduced B cells and immunoglobulins, typically producing recurrent infections in boys after maternal antibodies decline.
symptoms_in_common: Male child with recurrent pneumonia beginning after infancy
Fever, productive cough, and bilateral crackles
Recurrent viral infections can occur with selected pathogens
symptoms_not_in_common: An absent neutrophil oxidative burst is not explained by this disorder
Oropharyngeal ulcers are not a defining feature
Palpable liver and spleen are not typical primary findings

data.description: A CD40-ligand deficiency that impairs antibody class switching and cellular immune interactions, causing recurrent bacterial and opportunistic infections; neutropenia may also occur.
symptoms_in_common: Male child presenting with recurrent pneumonia early in life
Persistent pulmonary infection with fever and cough
Oropharyngeal ulcers, potentially associated with neutropenia
Palpable liver edge and spleen tip can accompany infection or immune dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent absent oxidative-burst pattern is not characteristic
The apparent mosaic oxidative-burst carrier pattern is not explained by CD40-ligand deficiency
Normal growth is less typical of severe disease with recurrent opportunistic infections

data.description: A disorder, often associated with ELANE variants, causing periodic reductions in neutrophil counts and recurrent fever, oral ulcers, and bacterial infections. Diagnosis requires serial blood counts demonstrating cycling.
symptoms_in_common: Normal growth between infectious episodes can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistent rather than clearly periodic pneumonia is less characteristic
Palpable liver and spleen are not usual defining features
An absent oxidative burst in tested neutrophils is not explained by cyclic neutropenia
Prior infections described specifically as viral are less characteristic

data.description: Primary phagocyte immunodeficiency caused by defective NADPH oxidase, leading to absent respiratory burst and recurrent bacterial and fungal infections with granuloma formation. The DHR flow cytometry assay shows absent neutrophil oxidation in affected males and a bimodal pattern in carrier mothers.
symptoms_in_common: Male sex with early childhood onset
Recurrent and persistent pneumonia with multiple prior hospitalizations
Fine crackles in both lung fields with consolidation and pleural effusion on chest imaging
DHR assay with absent rhodamine shift in one sample, bimodal pattern in another (consistent with patient and carrier mother) and a normal shift in the third
Sequencing showing a single nucleotide variant, apparently heterozygous in one tracing (carrier) and hemizygous in another
Non-consanguineous parents, consistent with X-linked inheritance
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior pneumonias were labeled viral rather than the typical catalase-positive bacterial or fungal infections
Normal growth without failure to thrive
No reported skin abscesses, suppurative lymphadenitis or perianal abscess

data.diagnosis: Autosomal recessive chronic granulomatous disease (e.g., NCF1/p47phox deficiency)
data.description: Chronic granulomatous disease caused by biallelic mutations in the autosomal NADPH oxidase components; usually milder and later in onset than the X-linked form, with reduced or absent respiratory burst.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal DHR assay with absent oxidative burst
symptoms_not_in_common: Bimodal (mosaic) DHR pattern in a family member, which indicates an X-linked carrier state rather than autosomal recessive inheritance
Non-consanguineous parents
Relatively early onset at 12 months
Prior pneumonias labeled viral

data.description: BTK mutation causing absent B cells and profoundly low immunoglobulins, with recurrent sinopulmonary infections by encapsulated bacteria beginning after maternal antibody wanes at around 6 months of age.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent pneumonia beginning around 12 months of age
symptoms_not_in_common: Hepatosplenomegaly (lymphoid tissue is usually scant or absent)
Abnormal DHR assay, which is normal in this disease
Uvular ulcers
Prior pneumonias labeled viral rather than due to encapsulated bacteria

data.description: Autosomal recessive defect of CD18 integrin that impairs neutrophil migration into tissues, causing recurrent bacterial infections without pus, delayed umbilical cord separation and marked leukocytosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of delayed umbilical cord separation or omphalitis
No reported severe periodontitis or non-purulent skin infections
Abnormal DHR assay, which is normal in this disease
Hepatosplenomegaly is not typical
Non-consanguineous parents

data.description: Primary immunodeficiency with eczema, recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses, recurrent pneumonias with pneumatocele formation and markedly elevated IgE.
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever (inflammatory responses are often blunted, with 'cold' infections)
No eczema, skin abscesses or characteristic facial features
No pneumatoceles on imaging
Hepatosplenomegaly
Abnormal DHR assay, which is normal in this disease

data.description: 50-year-old man presented with 2-week history of constant worsening headache affecting the whole head. No history of head trauma, but reported headbanging at a Motörhead concert 4 weeks prior to presentation. Medical history was unremarkable and patient denied substance misuse. Neurological examination and laboratory studies, including coagulation screening, were normal.

data.diagnosis: Right-sided subacute or chronic subdural hematoma
data.description: Blood collecting between the dura and arachnoid, potentially from bridging-vein injury during vigorous headbanging. The crescent-shaped right-sided extra-axial collection with mass effect on the supplied CT makes this the leading possibility and warrants urgent specialist assessment.
symptoms_in_common: Constant, progressively worsening headache over two weeks
Headbanging four weeks before presentation, providing a possible acceleration-deceleration mechanism
CT appearance of a right-sided crescent-shaped extra-axial collection with mass effect
A normal neurological examination can occur despite a subdural hematoma
Normal coagulation studies do not exclude mechanically induced bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly discordant reported symptoms; absence of direct head impact does not exclude this diagnosis

data.description: An extra-axial collection of cerebrospinal fluid that can develop after an arachnoid tear, sometimes following relatively minor mechanical injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: The collection appears denser than simple cerebrospinal fluid, favoring blood rather than a pure hygroma
Progressively worsening headache and appreciable mass effect are less typical of a small uncomplicated hygroma

data.diagnosis: Complicated middle cranial fossa arachnoid cyst
data.description: A cerebrospinal-fluid-filled arachnoid cyst, potentially suggested by the marked right temporal region, can predispose to subdural bleeding or fluid accumulation after minor mechanical stress. It could coexist with, rather than replace, a subdural hematoma.
symptoms_in_common: Possible right middle cranial fossa cystic abnormality on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: An uncomplicated arachnoid cyst would not usually explain newly progressive headache
A convexity collection with mass effect suggests an associated complication rather than an isolated cyst

data.description: Bleeding between the skull and dura, usually following direct head trauma and often associated with a skull fracture. This is a less likely alternative extra-axial hemorrhage.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported direct head trauma
Delayed, gradually progressive course is less typical of an acute epidural hematoma
The collection appears crescent-shaped rather than the typical lens-shaped epidural collection

data.description: Thrombosis of cerebral venous drainage can produce progressive headache, sometimes without neurological deficits. It is less favored by the supplied CT and would require venous imaging if clinically suspected.
symptoms_in_common: Normal neurological examination can occur with isolated headache
Normal routine laboratory and coagulation results do not exclude venous thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: The dominant CT finding is an extra-axial crescent-shaped collection rather than a typical venous thrombosis finding
The preceding headbanging is more directly compatible with a mechanically induced subdural collection

data.description: Slow accumulation of blood in the subdural space from torn bridging veins, often after minor or rotational acceleration-deceleration forces; presents weeks after the inciting event with headache. May be associated with a pre-existing arachnoid cyst.
symptoms_in_common: Constant worsening holocephalic headache over 2 weeks
Right-sided hemispheric extra-axial collection on CT with midline shift to the left
symptoms_not_in_common: Relatively young age without brain atrophy
No direct head trauma
No anticoagulant use or alcohol misuse
No focal deficits or cognitive change despite mass effect

data.diagnosis: Middle cranial fossa arachnoid cyst with rupture/intracystic or subdural hemorrhage
data.description: Congenital CSF-filled cyst, commonly in the temporal fossa, that can rupture or bleed after minor trauma, producing subdural hematoma or hygroma.
symptoms_in_common: Hypodense lesion in the right middle cranial fossa (asterisk) on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Arachnoid cysts are usually incidental and asymptomatic
No seizures or signs of long-standing raised intracranial pressure

data.description: Collection of CSF in the subdural space following an arachnoid tear, often after minor trauma; may be asymptomatic or cause headache.
symptoms_in_common: Normal neurological examination and laboratory studies
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive worsening of headache
Significant mass effect with midline shift is uncommon
Mixed or iso-dense components suggest blood rather than pure CSF

data.diagnosis: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension with secondary subdural collections
data.description: A spinal CSF leak (which can be triggered by vigorous neck movement) causes low CSF pressure, headache and subdural effusions or hematomas.
symptoms_in_common: Possible trigger from vigorous neck motion
Normal neurological examination and laboratory studies
symptoms_not_in_common: Headache described as constant rather than orthostatic
Collection is unilateral rather than bilateral
Marked unilateral mass effect
No neck stiffness, tinnitus or nausea reported

data.description: Tear in the arterial wall after neck hyperextension or rotation, causing headache or neck pain and potentially ischemic stroke; a known complication of headbanging.
symptoms_in_common: Middle-aged patient without vascular risk factors
symptoms_not_in_common: Whole-head headache rather than unilateral head, neck or facial pain
No Horner syndrome or focal neurological deficits
CT shows an extra-axial collection rather than ischemic infarction
No neck pain reported

data.description: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

data.diagnosis: Incarcerated right obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
data.description: Small bowel becomes trapped in the obturator canal, causing obstruction and potentially strangulation. Obturator nerve compression can cause referred knee pain (Howship–Romberg sign). The provided CT images strongly favor this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced age, severe underweight, and multiple vaginal deliveries are characteristic risk factors
Sudden right knee pain without knee swelling or tenderness
Flexion of the right knee for pain relief
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, and radiographic small-bowel obstruction
Small right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal examination
CT appearance suggesting a bowel loop herniating through the right obturator region
Absence of a palpable abdominal mass, consistent with a deeply located pelvic hernia

data.description: Bowel becomes trapped in the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. This occurs particularly in older women and can produce acute small-bowel obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal tenderness without peritoneal irritation can occur before bowel ischemia develops
symptoms_not_in_common: Isolated knee pain relieved by flexion is more characteristic of obturator nerve compression
Right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal examination is atypical
The CT abnormality appears centered in the obturator region rather than the femoral canal

data.description: A rare pelvic hernia in which bowel protrudes through a sciatic foramen, potentially causing intestinal obstruction and nerve-related leg pain.
symptoms_in_common: Older, thin woman with a history of multiple deliveries
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, and small-bowel obstruction
Leg or knee pain may result from pelvic nerve compression
A deep pelvic mass may be detectable on rectal examination
symptoms_not_in_common: Knee pain relieved by flexion is more suggestive of an obturator hernia
The CT abnormality appears anterior in the obturator region rather than posterior at a sciatic foramen

data.description: Small bowel becomes trapped in the inguinal canal, causing mechanical obstruction and possible loss of bowel blood supply.
symptoms_not_in_common: Isolated knee pain without local knee abnormalities
Pain relief with knee flexion
Right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal examination
CT localization to the obturator region rather than the inguinal canal

data.description: A pelvic tumor can compress or invade bowel and pelvic nerves, producing intestinal obstruction and referred leg pain.
symptoms_in_common: Very low BMI, although recent weight loss is not documented
Small extraluminal pelvic mass on rectal examination
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, and small-bowel obstruction
Referred knee pain could occur with pelvic nerve involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt knee pain followed shortly by obstruction is less typical than a progressive course
Pain relief with knee flexion more specifically suggests obturator nerve irritation from a hernia
The CT images suggest a herniated bowel loop rather than a solid pelvic tumor

data.description: Herniation of bowel through the obturator canal, classically in elderly, emaciated, multiparous women; causes small-bowel obstruction and referred medial thigh/knee pain from obturator nerve compression (Howship-Romberg sign).
symptoms_in_common: sudden right knee pain with normal knee exam
right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal exam
CT showing bowel loop between pectineus and obturator muscles on the right with dilated small bowel
symptoms_not_in_common: no peritoneal irritation signs (may appear later if strangulation develops)

data.description: Herniation of bowel through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament, common in elderly women and prone to incarceration with small-bowel obstruction.
symptoms_not_in_common: referred knee pain relieved by flexion
no palpable groin mass
mass felt on rectal exam
CT shows herniated loop deep in the obturator region rather than medial to the femoral vein

data.description: Protrusion of bowel through the inguinal canal (indirect or direct) that can become trapped and cause bowel obstruction.
symptoms_not_in_common: no groin bulge or tenderness
knee pain relieved by flexion
extraluminal mass on rectal exam
CT location of hernia sac deep to the pectineus
less common in elderly thin women

data.diagnosis: Small-bowel obstruction due to pelvic or intestinal tumour
data.description: Mechanical obstruction from a primary small-bowel, colorectal, or gynaecological malignancy or peritoneal metastasis compressing or invading bowel.
symptoms_not_in_common: sudden onset over 2 days
referred knee pain relieved by flexion
no abdominal mass
CT shows a herniated bowel loop rather than a solid tumour

data.description: Mechanical small-bowel obstruction caused by a gallstone passing through a cholecystoenteric fistula and impacting in the ileum, typically in elderly women.
symptoms_not_in_common: right knee pain relieved by flexion
extraluminal mass on rectal exam
no pneumobilia or ectopic gallstone described on imaging
CT shows bowel loop in obturator canal

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with complaints of anal pain, constipation, and tenesmus for 3 months before being referred to the hospital. There were no relevant prior illnesses. Rectal digital examination revealed a 6-cm smooth elastic mass on the rectal posterior left side 2 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy showed a rectal submucosal bulging. Computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the presence of a single 6-cm well-delimited mass, compressing and infiltrating the wall of the medium to low rectum.

A mesenchymal tumor arising in the gastrointestinal wall, often composed of spindle cells and associated with KIT or PDGFRA alterations. This is a leading possibility; confirmation requires identified immunohistochemical stains and molecular results.
symptoms_in_common: Anal pain, constipation, and tenesmus from rectal compression
Large, well-delimited mass in the middle to lower rectum
Spindle-cell appearance in the supplied histology

data.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor that can arise in the rectal muscular wall. Diagnosis depends on smooth-muscle markers and assessment of atypia, mitotic activity, and tumor necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Large rectal wall mass with infiltration
Spindle-cell morphology in the supplied histology
symptoms_not_in_common: The smooth, elastic, well-delimited appearance is less typical of an overtly aggressive sarcoma, although it does not exclude one

data.description: An uncommon, usually benign peripheral nerve-sheath tumor of the rectum that can form a circumscribed spindle-cell mass. S100 and SOX10 staining help distinguish it from other mesenchymal tumors.
symptoms_in_common: Constipation and tenesmus caused by mass effect
Spindle-cell morphology in the supplied histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Infiltrative involvement of the rectal wall is less typical of a benign schwannoma

data.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor that may arise in the rectal wall and produce obstructive symptoms when large. Smooth-muscle immunostaining and absence of malignant histologic features support the diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Constipation, tenesmus, and pain from local compression
Spindle-cell morphology in the supplied histology
symptoms_not_in_common: A 6-cm lesion is larger than most colorectal leiomyomas
Rectal wall infiltration is atypical for a benign leiomyoma

data.description: A rare fibroblastic spindle-cell tumor that can occur in the pelvis or perirectal tissues and compress the rectum. Nuclear STAT6 staining is an important diagnostic discriminator.
symptoms_in_common: Single, large, well-delimited pelvic or perirectal mass
Constipation and tenesmus from rectal compression
Spindle-cell morphology in the supplied histology
symptoms_not_in_common: An apparently intramural rectal lesion with submucosal bulging is less typical than an extrarectal mass
Rectal wall infiltration is less typical of a nonaggressive solitary fibrous tumor

diagnoses.name: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor
diagnoses.title: Gastrointestinal stromal tumour of unspecified gastrointestinal sites

data.description: Mesenchymal tumor arising from interstitial cells of Cajal in the gut wall, typically spindle-cell, positive for KIT (CD117), DOG1 and CD34, and driven by KIT or PDGFRA mutations; a second mutation may confer imatinib resistance.
symptoms_in_common: Anal pain, constipation and tenesmus from mass effect
Smooth elastic 6-cm submucosal mass in the low rectum
Submucosal bulging on colonoscopy with intact mucosa
Single well-delimited mass infiltrating the rectal wall on CT/MRI
Spindle-cell histology with mitoses and necrosis
Diffuse strong immunohistochemical staining consistent with KIT/CD34
Sequencing chromatograms showing mutations consistent with KIT/PDGFRA alterations
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectum is an uncommon site for GIST (about 5%)
No rectal bleeding reported

data.description: Malignant smooth muscle tumor of the rectal wall (muscularis propria or muscularis mucosae), positive for desmin and smooth muscle actin and negative for KIT.
symptoms_in_common: Spindle-cell proliferation with mitoses and necrosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Diffuse KIT/CD34-type staining is not expected
Mutations on sequencing consistent with KIT/PDGFRA are not a feature
Well-delimited, smooth elastic mass is less usual for an aggressive sarcoma

data.description: Benign smooth muscle tumor of the rectal wall, usually small and found incidentally, positive for desmin and smooth muscle actin.
symptoms_not_in_common: 6-cm size with wall infiltration
Hypercellularity, mitoses and necrosis on histology
Diffuse KIT/CD34-type staining
Mutations on molecular analysis
Usually asymptomatic rather than 3 months of pain and tenesmus

data.description: Benign nerve sheath tumor that can arise in the rectal wall or retrorectal space, strongly S100-positive and KIT-negative.
symptoms_not_in_common: Infiltration of the rectal wall
Necrosis and mitotic activity
Diffuse KIT/CD34-type staining
Mutations consistent with KIT/PDGFRA on sequencing

data.description: Epithelial neuroendocrine neoplasm arising in the deep mucosa/submucosa of the rectum, appearing as a submucosal nodule; positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin.

Spindle-cell fascicular histology rather than nested/trabecular pattern
KIT/CD34-type staining pattern
Mutations consistent with KIT/PDGFRA
Smooth elastic consistency (carcinoids are usually firm)

data.description: A 44-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presented with abnormal findings on 18-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography imaging. She had previously been diagnosed with breast cancer (T1N2M0, Stage IIIa, intraductal carcinoma, triple negative cancer) and had undergone adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy after a right breast conserving surgery 2 years prior. She was a non-smoker with no specific occupational or environmental exposure to known carcinogens and had been taking tamoxifen after chemotherapy. Laboratory results revealed mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.4 mg/dL) and leucopenia (3,300/μL), with all other results within normal limits. Additional laboratory findings included an elevated angiotensin I-converting enzyme level of 101 U/L, and her purified protein derivative skin test for tuberculosis was negative. The biopsy sample was also negative for tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon gamma.

A systemic granulomatous inflammatory disease commonly involving the lungs and thoracic lymph nodes. This is the leading possibility given the imaging, elevated ACE level, and apparent non-necrotizing granulomas; infectious causes must still be excluded.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on CT
Intense FDG uptake in thoracic lymph nodes
Biopsy images appear to show well-formed non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas
Mild anemia and leukopenia can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly discordant finding is reported; prior breast cancer raises an important competing explanation

data.description: A non-necrotizing granulomatous reaction associated with cancer or its treatment that can mimic metastatic disease on FDG-PET without establishing systemic sarcoidosis.
symptoms_in_common: History of breast cancer treated with surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation
Apparently non-necrotizing granulomas in the biopsy images
No specific respiratory or constitutional symptoms reported
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated ACE and pulmonary nodular involvement may favor systemic sarcoidosis, although neither excludes a sarcoid-like reaction
Mild anemia and leukopenia are not characteristic of a localized sarcoid-like reaction

data.diagnosis: Recurrent breast cancer with thoracic lymph node and pulmonary metastases
data.description: Recurrence of breast carcinoma involving thoracic lymph nodes or lungs, potentially producing FDG-avid lesions. The apparent granulomatous biopsy findings make this less likely in the sampled tissue.
symptoms_in_common: History of stage IIIA, node-positive breast cancer
New FDG-avid thoracic lesions two years after treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Relatively symmetric bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy favors a granulomatous process
Elevated ACE is not a typical marker of breast cancer recurrence
Biopsy images appear to show granulomas rather than metastatic carcinoma

data.description: A lymphoid malignancy that can cause intensely FDG-avid lymphadenopathy and cytopenias. Occasionally, associated granulomatous reactions can complicate biopsy interpretation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Well-formed non-necrotizing granulomas without an evident malignant lymphoid population are not typical diagnostic findings
Elevated ACE is more suggestive of granulomatous inflammation
No fever, night sweats, or weight loss are reported, although their absence does not exclude lymphoma

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause granulomatous thoracic lymphadenopathy and pulmonary nodules. Negative immune-based tests reduce support but do not independently exclude active tuberculosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative purified protein derivative skin test
Reported negative tuberculosis antigen-specific interferon-gamma testing
No obvious caseous necrosis in the supplied biopsy images
No cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss reported
Symmetric bilateral hilar involvement and elevated ACE favor sarcoidosis

data.description: Multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown cause characterized by non-caseating epithelioid granulomas, most often involving mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes and lungs; can occur after cancer treatment and mimic metastasis on FDG-PET.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral hilar and mediastinal FDG-avid lymphadenopathy
Symmetric distribution of enlarged nodes on CT
Non-caseating epithelioid granulomas on lymph node biopsy
Negative PPD and negative TB interferon-gamma testing
symptoms_not_in_common: History of stage IIIa triple-negative breast cancer raising suspicion of metastasis
Intense FDG uptake that is non-specific and also seen in malignancy

data.diagnosis: Metastatic breast cancer recurrence (mediastinal/hilar nodal and pulmonary metastases)
data.description: Recurrence of breast carcinoma with spread to thoracic lymph nodes and lungs, common in triple-negative disease within the first 2-3 years after treatment.
symptoms_in_common: History of node-positive (N2) triple-negative breast cancer 2 years earlier
FDG-avid mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas without malignant cells
Symmetric bilateral hilar pattern
Elevated ACE level
No clinical symptoms

data.description: Non-caseating granulomatous reaction in lymph nodes or organs in patients with cancer or after anticancer therapy, without meeting criteria for systemic sarcoidosis; thought to be an immune response to tumor antigens.
symptoms_in_common: History of breast cancer treated with chemotherapy and radiation
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated serum ACE (more suggestive of true systemic sarcoidosis)
Lung parenchymal involvement and extensive bilateral symmetric distribution
No evidence of active tumor at present

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of lymph nodes producing granulomatous inflammation, typically with caseous necrosis; common in endemic regions and in immunocompromised hosts.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative PPD skin test
Negative TB-specific interferon-gamma result
Granulomas are non-caseating without necrosis
Symmetric bilateral hilar involvement
Elevated ACE
No fever, night sweats, or weight loss reported

data.description: Malignant lymphoid proliferation (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) causing FDG-avid lymphadenopathy, sometimes as a therapy-related second malignancy; may be accompanied by granulomatous reactions.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple intensely FDG-avid mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes
symptoms_not_in_common: Biopsy showing well-formed non-caseating granulomas without atypical lymphoid cells or Reed-Sternberg cells
Elevated ACE
Symmetric hilar distribution
No B symptoms reported

data.description: 41-year-old right-handed man with neurologic history dating to his early twenties when he presented with seizures. In 2009, he developed headaches. Initial biopsy/resection pathology showed PXA (WHO grade 2) with BRAF V600E mutation confirmed by PCR testing.

data.diagnosis: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (PXA), CNS WHO grade 2, with possible residual or recurrent tumor
data.description: A circumscribed astrocytic tumor commonly affecting younger adults and frequently harboring BRAF V600E. This is the established initial pathological diagnosis; whether the pictured abnormality represents residual or recurrent tumor requires comparison with prior imaging.
symptoms_in_common: Right temporal enhancement and surrounding abnormal FLAIR signal on the supplied images

data.description: A higher-grade PXA that may develop through progression of a grade 2 tumor. Repeat tissue assessment is needed to establish transformation; enhancement alone is insufficient.
symptoms_in_common: Enhancing right temporal abnormality with surrounding FLAIR signal
symptoms_not_in_common: The initial specimen showed grade 2 rather than grade 3 disease
The prolonged seizure history is more consistent with an initially indolent tumor than an aggressive tumor from onset

data.description: A usually slow-growing mixed neuronal and glial tumor often arising in the temporal lobe and causing longstanding epilepsy. BRAF V600E can occur, but the documented PXA pathology makes this an alternative rather than the leading diagnosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: The reported biopsy/resection diagnosis was PXA rather than ganglioglioma

data.description: An aggressive glioma with epithelioid morphology that can harbor BRAF V600E and overlap pathologically with higher-grade PXA. It would require new tissue and integrated molecular evaluation to distinguish it from PXA progression.
symptoms_not_in_common: Longstanding seizures over many years are atypical for an untreated aggressive glioblastoma
The initial pathology established grade 2 PXA rather than glioblastoma

data.description: Scarring and reactive changes after brain tumor surgery can produce FLAIR hyperintensity and enhancement near a resection site. Serial imaging is needed to distinguish these changes from viable tumor.
symptoms_in_common: Right temporal FLAIR hyperintensity near an apparent operative region
Enhancement that could overlap with postoperative changes
Seizures, which can persist in association with cortical scarring
symptoms_not_in_common: Seizures began before the reported tumor surgery
Headaches developed before the initial biopsy/resection
BRAF V600E-positive PXA pathology indicates a true underlying neoplasm, which postoperative gliosis alone cannot explain

data.diagnosis: Anaplastic pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (WHO grade 3) – recurrence/malignant progression
data.description: Malignant transformation or recurrence of a previously resected PXA, typically BRAF V600E-mutant, showing new enhancing tumor and infiltrative FLAIR abnormality near the resection cavity.
symptoms_in_common: Prior PXA WHO grade 2 with BRAF V600E mutation
Long history of seizures since early twenties
Enhancing tissue around resection cavity on post-contrast T1
symptoms_not_in_common: Enhancement is patchy rather than a discrete nodular mass
No clear cyst with mural nodule on the current images

data.description: Local regrowth of a low-grade, superficially located astrocytic tumor of young people, often in the temporal lobe and causing chronic epilepsy, without anaplastic features.
symptoms_in_common: Known PXA grade 2 with BRAF V600E
Chronic seizures beginning in young adulthood
symptoms_not_in_common: Extensive infiltrative FLAIR signal extending posteriorly suggests more aggressive behavior
Long interval from the original diagnosis favors progression to a higher grade

data.description: Aggressive high-grade glioma variant that frequently harbors BRAF V600E and can arise from or coexist with PXA; presents with enhancing, infiltrative mass and edema.
symptoms_in_common: Pre-existing PXA as a possible precursor
Enhancing lesion with surrounding FLAIR hyperintensity
symptoms_not_in_common: Very long indolent course over about two decades
No marked mass effect or thick ring enhancement with central necrosis
No leptomeningeal dissemination evident

data.description: Treatment-related injury after surgery and/or radiotherapy producing enhancement and edema near the resection cavity that mimics tumor recurrence.
symptoms_in_common: Prior resection with cavity in right temporal lobe
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of radiotherapy is stated
Known tumor with a BRAF V600E driver makes true recurrence more likely
FLAIR change extends some distance from the cavity

data.description: Glioneuronal tumor of the temporal lobe in young patients causing long-standing epilepsy, often BRAF V600E-mutant, and a histologic mimic of or composite partner with PXA.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pathology already showed PXA rather than a neoplastic ganglion cell component
Infiltrative FLAIR abnormality is more extensive than typical for ganglioglioma
No calcification or classic cyst-nodule appearance described

data.description: 41-year-old white male with history of myelofibrosis. Past medical history includes splenectomy and allogeneic peripheral hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from single-antigen mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior. After sun exposure during sailing trip, developed nonpruritic rash on face, trunk and extremities, associated with intermittent fever, muscle pain and weakness. Only current medication is daily oral acyclovir. Vital signs normal. Physical exam showed impaired ability to dorsiflex wrists while bringing palms together ('prayer sign'). Lab results showed: AST 41 U/L, ALT 68 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 147 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL. Antinuclear antibody test positive (1:320) with speckled pattern.

data.diagnosis: Chronic graft-versus-host disease with cutaneous and musculoskeletal involvement
data.description: A delayed immune complication of allogeneic stem cell transplantation that can cause inflammatory skin eruptions, skin or fascial fibrosis, joint restriction, myositis, and liver abnormalities. This is a leading consideration given the transplant history and positive prayer sign.
symptoms_in_common: Rash involving the face, trunk, and extremities
Restricted wrist extension with a positive prayer sign, suggesting fascial or skin tightening
Positive antinuclear antibody, which can occur in chronic graft-versus-host disease
symptoms_not_in_common: A distinctly sun-triggered rash is less characteristic than in dermatomyositis or lupus
Intermittent fever is nonspecific and requires evaluation for infection or other causes

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory muscle disease associated with characteristic photosensitive skin eruptions. The facial and upper-chest erythema and reddish-purple dorsal hand lesions in the photographs raise this possibility, although muscle testing and further skin examination are needed.
symptoms_in_common: Reddish-purple lesions on the dorsal hands
Mild aminotransferase elevations, which may accompany muscle inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive prayer sign from restricted wrist extension is not typical of uncomplicated dermatomyositis
Alkaline phosphatase elevation is not explained by muscle inflammation alone

data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive rashes, fever, musculoskeletal inflammation, and positive antinuclear antibodies. Additional clinical and antibody findings would be necessary to establish the diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Rash on the trunk and extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Restricted wrist extension with a positive prayer sign is not a characteristic lupus finding
The reddish-purple dorsal hand lesions are more suggestive of dermatomyositis if centered over the joints
Mild alkaline phosphatase elevation is not a defining lupus feature

data.description: An autoimmune disease characterized by skin fibrosis and possible internal-organ involvement. Skin tightening can produce hand contractures and a positive prayer sign; inflammatory muscle involvement can occur in overlap syndromes.
symptoms_in_common: Restricted wrist extension with a positive prayer sign
Positive antinuclear antibody with a speckled pattern
Muscle pain and weakness, particularly if there is overlapping myositis
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute sun-triggered erythematous rash is not characteristic
Intermittent fever is not typical of uncomplicated systemic sclerosis
Diffuse facial and truncal erythema without documented skin thickening is not the usual presentation

data.description: An inflammatory fibrosing disorder of the fascia that can cause painful limb stiffness and restricted joint movement. An eosinophilic-fasciitis-like syndrome can also occur in chronic graft-versus-host disease.
symptoms_in_common: Restricted wrist extension with a positive prayer sign
Intermittent fever, which can occur during the inflammatory phase
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent facial and dorsal hand involvement is atypical because these areas are usually spared
Sun-triggered rash is not characteristic
High-titer antinuclear antibody positivity is not a typical defining finding
Mild liver enzyme abnormalities are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (photo-activated, with cutaneous, fascial/joint, muscular and hepatic involvement)
data.description: Immune-mediated multisystem disorder following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in which donor T cells attack host tissues; can be triggered by UV exposure and mimic autoimmune connective tissue diseases, with skin rash, fascial sclerosis causing joint contractures, myositis and liver involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Allogeneic stem cell transplant from mismatched unrelated donor 2 years prior
Rash onset after sun exposure (known trigger)
Rash on face, trunk and extremities including dorsal hands
Prayer sign indicating fascial/joint sclerosis and limited wrist dorsiflexion
Mildly elevated ALT and alkaline phosphatase (hepatic involvement)
Positive ANA (autoantibodies common in chronic GVHD)
symptoms_not_in_common: Nonpruritic rash (GVHD rash is often pruritic)
Fever is not a prominent feature of chronic GVHD
Malar-like photodistributed facial erythema more classically suggests lupus or dermatomyositis

data.description: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic photosensitive skin findings (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl/V sign) and proximal muscle weakness; may be paraneoplastic.
symptoms_in_common: Photosensitive rash on face, upper trunk and dorsal hands
Mildly elevated AST/ALT (may be of muscle origin)
symptoms_not_in_common: Prayer sign (sclerotic joint contracture) not typical
Elevated alkaline phosphatase
Post-transplant setting makes GVHD more likely
No described heliotrope rash or classic Gottron papules
Rash in dermatomyositis is often pruritic

data.description: Chronic multisystem autoimmune disease with photosensitive malar rash, arthritis, constitutional symptoms and antinuclear antibodies.
symptoms_in_common: Photosensitive rash triggered by sun exposure
symptoms_not_in_common: Prayer sign/fascial sclerosis not typical
Male sex makes it less common
Cholestatic liver enzyme elevation uncommon
Speckled ANA pattern is nonspecific
History of allogeneic transplant points to an alternative explanation

data.diagnosis: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) or overlap/mixed connective tissue disease
data.description: Autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by skin and fascial fibrosis, vasculopathy and internal organ involvement; overlap syndromes add myositis and lupus-like features, often with speckled ANA.
symptoms_in_common: Prayer sign from skin/fascial tightening of hands and wrists
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset after sun exposure
Photodistributed erythematous rash on face and trunk
Fever
No Raynaud phenomenon, digital ulcers or dysphagia reported
Elevated liver enzymes not typical

data.description: Cutaneous reaction in sun-exposed areas caused by interaction of UV light with a photosensitizing drug or by excessive sun exposure, producing sunburn-like or eczematous eruption.
symptoms_in_common: Rash developed after intense sun exposure while sailing
Distribution on face, upper chest/shoulders and dorsal hands
Mild liver enzyme elevation could be drug-related
symptoms_not_in_common: Acyclovir is not a typical photosensitizer
Fever, muscle pain and weakness
Prayer sign/joint contracture
Positive high-titer ANA
Rash extending beyond exposed sites to the trunk and extremities

data.description: An 8-year-old boy presented to his general practitioner with limping and complaints of occasional leg pain. He was otherwise healthy and afebrile. On physical examination, he walked with a limp and demonstrated painful, reduced internal rotation and abduction of his right hip. Plain radiographs were obtained to evaluate his symptoms.

Childhood osteonecrosis of the femoral head, most common in boys aged 4–10 years. The images appear to show femoral-head sclerosis, flattening, and fragmentation, strongly favoring this diagnosis. The more conspicuous abnormality appears on the image-right side, conventionally the patient's left, so laterality should be verified against the reported right-sided symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Occasional leg pain, which can represent referred hip pain
Painful, reduced hip internal rotation and abduction
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported symptom is clearly atypical; the apparent imaging laterality differs from the reported symptomatic side

data.description: A temporary, usually self-limited inflammation of the hip joint that commonly causes limping in otherwise well children. Femoral-head fragmentation or collapse would not be explained by this condition.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported symptom is clearly atypical, but the apparent structural femoral-head changes argue against isolated transient synovitis

data.description: Displacement of the proximal femoral epiphysis through the growth plate, generally occurring in adolescents. It can cause referred leg pain and limited internal rotation, but the apparent radiographic pattern is more suggestive of Perthes disease.
symptoms_in_common: Leg pain potentially referred from the hip
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation at age 8 is younger than typical
Occasional mild pain is less characteristic of an acute unstable slip, although it can occur with a stable slip

data.diagnosis: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the hip
data.description: Chronic inflammatory arthritis beginning before age 16 that can cause hip pain, stiffness, and restricted movement. Diagnosis requires persistent arthritis and exclusion of other causes; the described imaging is not typical of early disease.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of fever can occur in nonsystemic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Occasional leg pain without reported morning stiffness is less characteristic
An isolated hip presentation is less typical than involvement of other joints

data.description: A bacterial infection of the hip joint requiring urgent assessment when suspected. It usually causes acute severe pain, marked movement restriction, and often fever; this child's mild intermittent symptoms and well appearance make it less likely.
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Otherwise healthy appearance
Occasional rather than severe persistent pain
Ability to walk, although with a limp

data.description: Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in children aged 4-10, more common in boys, leading to collapse, fragmentation and later remodelling of the femoral head.
symptoms_in_common: painful reduced internal rotation and abduction of the hip
radiographs showing flattened, sclerotic/fragmented femoral epiphysis
serial films showing later pelvic surgery with pins, consistent with containment osteotomy
symptoms_not_in_common: possible involvement of both hips on imaging, which is less common (10-15%) and would prompt consideration of skeletal dysplasia

data.description: Displacement of the femoral head epiphysis through the physis, typically in overweight adolescents, causing limp and hip or knee pain.
symptoms_not_in_common: age of 8 is younger than typical (10-16 years)
no mention of obesity or endocrine disorder
radiographs show epiphyseal flattening/fragmentation rather than a slip

data.description: Self-limiting inflammatory hip effusion in children, often following a viral illness, causing acute limp and hip pain.
symptoms_not_in_common: usually acute onset and resolves within 1-2 weeks
radiographs are normal in transient synovitis, whereas there are femoral head changes here
intermittent, more chronic course

data.description: Inherited skeletal dysplasia with delayed, irregular ossification of epiphyses, often bilateral and symmetric at the hips, which can mimic Perthes disease.
symptoms_in_common: irregular or flattened femoral epiphyses on radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: symptoms are unilateral (right hip)
no short stature, family history or other joint involvement reported
changes are usually symmetric and synchronous without the staged sclerosis-fragmentation sequence

data.diagnosis: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis involving the hip
data.description: Chronic autoimmune arthritis of childhood causing joint pain, stiffness, limp and reduced range of motion.
symptoms_not_in_common: isolated hip involvement at onset is uncommon
no morning stiffness, swelling of other joints or uveitis reported
radiographic epiphyseal necrosis/fragmentation is not typical

data.description: 42-year-old man with coronary artery disease and dyslipidemia presented with 2 days of sudden left upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back in a bandlike pattern, worsening with movement, associated with nausea and early satiety. He also had substernal chest pressure similar to prior angina but not relieved by nitroglycerin. He denied trauma, vomiting, or GI bleeding. History notable for chronic diarrhea since coronary bypass surgery, worsening after a lipid medication dose increase 6 months earlier, along with 16 kg unintentional weight loss over 6 months, intermittent early satiety, daily headaches, nocturia, and nighttime warmth without fever or night sweats. Exam showed mild left upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. Vitals were stable. Labs showed elevated amylase, lipase, AST, and ALT with otherwise normal electrolytes, renal function, blood counts, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, calcium, and triglycerides; ECG and chest radiograph were normal.

An immune-mediated reaction to gluten causing small-intestinal injury and malabsorption. The biopsy appears to show villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, supporting this diagnosis; serology and formal pathology review are needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal discomfort and intermittent early satiety
Apparent mesenteric lymph node enlargement on CT
Small-intestinal biopsy changes suggestive of celiac disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden bandlike left upper quadrant pain radiating to the back is not a typical primary presentation
Elevated pancreatic enzymes suggest an accompanying pancreatic process
Substernal chest pressure
Nocturia and nighttime warmth

data.description: Acute pancreatic inflammation causing upper abdominal pain and pancreatic enzyme elevation. This is a strong explanation for the acute presentation, although the reported enzyme levels and formal imaging interpretation are needed to establish diagnostic criteria.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden upper abdominal pain radiating to the back
symptoms_not_in_common: Six months of substantial weight loss and longstanding diarrhea are not explained by an isolated acute episode
Small-intestinal villous injury and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes are not typical
Mesenteric lymph node enlargement is not a defining feature
Daily headaches and nocturia

data.diagnosis: Medication-induced gastrointestinal toxicity with possible drug-induced pancreatitis
data.description: An adverse medication reaction can cause diarrhea, liver enzyme elevations, and, rarely, pancreatitis. The association with a lipid-lowering medication dose increase warrants review, but does not establish causation.
symptoms_in_common: Diarrhea worsening after a lipid medication dose increase
Elevated pancreatic enzymes if pancreatitis is medication-related
Weight loss potentially associated with persistent diarrhea
symptoms_not_in_common: Diarrhea began before the reported dose increase
Marked weight loss requires evaluation beyond a presumed medication side effect
Apparent mesenteric lymphadenopathy
Biopsy changes suggestive of celiac disease are not typical of routine lipid-lowering medication intolerance
Nocturia and nighttime warmth

data.description: A lymphoid malignancy involving the intestine that can cause malabsorption, abdominal pain, weight loss, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy. Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma is a consideration if underlying celiac disease is confirmed, although the supplied biopsy does not establish lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent mesenteric lymph node enlargement on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden pancreatic-pattern pain with elevated amylase and lipase is not a usual presentation
The displayed biopsy appears more consistent with inflammatory enteropathy than overt malignant infiltration
Substernal pressure resembling prior angina
Daily headaches and nocturia

data.description: A rare systemic infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that can produce intestinal malabsorption, diarrhea, weight loss, and abdominal lymphadenopathy. Confirmation requires characteristic tissue findings and organism-specific testing.
symptoms_in_common: Headaches could occur with neurologic involvement, although they are nonspecific
symptoms_not_in_common: The biopsy does not clearly show the characteristic macrophage-rich intestinal infiltrate
Apparent increased intraepithelial lymphocytes favor celiac disease instead
Acute bandlike pain and elevated pancreatic enzymes are not typical
Substernal chest pressure
Nocturia

data.diagnosis: Celiac disease (with associated pancreatitis/hyperamylasemia and celiac hepatitis)
data.description: Immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten, causing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis; can be unmasked after surgery and is associated with mesenteric lymphadenopathy, elevated transaminases, and pancreatitis from papillary inflammation/stenosis.
symptoms_in_common: Mesenteric lymphadenopathy and small-bowel changes on CT
Duodenal biopsy with villous blunting, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden bandlike left upper quadrant pain radiating to back
Substernal chest pressure
Nocturia
Nighttime warmth
Normal blood counts (no anemia)

data.description: Acute inflammation of the pancreas; causes include gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia, and medications such as statins, fibrates or ezetimibe.
symptoms_in_common: Sudden upper abdominal pain radiating to the back in bandlike pattern
Chest pressure not relieved by nitroglycerin (referred pain)
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic diarrhea for a long period
16 kg weight loss over 6 months
Mesenteric lymphadenopathy
Villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytes on biopsy
Daily headaches
Nocturia
Normal triglycerides and calcium, no vomiting

data.description: Malignant lymphoid proliferation of the intestine, sometimes complicating celiac disease, presenting with weight loss, diarrhea, abdominal pain and mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated amylase and lipase
No documented fever or drenching night sweats
Normal blood counts
Biopsy showing benign-appearing enteropathy without atypical lymphoid infiltrate
Chest pressure
Nocturia

data.diagnosis: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma or chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency
data.description: Pancreatic neoplasm or chronic inflammation causing duct obstruction, malabsorption from enzyme deficiency, weight loss and pain radiating to the back.
symptoms_in_common: Upper abdominal pain radiating to the back
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age
Normal bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase
No pancreatic mass described on CT
Villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytosis on duodenal biopsy
Mesenteric rather than peripancreatic adenopathy
Headaches

data.diagnosis: Crohn's disease of the small bowel
data.description: Chronic transmural inflammatory bowel disease that can involve any GI segment, causing diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain, and mesenteric lymphadenopathy; may rarely be associated with pancreatitis.

symptoms_not_in_common: No GI bleeding

data.description: 80-year-old woman with 6-month history of slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. History of chronic renal failure requiring dialysis three times weekly for 10 years. Poor compliance with phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical exam showed firm, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in major axis. Laboratory findings: serum calcium 1.95 mmol/L (normal: 2.05-2.55), serum phosphorus 3.3 mmol/L (normal: 0.74-1.52), serum intact parathyroid hormone 142 ng/L (normal: 10-65), serum creatinine 787 μmol/L (normal: 53-106).

Mass-like calcium-phosphate deposition in soft tissues associated with advanced renal failure and disordered mineral metabolism. This is the leading diagnosis given the dialysis history, hyperphosphatemia, and lobulated calcified mass.

Marked hyperphosphatemia with poor adherence to phosphate binders

data.description: 56-year-old Ethiopian male with a history of resected type A thymoma 3 years earlier, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, and intermittent diarrhea/IBS-D symptoms, presented with persistent fever, chills, cough, night sweats, and weight loss. On admission he had low-grade fever with otherwise stable vitals and normal oxygen saturation. Labs showed lymphopenia, mild anemia, low albumin/protein, and markedly reduced CD19 B cells with low CD3/CD4 counts; he had absent pneumococcal antibody responses and impaired lymphocyte proliferation to tetanus and candida. Extensive infectious workup was negative except for induced sputum positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Moraxella catarrhalis. Biopsy of a cavitary lesion showed acute and chronic inflammation without malignancy.

The leading unifying diagnosis: an adult-onset combined immunodeficiency associated with thymoma, characterized by markedly reduced B cells, impaired antibody production, and variable T-cell dysfunction. It can persist or appear after thymoma resection.
symptoms_in_common: Markedly reduced CD19 B cells and absent pneumococcal antibody responses
Impaired lymphocyte proliferation to tetanus and Candida
Intermittent diarrhea, fatigue, and weight loss
symptoms_not_in_common: Focal cavitary pulmonary consolidation is not a direct manifestation of the immunodeficiency and suggests a secondary infection

data.description: An opportunistic fungal pneumonia occurring with impaired cellular immunity. Positive induced sputum supports this diagnosis, although detection alone does not always distinguish infection from colonization.

Recurrent sinopulmonary infections preceding the current illness

data.description: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. data.description: A 65-year-old male retired farmer presented with an inability to fully straighten the ring finger and little finger of his right hand, which had progressed over the past two years. His father had a similar deformity. On examination, he had palpable cords to his middle, ring, and little fingers with palpable nodules on the volar aspect of all proximal phalanges, causing flexion contractures of the proximal interphalangeal joints. The cord and nodules in the ring finger were adherent to the overlying skin.

data.description: Young female traveler presented to a clinic in central Australia with vaginal discharge. She reported sexual intercourse with a new partner 1 week earlier in Sydney.

data.description: 47-year-old homeless man with 1 month of intermittent bilateral leg pain and pins-and-needles sensation, starting in the toes and spreading to the shins. Exam: afebrile, BP 170/110 mmHg; otherwise normal cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, and skin exams. Neurologic exam showed normal cranial nerves, strength, and reflexes, but unsteady gait with limited ambulation due to pain and decreased pinprick, light touch, and temperature sensation in both lower extremities.

data.description: 57-year-old man with 8 years of well-controlled HIV infection (CD4 250/mm³, undetectable viral load) and a 10-year history of bilateral inguinal hernias, left larger than right, previously easily reducible. He presented with 3 weeks of worsening left inguinal pain and enlarging hernia, with increased pain over the prior 3 months. During the 3 weeks before presentation, he developed intermittent subjective fevers, night sweats, and hard, tender lumps adjacent to the hernia; oral temperature reached 38.1°C the night before presentation. Exam showed easily reducible bilateral inguinal hernias and bulky, slightly tender left inguinal lymphadenopathy, including three nodes up to 3 cm. Past history included Kaposi sarcoma, molluscum contagiosum, anal dysplasia, pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection, pneumocystis pneumonia, thrush, preseptal cellulitis, and cryptosporidium-related diarrhea.

Lymph-node inflammation caused by Treponema pallidum. The apparent numerous slender, curved organisms on the tissue stain favor this diagnosis, although the stain identity and syphilis serology are needed for confirmation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Enlargement of longstanding reducible inguinal hernias is not a direct manifestation of syphilis
Prominent unilateral painful lymphadenopathy is less typical than painless or generalized lymphadenopathy

data.description: An invasive infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3 that can produce painful inguinal lymphadenopathy and inflammatory lymph-node lesions.
symptoms_not_in_common: Longstanding bilateral reducible hernias are unrelated to the infection
The apparent slender organisms on the tissue stain are not characteristic of Chlamydia trachomatis

data.description: A malignant proliferation of lymphocytes, with increased risk in people with HIV, that can cause enlarging lymph nodes and systemic symptoms. Tissue morphology and immunophenotyping are required for diagnosis.

symptoms_not_in_common: Tender nodes are less typical than painless lymphadenopathy

data.description: Lymph-node infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacteria such as Mycobacterium avium complex. Diagnosis requires acid-fast staining, culture, or molecular testing.

data.description: A bacterial infection, commonly associated with cat exposure, that causes regional lymphadenopathy and may produce suppurative or stellate inflammatory lesions in lymph-node tissue.

data.description: 8-year-old Korean boy with severe global developmental delay and multiple exostoses. Developmental delay was first noted at 3 months of age with incomplete eye contact and poor head control. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, with low birth weight. Physical findings included hypotonia, ptosis, nystagmus, and microcephaly. By age 6 years, he had severe growth retardation, marked developmental impairment, and could not sit or walk independently. Facial features included sparse eyebrows, prominent nasal bridge, hypoplastic nare, down-turned mouth, and high-arched palate. Multiple exostoses were first observed at age 6 years as protrusions of the right wrist and knee. Karyotype was normal (46,XY).

A contiguous-gene deletion syndrome involving chromosome 11p11.2, including EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A. It causes multiple exostoses, enlarged parietal foramina, intellectual disability, and craniofacial abnormalities. The supplied skull images and chromosomal microarray strongly favor this diagnosis despite the normal conventional karyotype.

Hypotonia and inability to sit or walk independently
Chromosome 11p deletion encompassing EXT2, ALX4, and PHF21A on the supplied microarray
