data.description: A 39-year-old man with a history of current smoking and no other medical history presented with left-sided squeezing chest pain that was worse in the early morning after drinking alcohol and lasted 30 minutes. Initial vital signs showed blood pressure of 132/89 mmHg and pulse rate of 98 beats/minute. Initial laboratory findings revealed creatine kinase 118 U/L (normal 58-348), CK-MB 1.7 ug/L (normal 0-5.0), elevated highly sensitive troponin-T 0.027 ng/mL (normal 0-0.014), and microcytic hypochromic anemia with hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL. Echocardiography showed normal-sized cardiac chambers with good left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction of 61%) and no regional wall motion abnormality.

Transient coronary artery spasm causes myocardial ischemia, typically at rest during the night or early morning. This is a leading possibility given the timing, smoking history, and alcohol association.
symptoms_in_common: Chest pain associated with alcohol consumption
Current smoking, a major risk factor for coronary spasm
Mild troponin-T elevation consistent with ischemic myocardial injury
Preserved left ventricular function without regional wall motion abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Microcytic hypochromic anemia is not explained by coronary spasm

data.description: A segment of a coronary artery, usually the left anterior descending artery, travels through heart muscle and can be compressed during contraction. The angiographic and intravascular ultrasound images raise this possibility, although confirmation requires assessment of dynamic compression.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent variation in left anterior descending artery caliber between angiographic panels
An intravascular ultrasound appearance potentially compatible with a myocardial bridge
symptoms_not_in_common: Early-morning alcohol-associated pain is more characteristic of coronary spasm than isolated myocardial bridging
Microcytic hypochromic anemia is not caused by myocardial bridging

data.description: Acute coronary plaque disruption with thrombosis causes myocardial injury without persistent ST elevation. Serial troponin measurements and coronary assessment are needed to establish this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Squeezing left-sided chest pain lasting 30 minutes
Normal ventricular function can occur with a small infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Early-morning alcohol-associated episodes favor vasospasm over plaque disruption
The supplied angiographic images do not clearly demonstrate an obstructive culprit lesion or thrombus
Microcytic hypochromic anemia is not explained by plaque disruption

data.diagnosis: Coronary microvascular dysfunction with microvascular angina

Mild troponin elevation can occur with associated ischemic injury

Microcytic hypochromic anemia is not caused by microvascular dysfunction

Preserved ventricular function and no regional wall motion abnormality

Stable blood pressure and absence of marked tachycardia make a major acute demand stress less evident
Possible dynamic focal coronary narrowing is not explained by anemia alone

data.diagnosis: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal/variant) angina with fixed atherosclerotic stenosis

data.description: 83-year-old woman with hypertension and biopsy-proven vaginal melanoma diagnosed 4 months earlier, with invasive loco-regional disease and a 3-mm left upper lobe lung nodule on PET-CT. She received four cycles of ipilimumab, last dose 3 weeks before admission; after the third dose she developed pruritus, lethargy, and malaise, and after the fourth dose diarrhea. For 2 weeks before admission, she had worsening substernal chest pain and progressive dyspnea. On admission, ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 110/min with 1 mm ST elevations in leads I, V2, and V3; troponin-I was elevated at 0.98 ng/ml and ESR was 65 mm/hour. Echocardiography showed an ejection fraction of 50% with LV outflow tract obstruction, peak gradient 100 mmHg, and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Cardiac angiography showed isolated 30% proximal LAD stenosis without thrombus.

Ventriculographic appearance suggestive of apical ballooning
symptoms_not_in_common: Pruritus and diarrhea following ipilimumab are not intrinsic features
Elevated ESR is nonspecific and may suggest an additional inflammatory process

data.description: 35-year-old female with intermittent rhinitis presented with 5 days of urticaria, fever, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia. She developed pruritic, painful wheals and erythematous macules >1 cm with burning on the limbs; lesions lasted >24 hours and left skin pigmentation changes. Angioedema involved the hands, fingers, ankles, and feet without pitting. Symptoms included severe headache and myalgia limiting daily activities, with fever up to 39.5°C. She had taken over-the-counter diet pills 18 days before symptom onset and had been seen 6 days earlier for dehydration and violaceous hives on the palms, after which she stopped the pills. Examination showed large confluent wheals and macules on the limbs with pruritus rated 6/10 and muscle pain. Labs showed lymphopenia and elevated CRP (7.5 mg/L); other routine studies, complement, liver, renal, thyroid, glucose, sodium, and ANA were normal or negative. Skin biopsy showed mild vacuolar interface change, papillary dermal edema, superficial and perivascular lymphocytic/eosinophilic infiltrate, focal fibrin in vessel walls, and erythrocyte extravasation.

Small-vessel inflammation causing persistent urticarial lesions that burn or hurt and leave pigmentation. This is the leading consideration given the lesion duration and vascular biopsy findings; normal complement supports the normocomplementemic subtype.

Vessel-wall fibrin and erythrocyte extravasation on biopsy

Lymphopenia is nonspecific

Acute onset after drug exposure
Eosinophilic infiltrate
Normal renal studies
Marked pruritus

data.description: Systemic autoinflammatory disorder with high spiking fevers, arthralgia/arthritis, myalgia and an evanescent or sometimes persistent urticarial rash, with negative ANA.
symptoms_not_in_common: Lymphopenia rather than neutrophilic leukocytosis
Only mildly elevated CRP
Normal liver tests
Markedly pruritic, painful fixed wheals with pigmentation
Angioedema
Vascular fibrin and eosinophils on biopsy
Clear drug trigger
No sore throat reported

data.description: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.

A congenital segment of abnormal lung supplied by a systemic artery rather than the pulmonary circulation. The left basal lesion and apparent vessel arising near the descending aorta make this a leading possibility, although dedicated vascular imaging is needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Fever and elevated C-reactive protein consistent with superimposed infection
Left upper quadrant pain worsened by deep breathing, compatible with diaphragmatic irritation
Basal lung tissue-like lesion with internal vascularity and an apparent systemic feeding vessel
symptoms_not_in_common: No previous respiratory infections, although sequestration can first become symptomatic in childhood
Pain worsened by lying down is nonspecific

data.description: Infection of the left lower lung can produce consolidation and referred upper abdominal pain, sometimes with few abnormal respiratory examination findings in children.
symptoms_in_common: Left upper quadrant pain worsened by deep breathing
Tissue-like appearance of the basal pulmonary lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: An apparent systemic arterial feeding vessel is not typical of ordinary pneumonia
Absence of leukocytosis is less typical of substantial bacterial pneumonia, but does not exclude it

data.diagnosis: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation with superimposed infection
data.description: A developmental abnormality of the small airways that can remain undetected until infection occurs. Hybrid lesions may also have the systemic arterial supply characteristic of sequestration.
symptoms_in_common: Childhood presentation after previously being healthy
symptoms_not_in_common: The supplied images do not clearly show the cystic architecture commonly associated with this malformation
An apparent systemic feeding vessel favors sequestration or a hybrid lesion rather than an isolated airway malformation

data.description: A localized collection of pus within lung tissue, usually resulting from bacterial infection or infection of an underlying congenital pulmonary lesion.
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear thick-walled cavity or air-fluid level is demonstrated in the supplied images
Mild whitish sputum rather than copious purulent or foul-smelling sputum
No leukocytosis
An apparent systemic feeding artery is not explained by an uncomplicated abscess

data.description: Inflammation and fluid accumulation around the lung associated with pneumonia, potentially producing diaphragmatic irritation and referred abdominal pain.
symptoms_not_in_common: A discrete vascularized basal tissue lesion is not explained by pleural inflammation alone
An apparent systemic feeding vessel is not typical
The supplied images do not clearly establish a substantial pleural fluid collection

data.description: Congenital mass of non-functioning lung tissue with its own pleural covering and a systemic arterial supply, usually in the left lower thorax; it can twist on its vascular pedicle, causing infarction with acute pain and an inflammatory response.
symptoms_in_common: Acute left upper quadrant abdominal pain
Pain worse with deep breathing or lying down
Left paravertebral supradiaphragmatic mass on imaging
Small vessel near the aorta suggesting a systemic feeding pedicle
symptoms_not_in_common: Cough with whitish sputum is not typical, as the sequestration has no bronchial communication
Colour Doppler shows some internal flow, whereas a fully torted lesion would be expected to be avascular

data.description: Non-functioning lung tissue within the normal lobe's pleura, supplied by a systemic artery, that typically presents with recurrent or persistent lower lobe infection.
symptoms_in_common: Left lower thoracic lesion with systemic vessel from the aorta
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of recurrent pneumonia
Well-defined, discrete mass separate from lung rather than consolidation or cystic change within a lobe
Abdominal pain as the dominant symptom
No leukocytosis

data.diagnosis: Left lower lobe pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion (including round pneumonia)
data.description: Bacterial or atypical infection of the lung base; in children it commonly presents with referred abdominal pain and may appear as a round, mass-like consolidation.
symptoms_in_common: Pleuritic left upper quadrant pain referred from the lung base
symptoms_not_in_common: No leukocytosis (though possible with atypical organisms)
No abnormal chest findings on examination
Sharply marginated paravertebral mass with its own vascular pedicle rather than air-bronchogram-containing consolidation

data.diagnosis: Neurogenic tumour of the posterior mediastinum (neuroblastoma/ganglioneuroblastoma/ganglioneuroma)
data.description: Tumours arising from the sympathetic chain, the commonest posterior mediastinal paravertebral masses in children; often found incidentally or through mass effect.
symptoms_in_common: Paravertebral solid mass in a child
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset of pleuritic pain
Cough with sputum
Age of 10 years is older than typical for neuroblastoma
No calcification, intraspinal extension or rib/vertebral change described
Discrete feeding vessel from the aorta and pleural effusion are unusual

data.description: Ischaemic or infective lesion of the spleen causing left upper quadrant pain with diaphragmatic irritation, sometimes with a reactive left pleural effusion.
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesion on imaging is above the diaphragm in the paravertebral thorax, not in the spleen
No predisposing condition such as haemoglobinopathy, endocarditis or immunodeficiency
Cough with sputum
No splenomegaly or tenderness on examination

data.description: 16-year-old male with 4 weeks of weakness, malaise, anorexia, nausea, fever, and vomiting. No rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, or herbal/native medication use. Exam showed pallor, bilateral pitting pedal edema, and hypertension (160/90 mmHg); otherwise unremarkable. Labs revealed anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, proteinuria (3+; 2.4 g/24 h), hematuria with RBC casts, and rapidly worsening renal failure (urea 130 mg/dL; creatinine 3 mg/dL rising to 10 mg/dL in 7 days). ANA and ANCA were negative, hepatitis B/C and HIV tests were negative, complements were normal. Ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys; chest/abdominal CT and fundus exam were normal.

An inflammatory glomerular disease causing rapidly progressive kidney failure with little or no immune deposition. The biopsy image appears to show substantial extracapillary cellular proliferation suggestive of crescent formation; immunofluorescence is needed to establish the subtype. Negative ANCA does not exclude this disease.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent crescent formation in the biopsy image
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe thrombocytopenia is unusual and suggests an additional or alternative process
Anemia may accompany renal failure, but anemia with severe thrombocytopenia raises concern for thrombotic microangiopathy

data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, producing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Normal circulating complement levels do not exclude it; blood-smear and hemolysis studies are needed.
symptoms_not_in_common: RBC casts favor inflammatory glomerulonephritis rather than isolated thrombotic microangiopathy
Apparent cellular crescent formation in the biopsy image is not the characteristic lesion of atypical HUS

data.description: An autoantibody-mediated disease causing necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis, sometimes with pulmonary hemorrhage. Renal-limited disease is possible; diagnosis requires anti-GBM antibody testing and assessment for linear IgG staining on kidney immunofluorescence.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent crescent formation in the biopsy image
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe thrombocytopenia is not typical
Fever lasting several weeks is less characteristic
No pulmonary symptoms or chest CT abnormalities, although renal-limited disease can occur

data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy associated with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency, causing platelet consumption, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and organ injury. ADAMTS13 activity and hemolysis testing are needed to distinguish it from HUS and other causes.
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound kidney failure is less typical than in HUS
RBC casts and substantial proteinuria suggest a primary glomerular inflammatory process
Apparent crescent formation is not characteristic of TTP
No neurological abnormalities were reported

data.description: An IgA immune-complex glomerular disease that can rarely produce extensive crescents and rapidly progressive kidney failure. Diagnosis requires predominantly mesangial IgA deposition on kidney immunofluorescence.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent crescent formation in the biopsy image
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe thrombocytopenia is not typical
Persistent fever and marked constitutional symptoms are less characteristic
Anemia together with severe thrombocytopenia suggests a possible concurrent thrombotic microangiopathy

data.diagnosis: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease with crescentic glomerulonephritis, possibly with associated thrombotic microangiopathy
data.description: Autoimmune disease caused by antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane, producing rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis, sometimes with pulmonary hemorrhage (Goodpasture syndrome). It can rarely be accompanied by thrombotic microangiopathy, causing anemia and thrombocytopenia.
symptoms_in_common: Rapidly progressive renal failure (creatinine 3 to 10 mg/dL in 7 days)
Negative ANA and ANCA with normal complements
Biopsy image showing a circumferential cellular crescent compressing the glomerular tuft
Constitutional prodrome of malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and fever
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe thrombocytopenia (unusual unless there is concurrent thrombotic microangiopathy)
No pulmonary hemorrhage and normal chest CT (though renal-limited disease does occur)
Fever is not prominent in most cases

data.diagnosis: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy
data.description: Complement-mediated or secondary thrombotic microangiopathy characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury due to endothelial damage and microthrombi in the renal vasculature.
symptoms_not_in_common: RBC casts and crescent formation on biopsy are not typical of pure thrombotic microangiopathy
Normal complement levels (C3 is often low in complement-mediated disease, though it can be normal)
No diarrheal prodrome reported
Four-week subacute course with fever
Normal fundus despite severe hypertension-associated disease

data.description: Necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis with little or no immune deposits. About 10-30% of cases are ANCA-negative, and it may be renal-limited. It presents as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with constitutional symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe thrombocytopenia (vasculitis usually causes thrombocytosis)
Negative ANCA
Young age (more common in older adults)
No extrarenal vasculitic features (no rash, joint pain, or lung or sinus involvement)

data.diagnosis: Lupus nephritis (seronegative systemic lupus erythematosus) with crescentic glomerulonephritis
data.description: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis due to systemic lupus erythematosus. Class IV disease can present with crescents and rapidly progressive renal failure, and is often accompanied by cytopenias.
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative ANA (very rare in lupus)
Normal complement levels
No rash, joint pain, or oral ulcers
Male sex (less common)

data.diagnosis: Crescentic IgA nephropathy / IgA vasculitis nephritis
data.description: Mesangial IgA deposition disease, the most common primary glomerulonephritis in young people. It can rarely present with a crescentic, rapidly progressive course, and complement levels are normal.
symptoms_in_common: Normal complements with negative ANA and ANCA
Rapidly progressive renal failure with crescents (in the crescentic variant)
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe thrombocytopenia
Prolonged fever and marked constitutional symptoms
No purpuric rash, joint pain, or abdominal pain to suggest IgA vasculitis
No history of preceding mucosal infection or gross hematuria
Such fulminant renal failure is uncommon

data.description: A previously healthy 9-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of left chest pain and increasing respiratory distress. His vital signs showed a respiratory rate of 40/min and heart rate of 105/min. Physical examination revealed unremarkable cardiac auscultation, while auscultation of lung fields showed diminished breath sounds over the left side.

A congenital defect in the left diaphragm allows abdominal organs, particularly the stomach, to enter the chest. This is strongly suggested by the large left-sided air-fluid level and the apparent nasogastric tube looping within the intrathoracic stomach.
symptoms_in_common: Large air-fluid level in the lower left chest
Apparent intrathoracic positioning of the stomach on the tube-placement image
symptoms_not_in_common: First presentation at age 9 is less common than presentation during infancy, although delayed presentation is recognized

data.description: Marked distension of a stomach displaced into the chest compresses the adjacent lung and can compromise circulation. It is a potentially life-threatening complication of diaphragmatic herniation.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset of left chest pain
Large intrathoracic gas-filled structure with an air-fluid level
Apparent reduction of the gas-filled structure after gastric tube placement
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hypotension or circulatory collapse to establish severe tension physiology

data.description: Rotation of a herniated stomach can obstruct gastric emptying and cause rapid distension, respiratory compromise, and potentially gastric ischemia. The radiographs suggest an intrathoracic stomach but do not establish volvulus.
symptoms_in_common: Large gastric-appearing air-fluid level within the left chest
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported retching, vomiting, or epigastric pain
Apparent successful gastric tube placement is less typical of a completely obstructing volvulus

data.description: Air and fluid within the pleural space can produce a horizontal air-fluid level, compress the lung, and cause acute chest pain and dyspnea. This is an important imaging mimic, although the gastric tube course favors an intrathoracic stomach.
symptoms_in_common: Diminished breath sounds on the affected side
Horizontal air-fluid level in the left chest
symptoms_not_in_common: Apparent nasogastric tube looping within the left thoracic air-fluid structure is not explained by an uncomplicated hydropneumothorax
The rounded, bounded gas collection is less typical of freely distributed pleural air

data.diagnosis: Left diaphragmatic eventration with gastric distension
data.description: Abnormal elevation of an intact but weakened diaphragm can displace the stomach upward and compress the lung. Gastric distension can worsen respiratory symptoms and mimic diaphragmatic herniation.
symptoms_in_common: Curved elevated boundary above the left-sided gas collection
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt chest pain and deterioration over 6 hours are less typical of uncomplicated eventration
The apparent intrathoracic stomach favors a diaphragmatic hernia unless an intact elevated diaphragm is confirmed

data.diagnosis: Late-presenting congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek) with intrathoracic gastric herniation
data.description: A congenital posterolateral diaphragmatic defect that can stay silent until later childhood, when the stomach or other abdominal viscera herniate acutely into the chest. The distended intrathoracic stomach compresses the lung and can mimic a tension pneumothorax or hydropneumothorax.
symptoms_in_common: Previously healthy child with sudden onset of symptoms
Rapidly increasing respiratory distress with tachypnea (40/min)
Diminished breath sounds over the left side
Large left intrathoracic air-fluid level with a curved, dome-like wall on the chest films
Nasogastric tube appearing to coil upward into the left lower chest on the follow-up film, suggesting an intrathoracic stomach
Re-expansion of the left lung after gastric decompression
symptoms_not_in_common: No vomiting or abdominal pain reported
No bowel sounds in the chest described
No prior recurrent respiratory or gastrointestinal complaints

data.diagnosis: Tension gastrothorax (acute gastric volvulus through a diaphragmatic defect)
data.description: A massively distended stomach, often twisted, herniated into the left hemithorax through a diaphragmatic defect. It produces tension physiology with mediastinal shift and respiratory compromise, and is relieved by nasogastric decompression.
symptoms_in_common: Single very large air-fluid level in the left hemithorax
Apparent improvement after nasogastric tube placement
symptoms_not_in_common: No retching or unproductive vomiting reported
No epigastric pain or distension reported
No hypotension or shock described
Nasogastric tube could apparently be passed, which is often difficult in volvulus

data.description: Air, with or without fluid, in the pleural space under pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum. It is the main mimic of an intrathoracic stomach, and mistaking one for the other risks a chest drain being placed into the stomach.
symptoms_in_common: Diminished breath sounds on the left
Left-sided lucency with an air-fluid level
symptoms_not_in_common: Lucency is bounded above by a curved, wall-like line with aerated lung above it, rather than a visceral pleural line with lung collapsed toward the hilum
Normal left hemidiaphragm contour and gastric bubble not seen
No trauma or underlying lung disease
Nasogastric tube courses into the left chest
No fever to suggest an infected hydropneumothorax

data.diagnosis: Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture with visceral herniation
data.description: A tear in the diaphragm after blunt or penetrating trauma that allows abdominal organs into the chest, sometimes presenting days to years after the injury.
symptoms_in_common: Intrathoracic air-fluid level consistent with herniated stomach
Left side affected, as is usual for diaphragmatic rupture
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of trauma
Previously healthy child
No rib fractures or other signs of injury on imaging

data.diagnosis: Diaphragmatic eventration or large paraesophageal hiatal hernia with gastric distension
data.description: Eventration is an abnormally elevated, thinned but intact hemidiaphragm; a paraesophageal hernia lets the stomach pass through the hiatus into the chest. Either can place a distended stomach high in the left hemithorax.
symptoms_in_common: Large gas-filled structure with an air-fluid level in the left lower chest
Smooth dome-like upper contour that could represent an elevated diaphragm or stomach wall
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt onset over 6 hours in a previously healthy child, whereas these are usually chronic or incidental
Marked mediastinal shift and severe distress are unusual
No history of reflux, feeding problems, or recurrent chest infections
A hiatal hernia would typically lie retrocardiac in the midline rather than fill the left hemithorax

data.description: 35-year-old woman with severe hypertension, edema, and renal failure. She had preeclampsia 12 months earlier requiring Caesarean delivery at 29 weeks, followed by poorly controlled hypertension and proteinuria (>1 g/day). Over the preceding 6 months, she developed fatigue, headaches, severe hypertension, and facial/pedal edema. She denied fever, neurologic symptoms, or diarrheal prodrome. Exam showed pallor, hydration, and blood pressure 151/103 mmHg. Labs revealed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, marked renal dysfunction, elevated reticulocytes, schistocytes, heavy proteinuria (4.9 g/24h), microscopic hematuria, elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, and negative Coombs test; liver enzymes, immunologic tests, viral screening, and antiphospholipid antibodies were normal.

A thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulated complement activation, producing small-vessel thrombosis, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and predominantly renal injury. Pregnancy can trigger disease, and cutaneous vascular involvement can occur. This is the leading consideration.
symptoms_in_common: Severe renal dysfunction with heavy proteinuria and microscopic hematuria
Coombs-negative microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, elevated LDH and bilirubin, and low haptoglobin
History of pregnancy-associated disease followed by persistent renal abnormalities
Ankle ulceration and apparent dermal small-vessel thrombosis in the supplied images
symptoms_not_in_common: The prolonged course is less typical of an abrupt acute presentation, although chronic or recurrent disease is possible

data.description: Severe hypertension can injure small-vessel endothelium, causing renal failure, red-cell fragmentation, and platelet consumption. It can resemble or coexist with complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy.
symptoms_in_common: History of severe, poorly controlled hypertension
Marked renal dysfunction, proteinuria, and microscopic hematuria
symptoms_not_in_common: The recorded blood pressure of 151/103 mmHg is below the range usually associated with hypertensive emergency, although earlier pressures may have been higher
Cutaneous ulceration with apparent microvascular thrombosis is not a usual presenting feature
Severe thrombocytopenia is less typical than relatively modest platelet reduction

data.description: A thrombotic microangiopathy usually caused by autoantibodies producing severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. It causes platelet-rich microvascular thrombosis and requires urgent evaluation when suspected.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH, reticulocytes, and bilirubin with low haptoglobin
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked renal failure and heavy proteinuria are less typical than in hemolytic uremic syndrome
The prolonged renal-predominant course is atypical
No neurologic abnormalities or fever were reported, although their absence does not exclude this diagnosis
Severe persistent hypertension is not a defining feature

data.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome with renal thrombotic microangiopathy
data.description: An autoimmune thrombophilia that can cause pregnancy complications, renal small-vessel thrombosis, hypertension, and ischemic skin ulcers. The negative antiphospholipid testing substantially weakens this possibility.
symptoms_in_common: Severe preeclampsia requiring delivery before 34 weeks
Ulcerative ankle lesion with apparent dermal vascular thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative antiphospholipid antibodies do not support standard diagnostic criteria
No documented large-vessel thrombosis
Prominent ongoing hemolysis is less typical of uncomplicated antiphospholipid nephropathy

data.description: An infection-associated thrombotic microangiopathy, usually following Shiga toxin-producing bacterial gastroenteritis, characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: No diarrheal prodrome
Progression over months rather than an acute postinfectious illness
Persistent hypertension and proteinuria following pregnancy
Cutaneous ulceration and dermal vascular thrombosis are uncommon manifestations

data.diagnosis: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy)
data.description: Thrombotic microangiopathy caused by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, often triggered by pregnancy; causes microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and renal failure, and can rarely involve the skin with ulcerating lesions due to dermal microvascular thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: Renal failure with heavy proteinuria and microscopic hematuria
Coombs-negative microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes
Elevated LDH and bilirubin, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocytes
Negative immunologic, viral and antiphospholipid tests
Ulcerated ankle skin lesions with dermal small-vessel thrombi on biopsy, later healing
symptoms_not_in_common: Subacute/chronic course over 6-12 months
Nephrotic-range proteinuria is less common
Skin involvement is rare

data.description: Thrombotic microangiopathy due to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency (acquired autoantibody or congenital), causing platelet-rich microthrombi, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and organ ischemia, especially neurologic.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, negative Coombs
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked renal failure (usually mild in TTP)
Heavy proteinuria
Absence of fever and neurologic symptoms
Prolonged course over months
Ulcerating skin lesions

data.description: Severe hypertension causing endothelial injury with fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, leading to microangiopathic hemolysis and progressive renal failure.
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure of 151/103 mmHg at presentation is not in the malignant range
Severe anemia and thrombocytopenia are disproportionate
Nephrotic-range proteinuria
Thrombotic skin ulcers
No reported retinopathy or encephalopathy

data.description: Pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder with endothelial dysfunction; HELLP involves hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets, normally resolving within days to weeks after delivery.
symptoms_in_common: History of preeclampsia with preterm Caesarean delivery
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistence and worsening 12 months postpartum
Normal liver enzymes
Severe renal failure
Skin ulcers with microvascular thrombi

data.diagnosis: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome / lupus nephritis-associated thrombotic microangiopathy
data.description: Autoimmune disorders causing small-vessel thrombosis and/or immune-complex glomerulonephritis, associated with pregnancy morbidity, renal disease, cytopenias and skin ulcers or livedo.
symptoms_in_common: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with hematuria and renal failure
Thrombotic skin ulcers around the ankle
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative antiphospholipid antibodies
Normal immunologic tests
Negative Coombs test
No arthritis, rash, serositis or fever
No large-vessel thrombosis

data.description: A 14-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain for 2 days, accompanied by non-bilious vomiting. Physical examination revealed pallor, diffuse abdominal tenderness with guarding, and sluggish bowel sounds but no rigidity. Her recent history included two episodes of multiple oral ulcers that had resolved spontaneously. Laboratory findings showed hemoglobin 88 g/L, total leucocyte count 3.6 × 10⁹/L, platelets 96 × 10⁹/L, and ESR 54 mm/h. Urinalysis was normal, and blood and urine cultures were sterile. Initial ANA testing by indirect immunofluorescence with HEp-2 cell substrate was negative. Subsequent repeat ANA testing at a different laboratory remained negative, but dsDNA and anti-Ro antibodies were strongly positive with low concentrations of C3 and C4. Echocardiography showed a mild pericardial effusion.

data.diagnosis: ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus enteritis
data.description: The leading possibility is systemic lupus with inflammatory or vasculitic bowel involvement. CT appears to show bowel-wall thickening with layered enhancement, compatible with lupus enteritis. Persistently negative ANA is unusual but does not completely exclude lupus; the strongly positive anti-dsDNA result warrants assay confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and diffuse tenderness
Bowel-wall thickening with a target-like appearance on CT
Strongly positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro antibodies
symptoms_not_in_common: Repeatedly negative ANA testing is atypical for systemic lupus

data.description: Autoimmune impairment of intestinal smooth muscle or its innervation can cause bowel dilation and obstruction-like symptoms without a mechanical blockage. Associated urinary tract dysmotility can produce hydroureteronephrosis; the CT appears to show bilateral collecting-system dilation.
symptoms_in_common: Dilated bowel loops on abdominal imaging
Apparent bilateral renal collecting-system dilation on CT
Oral ulcers, cytopenias, hypocomplementemia, and lupus-associated antibodies
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked layered bowel-wall thickening favors concomitant enteritis rather than isolated dysmotility
Repeatedly negative ANA is atypical for the underlying lupus association

data.description: A systemic inflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent oral ulcers and sometimes intestinal ulceration, which can cause severe abdominal pain or perforation. Only two reported episodes of oral ulcers provide limited support.
symptoms_not_in_common: Strongly positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro antibodies
Low C3 and C4 concentrations
Combined anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia
Pericardial effusion is an uncommon manifestation
Apparent bilateral renal collecting-system dilation

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can present during adolescence with abdominal pain, oral ulcers, anemia, and bowel inflammation. A severe flare or intestinal narrowing may cause vomiting and obstructive symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia before any treatment
Strongly positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro antibodies
Low C3 and C4 concentrations
Pericardial effusion is uncommon
Apparent bilateral renal collecting-system dilation

data.description: A small-vessel vasculitis that can cause bowel-wall edema, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and occasionally intussusception. Abdominal symptoms may precede the characteristic purpuric rash, although the overall findings here favor lupus.
symptoms_not_in_common: Recurrent oral ulcers
Thrombocytopenia and leukopenia
Strongly positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro antibodies
Low C3 and C4 concentrations
Pericardial effusion
Apparent bilateral renal collecting-system dilation

data.diagnosis: ANA-negative systemic lupus erythematosus with lupus enteritis (mesenteric vasculitis)
data.description: Multisystem autoimmune disease; lupus enteritis is an immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitis of the bowel causing wall edema with target sign on CT, often accompanied by ureterohydronephrosis and serositis. Rarely ANA by immunofluorescence is negative, especially with isolated anti-Ro or prozone effects.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse tenderness with guarding and sluggish bowel sounds
Dilated bowel loops on abdominal radiograph
Bowel wall thickening with target sign on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative ANA on repeated testing
Normal urinalysis
No rash or arthritis reported

data.description: Variable-vessel vasculitis characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions and possible gastrointestinal ulceration, typically ileocecal.
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro
Low C3 and C4
Pancytopenia
Bilateral hydroureteronephrosis
No genital ulcers, uveitis or skin lesions
Diffuse rather than ileocecal bowel involvement

data.description: Chronic transmural inflammatory bowel disease that may affect any part of the gut, with aphthous oral ulcers, abdominal pain, anemia and raised inflammatory markers.
symptoms_in_common: Hydronephrosis can occur from ureteral compression (usually unilateral)
symptoms_not_in_common: Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia (thrombocytosis expected)
Positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro
Low complement
Pericardial effusion
Bilateral hydroureteronephrosis
No chronic diarrhea or weight loss reported
Acute 2-day onset

data.description: Childhood IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis causing palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain with bowel wall edema or intussusception, and nephritis.
symptoms_in_common: Severe colicky abdominal pain with vomiting
Bowel wall edema with target appearance on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No palpable purpura
No arthralgia
Thrombocytopenia and leukopenia (platelets normal or high expected)
Low C3 and C4
Positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro
Oral ulcers
Pericardial effusion
Normal urinalysis

data.diagnosis: Infectious enterocolitis (including intestinal tuberculosis or bacterial enteritis)
data.description: Infection of the bowel causing inflammation, wall thickening, pain, vomiting and sometimes ileus; tuberculosis may also cause serositis and cytopenias.
symptoms_in_common: Bowel wall thickening and dilated loops
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever or diarrhea reported
Sterile cultures
Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia
Positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Ro
Low complement
Recurrent oral ulcers
Bilateral hydroureteronephrosis

data.description: 45-year-old woman presented with syncope and severe anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL) with lower GI bleeding. A diagnostic colonoscopy was negative. CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3.2 x 3 x 2.9 cm contrast-enhancing right lower-quadrant mass arising from the wall of the ileum. No evidence of metastatic disease. Subsequent laparotomy found a 3.5 cm mass that was resected with negative margins. Molecular studies showed a 42-base pair deletion in exon 11 of the KIT gene (V559_D572del) that would delete all or part of codons 558 to 572 and would change the 558-encoding amino acid from Lys to Asn (K558N).

data.diagnosis: Ileal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), KIT exon 11-mutant
data.description: A mesenchymal gastrointestinal tumor associated with activating KIT or PDGFRA mutations. This is overwhelmingly the most likely diagnosis given the ileal wall mass and KIT exon 11 deletion; the illustrated spindle-to-epithelioid morphology is also compatible.
symptoms_in_common: Severe anemia with hemoglobin of 6 g/dL
Syncope attributable to severe blood loss
Contrast-enhancing mass arising from the ileal wall
Negative colonoscopy despite a small-bowel bleeding source
KIT exon 11 deletion involving the juxtamembrane region

data.diagnosis: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the ileum

data.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma to the small bowel

data.description: 18-year-old male with 4 days of fatigue, subjective fever/chills, headache, non-bloody non-bilious vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, low back pain, dysuria, and fever with lower abdominal, groin, and scrotal pain. Past history: exercise-induced asthma and childhood hospitalization for diarrhea. Born in Central America, moved to the US at age 15. Recent testing was negative for TB (IGRA), HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, and chlamydia. On exam, he appeared tired, febrile to 39.4°C, tachycardic, tachypneic, and had tenderness of the low back paraspinal muscles.

A potentially life-threatening syndrome of excessive immune activation, often triggered by infection or malignancy. The marrow images appear to show histiocytes engulfing blood cells, which supports consideration of HLH but is not diagnostic without laboratory and clinical criteria.

Apparent hemophagocytosis in the supplied marrow images

data.description: A bacterial infection of the iliopsoas muscles that may progress to abscess formation and sepsis. symptoms_in_common: Low back pain and muscle tenderness
Apparent iliopsoas-region inflammatory changes on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Diarrhea
Dysuria
Headache

data.description: A systemic bacterial zoonosis usually acquired through unpasteurized dairy products or animal exposure. data.description: A systemic fungal infection that can involve the gastrointestinal tract and bone marrow and occasionally trigger HLH. symptoms_not_in_common: Dysuria
Scrotal pain

data.description: An acute bacterial infection of the prostate that can cause fever, urinary symptoms, pelvic pain, and systemic illness. It could explain much of the urinary and genital presentation, but would not readily explain the apparent iliopsoas abnormalities or marrow findings.
symptoms_not_in_common: Diarrhea
Focal paraspinal muscle tenderness
Apparent iliopsoas-region inflammatory changes

data.diagnosis: Typhoid (enteric) fever due to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi with secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
data.description: Systemic infection by Salmonella Typhi/Paratyphi acquired by the fecal-oral route, causing sustained fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, mesenteric adenitis and ileocolitis; it can seed distant sites (psoas, epididymis, bone) and can trigger secondary hemophagocytosis in the bone marrow.
symptoms_in_common: Low back and paraspinal pain (possible psoas or iliacus involvement)
Groin and scrotal pain (possible focal seeding or epididymo-orchitis)

No documented recent travel after living in the US for 3 years
Short 4-day course (typhoid is often more insidious)

data.description: Life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome of uncontrolled macrophage and T-cell activation, usually triggered by infection, malignancy or autoimmune disease, with fever, cytopenias, high ferritin and hemophagocytosis in the marrow.

Strong histiocyte staining on immunohistochemistry (likely CD163 or CD68)

data.description: Zoonotic infection from unpasteurized dairy or animal exposure, common in Latin America, causing undulant fever, sacroiliitis or spondylitis, epididymo-orchitis and occasionally psoas abscess or hemophagocytosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent vomiting and diarrhea

data.description: A 73-year-old man presented with abdominal distention and maldigestion for 1 month. The patient had a medical history of diabetes and hypertension. On physical examination, an intraabdominal mass was palpated in the epigastric area, and the patient did not complain of pain and tenderness. Laboratory findings showed no abnormalities except an elevated fasting glucose level.

data.diagnosis: Gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), possibly epithelioid type
data.description: A mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract that can grow outward from the stomach into a large, heterogeneous mass with hemorrhage and necrosis. This is a leading consideration from the supplied images, but confirmation requires identification of the immunostains and expert pathology review.

Large heterogeneous upper-abdominal mass with hemorrhagic or necrotic areas

data.diagnosis: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the stomach, epithelioid type, KIT-negative (likely PDGFRA-mutant)

data.description: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1-week history of shortness of breath and sore throat. Her medical history included smoking, obesity, type 2 diabetes On examination, her oxygen saturation was 81% on room air, dropping to 71% with exertion. She was afebrile with a normal white blood cell count. Chest examination revealed soft heart sounds, decreased air entry, wheeze, and aegophony at the lung bases bilaterally. Abdominal examination was normal except for obesity.

data.diagnosis: Large pericardial cyst with compressive atelectasis

The rounded right cardiophrenic opacity and large, apparently fluid-density anterior lesion on CT favor this possibility; compression of nearby lung can cause breathlessness. The profound hypoxemia requires urgent clinical assessment.

Hypoxemia potentially aggravated by lung compression
Afebrile presentation with normal white blood cell count
symptoms_not_in_common: Sore throat

Profound hypoxemia is unusual for an uncomplicated pericardial cyst

data.description: A localized collection of fluid within the pericardial space that can resemble a cystic mass. A large collection can compress adjacent structures or impair cardiac filling; echocardiography would help assess this possibility.

Hypoxemia if there is significant cardiopulmonary compromise

Wheeze
Basal aegophony is not a direct manifestation of pericardial fluid

Basal aegophony if compression produces atelectasis
Afebrile presentation with normal white blood cell count if uninfected

Profound hypoxemia is uncommon without substantial compression or additional lung disease

Wheeze if there is airway compression

data.description: 30-year-old male with 6 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, and progressive symmetric large-joint polyarthritis involving knees, hips, and elbows, without small joint involvement. Examination showed fever (38.9°C), multiple tender dull red nodules on the forehead, left cheek, and sternum, a solitary firm 1×1 cm right cervical lymph node, and hepatomegaly (liver palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin). No relevant past history. Laboratory tests showed elevated CRP (131 mg/L) with normal blood count and ESR (6 mm/h); ANA, rheumatoid factor, ANCA, ASO, anti-DNase B, blood cultures, gonococcal and syphilis tests were negative. Serum calcium and ACE were normal.

data.diagnosis: Active tuberculosis with Poncet disease (tuberculosis-associated reactive polyarthritis)

The apparent upper-lung opacities and granulomatous histology with a broad necrotic-appearing area raise concern for tuberculosis, but tissue mycobacterial testing is needed for confirmation.

Tender red skin nodules potentially representing a tuberculosis-associated skin manifestation
Apparent upper-lung opacities and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation

Facial and sternal nodules are less typical than the lower-leg nodules of erythema nodosum

data.diagnosis: Systemic sarcoidosis with cutaneous involvement and sarcoid arthropathy

data.description: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis that can cause pulmonary lesions, systemic inflammation, arthritis, and skin abnormalities. data.description: 59-year-old man with multiple nodules on his joints. Laboratory findings showed elevated creatine (137 μmol/L; normal range 62–115 μmol/L) and uric acid (725 μmol/L; normal range 208–428 μmol/L).

Longstanding monosodium urate crystal deposition causing large tophi, destructive arthritis, and contractures. This is overwhelmingly the most likely diagnosis given the crystal-confirmed gout, marked hyperuricemia, and extensive nodular hand deformity in the photographs.

data.description: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. data.description: This is a 56-year-old woman who underwent radical nephrectomy and lymph-node resection for clear-cell renal-cell carcinoma in February 2012. Over days, there was an increase in bone exposure and necrosis without evidence of acute secondary infection.

Onset after coronary angiography and bypass surgery is not a typical association

data.description: Showering of cholesterol crystals from disrupted aortic atherosclerotic plaques after vascular instrumentation or surgery, occluding small arteries in skin, kidneys, brain and gut, with an inflammatory response.
symptoms_in_common: Recent coronary angiography and CABG (3 weeks prior)
Subacute acute kidney injury requiring dialysis
Altered mental status (cerebral emboli or uremia)
Elderly man with atherosclerotic disease (CAD, hypertension)
symptoms_not_in_common: 2+ proteinuria is somewhat more than the bland sediment usually seen
Palmar involvement is less common than lower extremity involvement

data.description: Infection of cardiac valves (risk increased by valvular disease and recent cardiac surgery) causing embolic phenomena, immune-complex glomerulonephritis and neurologic complications.
symptoms_in_common: Aortic stenosis as predisposing valvular lesion
Painful acral lesions on digits and palms (resembling Osler nodes/Janeway lesions)
Acute kidney injury with hematuria and proteinuria
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked eosinophilia
Normal white blood cell count
No fever reported
No new murmur or positive blood cultures described

data.diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) or other ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis
data.description: Systemic necrotizing small-to-medium vessel vasculitis with eosinophilia, affecting skin, kidneys and nerves, typically in patients with asthma and sinus disease.
symptoms_in_common: Acute kidney injury with hematuria and proteinuria (possible glomerulonephritis)
Purpuric/ischemic skin lesions of the extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of asthma, sinusitis or pulmonary infiltrates
Onset closely following vascular procedure
Digital ischemia with blue toes more than palpable purpura
Only mild urinary abnormalities rather than active nephritic sediment

data.diagnosis: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (allergic drug reaction)
data.description: Hypersensitivity reaction to medications (e.g., antibiotics, PPIs, NSAIDs started perioperatively) causing renal interstitial inflammation, often with rash, fever and eosinophilia.
symptoms_in_common: Recent hospitalization with likely new medications
Erythematous skin changes of the palms
symptoms_not_in_common: Painful dusky ischemic toes are not explained
Skin findings are acral and ischemic rather than a diffuse maculopapular rash
No fever reported
Altered mental status explained only indirectly by uremia

data.diagnosis: Contrast-induced nephropathy / postoperative acute tubular necrosis
data.description: Acute kidney injury from iodinated contrast toxicity or perioperative renal hypoperfusion, usually beginning within 1–3 days of the insult and often recovering within 1–2 weeks.
symptoms_in_common: Recent coronary angiography with contrast exposure
Recent cardiac surgery with possible hypoperfusion
Acute kidney injury with elevated BUN and creatinine
Altered mental status attributable to uremia
symptoms_not_in_common: Eosinophilia
Painful dusky discoloration of toes and palms
Delayed, progressive course 3 weeks after procedure
Hematuria and proteinuria rather than muddy brown casts

data.description: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

data.diagnosis: Delayed pharyngoesophageal perforation caused by cervical spinal hardware erosion
data.description: A late complication of cervical fixation in which hardware erodes into the hypopharynx or esophagus, allowing contamination of deep neck and mediastinal tissues. The supplied images appear to show exposed hardware and a defect communicating with a pus-containing cavity, making this the leading diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Fever and chills from secondary infection
Cervical metal plates implanted five years earlier
symptoms_not_in_common: Preexisting traumatic quadriplegia is not caused by the perforation

data.diagnosis: Retropharyngeal abscess with extension into the danger space
data.description: A deep neck infection behind the pharynx that can spread through fascial planes into the thorax. It may occur secondary to pharyngoesophageal injury or infected cervical hardware.
symptoms_not_in_common: Apparent exposed hardware and a pharyngoesophageal defect suggest an underlying perforation rather than an isolated retropharyngeal infection
Preexisting traumatic quadriplegia is not explained by this infection

data.diagnosis: Descending mediastinitis secondary to pharyngoesophageal perforation
data.description: A potentially life-threatening mediastinal infection caused by spread of contamination from the neck or esophagus. The apparent communication with a purulent mediastinal cavity and thoracic extension support this possibility.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia and odynophagia associated with the cervical source
Abscess extending into the thoracic region
Purulence in the cavity labeled mediastinum
symptoms_not_in_common: Preexisting traumatic quadriplegia is unrelated to mediastinitis

data.description: Infection involving implanted cervical fixation hardware, potentially associated with biofilm formation, adjacent tissue destruction, and paraspinal abscess. It can coexist with hardware erosion into the esophagus.
symptoms_in_common: Prior cervical stabilization with metal plates
symptoms_not_in_common: Dysphagia and odynophagia are less typical unless infection extends to the pharynx or esophagus
A pharyngoesophageal defect is not explained by implant infection alone
Preexisting traumatic quadriplegia does not establish infection-related neurologic injury

data.description: Infection of vertebral bone, sometimes involving adjacent discs, that can produce a paraspinal abscess. Prior instrumentation or contiguous spread from an esophageal perforation are possible sources; vertebral or disc involvement would need confirmation on imaging.
symptoms_not_in_common: Dysphagia and odynophagia are not typical unless there is associated prevertebral or pharyngoesophageal involvement
Apparent hardware exposure within the pharyngoesophageal lumen suggests an additional structural complication
The longstanding traumatic quadriplegia is not evidence of new neurologic injury from spinal infection

data.diagnosis: Pharyngoesophageal (hypopharyngeal) perforation due to cervical spine hardware erosion with paraspinal/mediastinal abscess
data.description: Delayed erosion of an anterior cervical fixation plate or screws through the posterior hypopharyngeal or esophageal wall, creating a fistula that seeds the retropharyngeal and prevertebral space and mediastinum with infection.
symptoms_in_common: History of cervical spine stabilization with metal plates
Metal hardware visible through the pharyngeal wall on endoscopy
Pus draining from the mediastinum near the upper esophageal sphincter
Large paraspinal abscess from C4 to T11
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation 5 years after surgery is unusually late, though delayed erosion is reported
No reported subcutaneous emphysema

data.diagnosis: Retropharyngeal abscess with descending necrotizing mediastinitis
data.description: Deep neck space infection, usually of oropharyngeal or odontogenic origin, that spreads down fascial planes into the mediastinum.
symptoms_in_common: Collection extending from the neck into the thorax
symptoms_not_in_common: No preceding dental or tonsillar infection reported
Exposed metal hardware in the pharyngeal wall points to a perforation source
Contrast extravasation indicates a luminal defect rather than a primary deep neck infection

data.diagnosis: Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis with paraspinal and epidural abscess (late hardware-associated infection)
data.description: Infection of the vertebral bodies and discs, often haematogenous (commonly Staphylococcus aureus) or implant-related, extending into the paraspinal soft tissues.
symptoms_in_common: Large paraspinal abscess spanning multiple vertebral levels
Presence of spinal hardware as a nidus
Quadriplegia as a risk factor (urinary sepsis, pressure ulcers as haematogenous sources)
symptoms_not_in_common: Dysphagia and odynophagia are not typical primary features
Exposed hardware in the pharyngeal lumen on endoscopy
Contrast leak from the pharynx/esophagus
No bone destruction described on imaging

data.diagnosis: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with cold paraspinal abscess
data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the spine that characteristically produces large multilevel paraspinal abscesses tracking beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament.
symptoms_in_common: Extensive multilevel paraspinal abscess (C4 to T11)
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute presentation with chills and odynophagia rather than an indolent course
No weight loss, night sweats or TB exposure reported
Exposed cervical hardware and pharyngeal perforation on endoscopy
Contrast leak on fluoroscopy
No vertebral destruction or kyphosis described

data.diagnosis: Esophageal perforation from another cause (foreign body, iatrogenic, or Boerhaave syndrome) with mediastinitis
data.description: Transmural esophageal tear from an ingested foreign body, instrumentation or forceful vomiting, leading to mediastinal contamination and abscess formation.
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of vomiting, foreign body ingestion or recent instrumentation
Defect is at the hypopharynx/upper esophageal sphincter with visible metal plate, whereas Boerhaave tears are typically in the distal esophagus
Abscess is predominantly paraspinal and tracks along the hardware
No chest pain or subcutaneous emphysema reported

data.description: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

A lymphatic malignancy characterized by Hodgkin and Reed–Sternberg cells. The bulky abdominal and thoracic lymphadenopathy, apparent liver lesion, and large atypical cells in an inflammatory background make this a leading possibility; confirmation requires the biopsy report and identified immunostains.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal pain and distension associated with bulky abdominal lymphadenopathy
Severe anemia with pallor and dizziness
Extensive metabolically active lymphadenopathy on the supplied imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent bloody stools and diarrhea are not usual presenting features
Marked longstanding short stature is not a typical direct manifestation
Shin ecchymoses are not typical without an associated bleeding or platelet abnormality

data.description: A group of lymphoid malignancies that can produce bulky abdominal masses, gastrointestinal involvement, and systemic symptoms in children. Tissue morphology, immunophenotyping, and molecular testing distinguish it from Hodgkin lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Bulky abdominal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy on imaging
Blood in stools if the gastrointestinal tract is involved
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked longstanding growth impairment is less typical of an aggressive lymphoma
The supplied biopsy appears to show scattered large atypical cells in a mixed inflammatory background rather than the uniform malignant population seen in many non-Hodgkin lymphomas
Headache and myalgias are nonspecific rather than characteristic manifestations

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, anemia, weight loss, and impaired childhood growth. The extensive bulky lymphadenopathy and supplied biopsy findings are less supportive than the gastrointestinal symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent periumbilical and lower abdominal pain
Occasional diarrhea and blood in stools
Fevers, fatigue, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers
symptoms_not_in_common: Extensive bulky thoracic and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy is atypical
An apparent focal liver lesion is not a usual uncomplicated manifestation
Large atypical cells in the supplied lymphoid biopsy are not characteristic
Shin ecchymoses are not a typical intestinal manifestation

data.description: Tuberculosis can involve abdominal lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract, causing prolonged fever, abdominal pain, anemia, and weight loss. Diagnosis requires compatible pathology and microbiologic testing; travel alone does not establish exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Occasional diarrhea or gastrointestinal bleeding with intestinal involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: The supplied biopsy does not clearly show the caseating granulomas expected in typical tissue tuberculosis
Scattered large atypical cells are more suggestive of a lymphoid malignancy
Shin ecchymoses are not a usual feature
Profound microcytic anemia is less typical unless substantial chronic inflammation or gastrointestinal blood loss is present

data.description: A systemic fungal infection that can affect lymph nodes, liver, bone marrow, and gastrointestinal tract. Caribbean travel provides a possible exposure context, but disseminated disease is less common in otherwise healthy children and requires fungal identification or antigen testing.
symptoms_in_common: Gastrointestinal bleeding if intestinal lesions are present
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked longstanding short stature is not a typical consequence of a recently acquired infection
Profound isolated microcytic anemia is less characteristic than broader blood-count abnormalities in disseminated infection
The supplied biopsy shows large atypical cells rather than clearly identifiable intracellular fungal organisms
Shin ecchymoses are not typical without associated thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy

diagnoses.name: Mixed-cellularity subtype of classic Hodgkin's lymphoma
diagnoses.title: Mixed cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma

data.diagnosis: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma (advanced stage, likely EBV-positive)
data.description: B-cell derived lymphoma characterized by Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells (CD30+, CD15+, weak PAX5, often EBV+) in an inflammatory background; presents with lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, and anemia of chronic inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: bulky mediastinal, retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy on CT
FDG-avid nodes above and below diaphragm with liver lesion
microcytic anemia with elevated ferritin (anemia of inflammation)
biopsy with large atypical Reed-Sternberg-like cells in mixed inflammatory background with CD30/CD15 positive staining
abdominal pain and distension from nodal mass
symptoms_not_in_common: blood in stools
diarrhea
predominantly abdominal presentation without palpable peripheral nodes
growth at 1st percentile
ecchymoses on shins

data.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (Burkitt lymphoma or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
data.description: Aggressive B-cell lymphomas of childhood that commonly present with rapidly growing abdominal masses, bowel involvement, and systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: bulky mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymph node masses
symptoms_not_in_common: histology showing scattered large cells in inflammatory background rather than sheets of monomorphic cells
CD30/CD15 positive pattern
relatively subacute 1-month course for Burkitt
prominent mediastinal involvement less typical for Burkitt

data.description: CD30-positive T-cell lymphoma, often ALK-positive in children, presenting with advanced-stage nodal and extranodal disease and prominent systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: generalized lymphadenopathy including mediastinum and abdomen
symptoms_not_in_common: CD15 positivity and PAX5 weak staining favor Hodgkin
no skin lesions
blood in stools
mixed inflammatory background with Reed-Sternberg-like morphology

data.description: Chronic transmural granulomatous inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract causing abdominal pain, diarrhea, bleeding, growth failure, and anemia.
symptoms_in_common: diarrhea with occasional blood in stools
symptoms_not_in_common: bulky mediastinal and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy
FDG-avid liver lesion
biopsy showing large atypical CD30-positive cells
elevated ferritin
headache and myalgias

data.diagnosis: Disseminated infection (abdominal tuberculosis or enteric/typhoid fever, travel-related)
data.description: Systemic infections acquired in endemic areas; tuberculosis causes necrotic lymphadenitis and bowel disease, typhoid causes prolonged fever with abdominal symptoms and mesenteric adenitis.
symptoms_not_in_common: onset 2 months after travel is late for typhoid
massive bulky non-necrotic lymphadenopathy
biopsy showing atypical large CD30-positive cells rather than caseating granulomas
no respiratory symptoms
ecchymoses

data.description: A 52-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with acute onset shortness of breath and confusion. On physical examination, he was agitated and taking deep breaths at a rate of 28/min. Initial venous blood gas on ambient air showed pH 7.02, partial pressure of carbon dioxide 3.4 kPa, and partial pressure of oxygen 4.1 kPa. Laboratory studies revealed blood glucose 7.1 mmol/L (reference range 4.4-6.1), lactic acid 6.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), serum anion gap 19 mmol/L (8-16), serum osmolality 318 mmol/kg (275-295), serum osmolal gap 20 mmol/kg (<10), and acute kidney injury with creatinine 141 μmol/L (70-120). Blood ethanol was undetectable and urine drug screen was negative. Urinalysis showed haematuria and no ketones.

The most likely diagnosis: toxic alcohol ingestion produces acidic metabolites and calcium oxalate deposition in the kidneys. The urine microscopy appears to show elongated calcium oxalate monohydrate crystals, supporting this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Deep, rapid breathing due to severe metabolic acidosis
Severe acidemia with an elevated anion gap
Elevated serum osmolality and osmolal gap
Urinary crystals consistent with calcium oxalate
Elevated measured lactate, which may reflect true elevation or assay interference by toxic metabolites

data.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion causing formate accumulation, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, neurological dysfunction, and often visual injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: Calcium oxalate-like urinary crystals are not characteristic
Haematuria and acute kidney injury are less characteristic than in ethylene glycol poisoning

data.description: Toxic alcohol exposure that can cause metabolic acidosis, acute kidney injury, and neurological impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Severe metabolic acidosis with deep, rapid breathing
symptoms_not_in_common: Calcium oxalate-like urinary crystals are not characteristic
Haematuria is less characteristic

data.description: Accumulation of a solvent used in some medications or other products, producing hyperosmolality, lactic acidosis, and sometimes renal or neurological dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated osmolal gap and serum osmolality
symptoms_not_in_common: Calcium oxalate-like urinary crystals are not characteristic
Haematuria is not a typical defining feature

data.description: Severe infection can cause tissue hypoperfusion, elevated lactate, metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy, and acute kidney injury; however, it explains the toxic-alcohol pattern less well.
symptoms_not_in_common: An elevated osmolal gap is not a typical defining finding
Calcium oxalate-like urinary crystals are not characteristic
Haematuria is not a typical defining feature

data.description: Ingestion of antifreeze or similar products; ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acid, causing severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis, raised osmolal gap, calcium oxalate crystalluria and acute kidney injury. Glycolate can cause a falsely elevated lactate on some analysers.
symptoms_in_common: Severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.02) with low pCO2
Raised osmolal gap (20 mmol/kg) and serum osmolality
Needle/dumbbell-shaped crystals on urine microscopy consistent with calcium oxalate monohydrate
Undetectable ethanol, negative drug screen, no ketones
symptoms_not_in_common: No ingestion history given
Mild hyperglycaemia is nonspecific

data.description: Toxic alcohol ingestion (e.g. windscreen washer fluid, adulterated spirits) metabolised to formic acid, causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis, raised osmolal gap, visual disturbance and CNS depression.
symptoms_in_common: Severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Undetectable ethanol and negative drug screen
symptoms_not_in_common: Urinary crystals (calcium oxalate) are not a feature
Haematuria
Acute kidney injury is less typical
No visual symptoms reported

data.diagnosis: Lactic acidosis (type A/B, e.g. sepsis, hypoperfusion or metformin-associated)
data.description: Accumulation of lactate from tissue hypoperfusion, sepsis, or drugs/toxins, producing high anion gap metabolic acidosis; can be accompanied by acute kidney injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: Raised osmolal gap of 20 is not explained
Urinary crystals
Haematuria
Acidosis (pH 7.02) is more severe than expected for this lactate level
No reported hypotension, infection or metformin use

data.description: Insulin deficiency causing ketone production, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, dehydration and altered mental state; the euglycaemic form occurs with SGLT2 inhibitors.
symptoms_in_common: Modestly raised osmolal gap can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: No ketones on urinalysis
Glucose only 7.1 mmol/L
Urinary crystals
Haematuria
No history of diabetes or SGLT2 inhibitor use reported

data.description: High anion gap metabolic acidosis in chronic alcohol users after a binge followed by starvation and vomiting; ethanol is often undetectable at presentation and osmolal gap and lactate may be mildly elevated.
symptoms_not_in_common: No ketones on urinalysis (though beta-hydroxybutyrate can be missed by dipstick)
Urinary crystals
Haematuria
Acidosis this severe and marked confusion are unusual
No alcohol history, vomiting or abdominal pain reported

data.description: A 79-year-old man with a history of hypertension, stroke, and glaucoma was brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive by a caregiver. He was cold to the touch with vital signs showing blood pressure of 85/55 mm Hg, heart rate of 36/min, respiratory rate of 14/min, and pulse oximetry of 100% on ambient air. Multiple temperature measurements, including core temperature assessment via rectal method, did not yield a detectable temperature. Physical examination revealed clear bilateral chest auscultation. Chest radiographs and computed tomography of the head were negative for any acute pathology.

A critically low core temperature can depress consciousness, circulation, and cardiac conduction. The ECG appears to show prominent J-point elevations (Osborn waves), strongly supporting hypothermia in this clinical setting. A low-reading core thermometer is needed to confirm the temperature.
symptoms_in_common: Temperature below the measurement range of the available thermometers
Apparent Osborn waves on the ECG

data.description: Life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism that can cause profound hypothermia, altered consciousness, bradycardia, and hypotension. Thyroid hormone testing is required, and classic external signs of hypothyroidism may be absent.
symptoms_not_in_common: Preserved respiratory rate and oxygen saturation are less typical of advanced cases with hypoventilation

data.description: Excessive beta-adrenergic blockade can cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, and impaired consciousness. Medication review should include oral antihypertensives and ophthalmic timolol, which can be systemically absorbed; exposure is not established here.
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound apparent hypothermia is not a characteristic primary finding
Osborn waves are not typical unless hypothermia is also present

data.description: Severe infection in an older adult may present with hypothermia rather than fever, along with hypotension and altered consciousness. Normal chest imaging does not exclude an infection elsewhere.
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound bradycardia is less typical than tachycardia
Osborn waves are not a direct feature of sepsis, although secondary hypothermia can produce them

data.description: A critically low blood glucose level can cause coma and impaired thermoregulation. Immediate bedside glucose measurement is needed to evaluate this reversible cause of unresponsiveness.
symptoms_in_common: Cold body temperature consistent with impaired thermoregulation
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked bradycardia is less typical than an adrenergic response with tachycardia
Profound hypotension is not a usual isolated manifestation
Osborn waves suggest associated hypothermia rather than hypoglycemia itself

data.description: Core body temperature below 28-30°C from cold exposure, common in elderly patients with impaired thermoregulation or immobility; causes bradycardia, hypotension, depressed consciousness and characteristic Osborn (J) waves on ECG.
symptoms_in_common: Osborn (J) waves at the QRS-ST junction on ECG (arrowhead in V3)
Baseline artifact on ECG possibly from shivering
Elderly with prior stroke (risk factor for immobility and impaired thermoregulation)
Normal head CT and chest radiograph
symptoms_not_in_common: No explicit history of cold exposure provided
Respiratory rate of 14/min is relatively preserved for severe hypothermia

data.description: Life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism, typically in elderly patients, causing hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation and altered mental status.
symptoms_not_in_common: No known history of thyroid disease
No described myxedematous features (facial puffiness, macroglossia, non-pitting edema)
Normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation without hypoventilation
No pleural or pericardial effusion on chest imaging
Prominent Osborn waves are more typical of primary hypothermia than of low-voltage hypothyroid ECG

data.description: Dysregulated host response to infection; elderly patients may present with hypothermia rather than fever, along with hypotension and altered mentation.
symptoms_in_common: Hypothermia (can occur in elderly septic patients)
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound bradycardia rather than tachycardia
Normal respiratory rate rather than tachypnea
Clear chest and normal chest radiograph with no evident infectious source
Temperature so low as to be unmeasurable is atypical for sepsis
Osborn waves not explained by sepsis alone

data.diagnosis: Beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity (including systemic absorption of ophthalmic beta-blocker for glaucoma)
data.description: Excess of AV nodal or negative chronotropic agents causes bradycardia, hypotension and depressed consciousness; elderly patients on antihypertensives or timolol eye drops are at risk.
symptoms_in_common: History of hypertension and glaucoma (likely exposure to these drugs)
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound, unmeasurable hypothermia is not explained by drug toxicity alone
Osborn waves are not typical
No documented overdose or medication list
No high-grade AV block clearly described

data.description: Acute cortisol deficiency causing refractory hypotension, altered mental status, hypoglycemia and sometimes hypothermia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Bradycardia rather than the usual tachycardia
No history of steroid use or known adrenal disease
No reported hyperpigmentation, vomiting or abdominal pain
No electrolyte or glucose abnormalities reported
Osborn waves and unmeasurable core temperature are not typical

data.description: 12-year-old Saudi boy presented with severe spontaneous dental pain for 3 days. He was the fourth of five siblings. Parents were not related. His mother had 5 previous spontaneous abortions in first trimester. Mother took acetazolamide 1000mg/day for idiopathic intracranial hypertension before and throughout pregnancy. Patient was born at full term via spontaneous vaginal delivery, weighing 2,270g (below 5th percentile). He presented without major dysmorphic features, was intelligent with good behavior, and had normal skin, hair and nails. Intraoral exam showed mixed dentition with retained primary lower central incisors, hypocalcified permanent upper incisors, and multiple carious teeth. Tongue, floor of mouth, upper lip, hard and soft palate were normal.

A possible exposure-related developmental disorder involving congenital limb and dental abnormalities. Prenatal acetazolamide exposure has been reported in association with such findings, but causation in humans is not established.
symptoms_in_common: Maternal acetazolamide use at 1000 mg/day before and throughout pregnancy
Congenital reduction or absence of digits in both hands and feet, apparent in the photographs
Apparent absence of multiple permanent teeth on the panoramic radiograph
Low birth weight at full term
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe acute spontaneous dental pain is more directly attributable to caries or pulpal inflammation than to prenatal exposure
Hypocalcified incisors are nonspecific and do not establish an exposure-related diagnosis

data.description: A usually TP63-related developmental syndrome combining split-hand/split-foot malformations, ectodermal abnormalities, and variably present cleft lip or palate.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral hand and foot digit abnormalities compatible with ectrodactyly
