symptoms_not_in_common: Normal skin, hair, and nails argue against prominent ectodermal dysplasia
Normal upper lip and palate, without clefting
Severe dental pain is not a defining syndrome feature and is likely secondary to caries

data.description: A genetically heterogeneous congenital limb malformation characterized by missing or underdeveloped central digits, sometimes producing cleft hands and feet, without a broader syndromic phenotype.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent reduction of central digits in both hands and feet
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple apparently absent permanent teeth suggest abnormalities beyond an isolated limb disorder
Hypocalcified permanent incisors
Retained primary lower incisors
Low birth weight is not a characteristic feature

data.description: An inherited disorder of ectodermal development that typically causes missing or abnormally shaped teeth, sparse hair, and reduced sweating.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent absence of multiple permanent teeth
Retained primary teeth associated with absent permanent successors
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal hair and skin
Normal nails, although nail abnormalities are not obligatory
Marked congenital digit reduction is not characteristic
Low birth weight is not a defining feature

data.diagnosis: Symptomatic irreversible pulpitis secondary to dental caries
data.description: Persistent inflammation of the dental pulp, commonly caused by deep caries, that can produce severe spontaneous pain. This could explain the presenting complaint but not the congenital limb and dental-development abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Severe spontaneous dental pain lasting three days
Hypocalcified enamel, which may increase susceptibility to dental breakdown
symptoms_not_in_common: Congenital hand and foot digit abnormalities
Apparent absence of multiple permanent teeth
Retained primary lower central incisors
Low birth weight

data.diagnosis: Acetazolamide embryopathy (prenatal carbonic anhydrase inhibitor teratogenicity)
data.description: Teratogenic syndrome from in-utero exposure to acetazolamide, associated in animal models and case reports with distal limb reduction defects (ectrodactyly, oligodactyly, syndactyly), growth restriction and dental anomalies including missing teeth.
symptoms_in_common: Maternal acetazolamide 1000 mg/day before and throughout pregnancy
Hand anomalies on photograph with missing digits/cleft-like (ectrodactyly, oligodactyly) appearance
Foot anomalies on photograph with missing, fused or malformed toes
Multiple congenitally missing permanent teeth (oligodontia) on panoramic radiograph
Low birth weight at term (2,270 g, below 5th percentile)
Non-consanguineous parents and no affected siblings reported
symptoms_not_in_common: Mother's 5 first-trimester spontaneous abortions that may suggest an alternative genetic or chromosomal cause
Enamel hypocalcification of upper incisors is not well documented
Severe spontaneous dental pain and multiple caries are nonspecific

data.description: Autosomal dominant TP63 disorder characterised by split hand/foot malformation, ectodermal dysplasia (sparse hair, dystrophic nails, dry skin, hypodontia, enamel defects) and cleft lip/palate, with variable expressivity.
symptoms_in_common: Split hand/foot-type limb anomalies of hands and feet
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal skin, hair and nails
Normal lip and hard and soft palate (no cleft)
No lacrimal duct or genitourinary anomalies reported
No family history of similar findings
Maternal acetazolamide exposure offers an alternative explanation
Low birth weight is not typical

data.description: Genetically heterogeneous congenital limb malformation with median clefts of the hands and feet, absent central rays and syndactyly, usually autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance; typically no other system involved.
symptoms_in_common: Hand anomalies with missing digits/cleft-like appearance
Foot anomalies with missing or fused toes
symptoms_not_in_common: Oligodontia with multiple missing permanent teeth
Hypocalcified upper incisors
Low birth weight
No family history
Maternal acetazolamide exposure during pregnancy

data.diagnosis: Limb-mammary syndrome / ADULT syndrome (TP63-related disorders without clefting)
data.description: Allelic TP63 conditions featuring split hand/foot or other limb anomalies, hypodontia and early loss of permanent teeth, mammary gland/nipple hypoplasia and lacrimal duct obstruction, with milder skin and hair involvement than EEC and often no cleft lip.
symptoms_not_in_common: No nipple or mammary hypoplasia reported
No lacrimal duct obstruction reported
Normal nails and no excessive freckling
No family history
Low birth weight
Maternal acetazolamide exposure

data.description: X-linked dominant ciliopathy (OFD1) with oral anomalies (lobulated tongue, hamartomas, accessory frenula, cleft palate, missing teeth), facial dysmorphism and digital anomalies (brachydactyly, syndactyly, clinodactyly, polydactyly); usually lethal in males, which can produce recurrent male miscarriages.
symptoms_in_common: Digital anomalies of hands and feet
symptoms_not_in_common: Patient is a surviving male
Normal tongue, floor of mouth, upper lip and palate
No major facial dysmorphic features
Normal intelligence
Split/reduction-type limb defects rather than brachydactyly or polydactyly
No renal cystic disease reported
Normal hair and skin (no milia or alopecia)

data.description:
47-year-old man with hypertension presented with 3 days of left periorbital swelling, throat tightness, hoarseness, and dysphagia to solids. He denied pain, pruritus, visual symptoms, headache, dyspnea, wheezing, fever, or recent illness. Exam showed left periorbital edema with faint erythema, mildly enlarged tongue, hoarse muffled voice, and no stridor or extraocular movement deficits; vital signs were stable.

Two weeks later, he developed worsening dysphonia, increased throat swelling sensation, nasal regurgitation of liquids, shoulder and hip pain, difficulty jumping, neck muscle tenderness, edema of both upper arms, preserved arm strength, reduced hip strength, and difficulty rising from a seated position. Labs showed markedly elevated CK and transaminases, mild ESR/CRP elevation, normal TSH, positive ANA, and negative myositis-specific antibodies. Muscle biopsy from the left deltoid showed mild fiber size variability, perivascular inflammatory infiltrate, and patchy MHC class I expression on nonnecrotic fibers.

An autoimmune inflammatory muscle disease with characteristic skin changes; the edematous variant can cause substantial facial, limb, and oropharyngeal swelling. This is the leading possibility, although the biopsy is not definitive.
symptoms_in_common: Periorbital edema with erythematous-to-violaceous eyelid discoloration in the photographs
Proximal hip weakness and difficulty rising from a chair or jumping
Shoulder, hip, and neck muscle pain
MRI-demonstrated facial, tongue, palatal, and pharyngeal muscle edema
Positive ANA and perivascular inflammation with muscle-fiber MHC class I expression
symptoms_not_in_common: Initially unilateral rather than bilateral periorbital swelling
Preserved arm strength despite upper-arm swelling
No reported Gottron papules or other characteristic body rash

data.description: An inflammatory myopathy causing proximal muscle weakness and elevated muscle enzymes, sometimes with pharyngeal involvement. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the reported biopsy does not demonstrate its classic endomysial pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty rising from a seated position
symptoms_not_in_common: Periorbital erythema and edema
Prominent tongue and subcutaneous swelling
Bilateral upper-arm edema with preserved arm strength
Perivascular rather than classic endomysial inflammation on biopsy

data.description: An autoimmune myopathy associated with severe proximal weakness and very high CK levels. Some cases lack recognized myositis antibodies, but muscle biopsy typically shows prominent necrosis and regeneration.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty rising from a chair and jumping
Muscle pain and MRI-demonstrated muscle edema
Negative myositis-specific antibodies, which can occur in seronegative disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Periorbital erythema and swelling
Prominent facial, tongue, and upper-arm edema
Preserved arm strength
Biopsy showing perivascular inflammation without reported prominent myofiber necrosis

data.description: Nonallergic swelling of deep tissues, potentially associated with ACE-inhibitor use or C1-inhibitor deficiency. It can threaten the airway but does not adequately explain the subsequent inflammatory myopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of wheezing or other typical allergic symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive proximal hip weakness
Shoulder, hip, and neck muscle pain
Markedly elevated CK
Diffuse muscle edema on MRI
Inflammatory muscle-biopsy abnormalities
Nasal regurgitation suggesting pharyngeal muscle dysfunction

data.description: A connective-tissue disease that can cause inflammatory muscle injury and occasionally facial or generalized edema. ANA positivity supports consideration, but additional lupus-specific clinical and laboratory findings would be required.
symptoms_not_in_common: Isolated unilateral periorbital swelling as the initial manifestation
Prominent tongue and pharyngeal muscle edema
Bilateral upper-arm edema without documented renal disease
No reported systemic lupus features such as oral ulcers, photosensitivity, or characteristic multisystem involvement

data.description: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with complement-mediated microangiopathy affecting muscle and skin, causing proximal weakness, dysphagia, periorbital (heliotrope-like) edema and sometimes marked subcutaneous and muscle edema; capillary staining (e.g., membrane attack complex deposition) and perivascular inflammation on biopsy are characteristic.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia, dysphonia and nasal regurgitation from pharyngeal/palatal muscle involvement
Proximal hip-girdle weakness (difficulty rising from seat, jumping)
Shoulder and hip myalgia, neck muscle tenderness
MRI showing muscle and subcutaneous edema of head and neck
Biopsy with perivascular inflammation, MHC class I expression and capillary staining
symptoms_not_in_common: Unilateral rather than bilateral periorbital involvement
Negative myositis-specific antibodies
No Gottron papules or other classic rash
Tongue enlargement
Preserved arm strength
No perifascicular atrophy described

data.diagnosis: Polymyositis / overlap myositis associated with connective tissue disease
data.description: Immune-mediated inflammatory myopathy, often overlapping with lupus, scleroderma or mixed connective tissue disease, causing subacute proximal weakness with elevated CK and ANA positivity.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute proximal weakness of the hips
MHC class I upregulation on nonnecrotic fibers
symptoms_not_in_common: Periorbital edema and erythema
Prominent subcutaneous and limb edema
Tongue enlargement
Perivascular rather than endomysial inflammation with fiber invasion
No arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon or other connective tissue disease features

data.description: Autoimmune myopathy (anti-SRP, anti-HMGCR or seronegative) with severe proximal weakness, very high CK, and prominent dysphagia; biopsy shows fiber necrosis with scant inflammation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Periorbital edema and erythema
Subcutaneous edema of arms and neck
Tongue enlargement
Biopsy lacks prominent necrosis and shows perivascular inflammation
No statin exposure reported

data.description: Parasitic infection from undercooked meat (Trichinella) in which larvae encyst in striated muscle, causing periorbital edema, myalgia, weakness, elevated CK and eosinophilia.
symptoms_in_common: Dysphagia and hoarseness from involvement of tongue, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No preceding gastrointestinal illness or exposure history
No eosinophilia reported
Unilateral periorbital edema
No larvae on muscle biopsy
Positive ANA

data.diagnosis: Angioedema (ACE inhibitor-induced or hereditary/acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency)
data.description: Bradykinin-mediated episodic, non-pruritic swelling of the face, tongue, and upper airway, common in hypertensive patients taking ACE inhibitors.
symptoms_in_common: History of hypertension (possible ACE inhibitor use)
symptoms_not_in_common: Persistence and progression over weeks
Proximal muscle weakness
Markedly elevated CK and transaminases
Nasal regurgitation
Muscle edema on MRI
Inflammatory muscle biopsy
Positive ANA

data.description: 24-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with 2 days of left leg pain and swelling after training for a 5-km race. Pain was crampy, extending to the left lower abdomen and buttock, with exertional dyspnea. She denied fever, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or trauma. Examination showed tachycardia (102 bpm), pitting edema, erythema, and increased warmth of the left leg from thigh to calf. History included oral contraceptive use since age 15, prior smoking, and family history of DVT in her father after surgery. Labs showed mild leukocytosis; coagulation studies and cardiac markers were normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis
data.description: Thrombosis of the deep veins draining the thigh and pelvis. The pelvic CT appears to show an enlarged, poorly opacified left iliac vein, concerning for thrombus. Normal routine coagulation studies do not exclude DVT. This requires urgent evaluation and treatment.
symptoms_in_common: Acute unilateral leg pain and swelling
Pitting edema involving the thigh and calf
Pain extending into the lower abdomen and buttock, consistent with proximal venous involvement
Oral contraceptive use and family history of DVT increase suspicion
symptoms_not_in_common: Exertional dyspnea is not explained by isolated DVT and raises concern for associated pulmonary embolism

data.description: Blood clots obstructing pulmonary arteries, usually originating in deep leg or pelvic veins. The chest CT appears to demonstrate bilateral pulmonary arterial filling defects at the arrows, strongly supporting pulmonary embolism. This is an urgent condition even without chest pain or dyspnea at rest.
symptoms_in_common: Concurrent unilateral leg swelling and pain suggesting a venous clot source
symptoms_not_in_common: Leg erythema, warmth, and pitting edema are not direct manifestations of pulmonary embolism but fit associated DVT
Lower abdominal and buttock pain are not typical direct manifestations

data.diagnosis: May-Thurner syndrome with secondary left iliac vein thrombosis
data.description: Compression of the left common iliac vein by the crossing right common iliac artery, predisposing to left-sided iliofemoral DVT, particularly in young women. The clinical pattern is suggestive, but the supplied pelvic image alone does not establish the characteristic compression.
symptoms_in_common: Pain involving the leg, buttock, and lower abdomen
Pitting edema consistent with impaired proximal venous drainage
Acute painful, warm, erythematous leg when complicated by thrombosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Exertional dyspnea and tachycardia are not typical of uncomplicated venous compression and suggest associated pulmonary embolism

data.description: A bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues that can produce unilateral painful redness and swelling. It is a less likely alternative because the imaging appears to support venous thromboembolism.
symptoms_not_in_common: Exertional dyspnea
Pain extending into the lower abdomen and buttock
Extensive thigh-to-calf pitting edema is less characteristic than localized inflammatory swelling

data.description: Overstretching or tearing of muscle fibers during training can cause acute pain and localized swelling. This is substantially less likely given the diffuse venous-pattern edema and apparent thromboembolic imaging findings.
symptoms_not_in_common: Diffuse pitting edema from thigh to calf
Extensive erythema and warmth
Exertional dyspnea
Tachycardia
Lower abdominal pain

data.diagnosis: May-Thurner syndrome (iliac vein compression syndrome) with iliofemoral DVT and pulmonary embolism
data.description: Anatomic compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery against the lumbar spine, predisposing to extensive left-sided iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, often in young women with additional risk factors such as oral contraceptives.
symptoms_in_common: Left-sided leg pain and swelling from thigh to calf
Pain extending to left lower abdomen and buttock (suggesting iliac vein involvement)
CT showing filling defects in pulmonary arteries bilaterally
Pelvic CT showing abnormality at the left common iliac vein
Oral contraceptive use as a trigger
symptoms_not_in_common: Family history of DVT (suggests a possible additional inherited component)
Mild leukocytosis is nonspecific
No prior chronic left leg swelling or venous insufficiency

data.diagnosis: Oral contraceptive-associated (provoked) deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism
data.description: Venous thromboembolism provoked by estrogen-containing contraceptives, which increase clotting factor levels and reduce natural anticoagulants; risk is further increased by smoking.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral leg pain, swelling, erythema, warmth, pitting edema
Pulmonary artery filling defects on CT
Normal cardiac markers consistent with non-massive PE
symptoms_not_in_common: Risk is highest in the first year of use, whereas she has used it for about 9 years
Extensive proximal iliofemoral thrombosis with abdominal and buttock pain suggests an underlying anatomic cause
Pelvic CT finding at the iliac vein is not explained by contraceptive use alone

data.diagnosis: Inherited thrombophilia (e.g., Factor V Leiden or prothrombin G20210A mutation) with venous thromboembolism
data.description: Genetic hypercoagulable states that increase the risk of venous thrombosis, especially at a young age and when combined with estrogen exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Family history of DVT in father
Normal routine coagulation studies (do not exclude thrombophilia)
symptoms_not_in_common: Father's DVT was provoked by surgery, weakening the hereditary link
No prior personal thrombotic events despite 9 years of contraceptive use
Strict left-sided iliofemoral location with pelvic imaging abnormality points to an anatomic cause
Erythema and leukocytosis are nonspecific

data.description: Acquired autoimmune hypercoagulable disorder with antiphospholipid antibodies causing venous and/or arterial thromboses and pregnancy morbidity, typically affecting young women.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal coagulation studies (aPTT often prolonged with lupus anticoagulant)
No history of autoimmune disease, pregnancy loss, livedo or arterial thrombosis
No thrombocytopenia reported
Other clear provoking factors are present
Family history of provoked DVT is not relevant to this acquired disorder

data.description: Acute bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue causing a red, warm, swollen, painful limb, often with fever and leukocytosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No skin break, trauma or portal of entry
Crampy pain extending to the lower abdomen and buttock
Exertional dyspnea
Pulmonary artery filling defects on chest CT
Pelvic venous abnormality on CT
Diffuse thigh-to-calf pitting edema is more typical of venous obstruction

data.description: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. Several hours after intravenous urography was performed with iodinated contrast material, generalized pustular eruptions developed, with multiple coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae observed on the trunk, arms, and legs. Laboratory studies revealed neutrophilia and mild eosinophilia with 55% neutrophils and 8% eosinophils, and a white-cell count of 6500 per cubic millimeter. Histopathological examination of the lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. Microbiologic studies were negative.

A rare inflammatory skin reaction to iodine-containing agents, including iodinated contrast, that can produce sterile pustules, vegetating plaques, and bullae. This is the leading consideration given the exposure and biopsy findings.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt eruption several hours after iodinated contrast administration
Generalized pustules with coalescing vesicles and pus-filled bullae
Prominent facial and auricular lesions in the photographs
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and a diffuse neutrophilic dermal infiltrate
symptoms_not_in_common: Hematuria preceding contrast exposure is not a typical manifestation and may represent a separate condition

data.description: An acute, usually medication-induced eruption of numerous sterile, nonfollicular pustules; iodinated contrast can be a trigger.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid onset after exposure to iodinated contrast
Widespread pustular eruption involving the trunk and extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Large coalescing pus-filled bullae and prominent vegetating facial lesions are less typical than small superficial pustules
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and full-thickness epidermal necrosis are not characteristic biopsy findings
Hematuria preceding the eruption is not typical

data.description: A variant of acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis that produces inflammatory plaques with vesicles or bullae and sterile dermal neutrophilic infiltration.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt onset of widespread inflammatory skin lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly pus-filled, coalescing lesions with pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia are less typical
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis is not a characteristic finding
Mild eosinophilia is less characteristic than neutrophilia
Hematuria is not a usual manifestation

data.description: A potentially severe inflammatory disorder causing widespread sterile pustules on erythematous skin, sometimes triggered by medications.
symptoms_in_common: Generalized pustules on the trunk and extremities
Coalescence of pustules into larger collections of pus
symptoms_not_in_common: Immediate temporal association with iodinated contrast is less characteristic
Prominent vesicles and bullae are less typical
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis and diffuse dermal neutrophilic infiltration do not represent the usual psoriatic biopsy pattern
Mild eosinophilia and preceding hematuria are not typical

data.description: A severe, usually medication-associated skin reaction characterized by widespread epidermal death, blistering, and detachment, often with mucosal involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Recent exposure to a potential medication trigger
symptoms_not_in_common: A predominantly pustular eruption with pus-filled bullae is atypical
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and a dense neutrophilic dermal infiltrate favor another diagnosis
Onset within several hours is less typical without prior sensitization
Hematuria preceding the contrast exposure is not characteristic

data.description: Rare neutrophilic skin reaction to iodine-containing compounds, often in patients with impaired renal clearance, producing acneiform pustules, vegetating plaques, and pus-filled bullae, particularly on the face and other seborrheic areas, hours to days after exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Onset several hours after iodinated contrast material
Vegetating pustular lesions on face and ear seen in images
Hematuria suggesting possible underlying urinary tract or renal disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal total white-cell count (leukocytosis is sometimes seen)
No documented renal failure, which is the usual predisposing factor

data.description: Acute drug-induced eruption of numerous small, nonfollicular sterile pustules on an erythematous, edematous base, usually with fever and neutrophilia, appearing within hours to days of drug exposure, including contrast media.
symptoms_in_common: Involvement of trunk, arms, and legs
symptoms_not_in_common: Large pus-filled bullae and vegetating plaques rather than pinhead pustules
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis
Normal white-cell count without marked neutrophilia
No fever reported
Hematuria

data.diagnosis: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis), bullous or pustular variant
data.description: Neutrophilic dermatosis with abrupt onset of tender erythematous plaques, nodules, or pseudovesicular or pustular lesions, typically with fever and neutrophilia; may be drug-induced or associated with malignancy or infection.
symptoms_in_common: Pustular and bullous lesions on face and limbs
Hematuria could reflect an underlying malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis
Normal white-cell count
No fever reported
Eosinophilia
Onset within hours of contrast exposure

data.description: Chronic vegetating pustular disorders with exuberant plaques studded with pustules, showing pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and neutrophilic or eosinophilic abscesses; associated with inflammatory bowel disease (pyoderma vegetans) or autoimmune acantholysis (pemphigus vegetans).
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset within hours of contrast administration
Generalized distribution rather than intertriginous predominance
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis
No acantholysis reported
No history of inflammatory bowel disease
Hematuria

data.description: Severe psoriasis variant with sudden widespread sterile pustules on erythematous skin, often coalescing into lakes of pus, accompanied by fever and leukocytosis; may be triggered by drugs or steroid withdrawal.
symptoms_not_in_common: Large bullae and vegetating lesions
Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia
Full-thickness epidermal necrosis
Eosinophilia
No history of psoriasis
Normal white-cell count and no fever reported
Hematuria
Onset within hours of iodinated contrast

data.description: 65-year-old Haitian man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve, ascending and aortic-root aneurysm, prior secondary syphilis treated with penicillin, positive tuberculin skin test 13 years earlier with negative chest radiograph, and recent HTLV-1 positivity. He had 12 kg unintentional weight loss over 2 years and presented with a leg injury and diffuse pruritic rash. Examination showed bilateral wrinkled axillary plaques, multiple thin brown macules and patches with collarette of scale on the palms and some soles, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data.diagnosis: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with cutaneous involvement
data.description: An HTLV-1-associated mature T-cell malignancy that can cause pruritic skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, and weight loss. This is a leading consideration, but confirmation requires immunophenotyping, blood evaluation, and HTLV-1-related molecular testing.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse pruritic rash with macules, patches, and plaques
HTLV-1 positivity and origin from an endemic region
Biopsy images show epidermotropic lymphocytes with prominent intraepidermal collections, compatible with a cutaneous T-cell malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Palmoplantar lesions with collarette scale are not a characteristic presentation
Bicuspid aortic valve and aortic aneurysms are not typical manifestations
End-stage renal disease requiring hemodialysis is not a defining feature

data.diagnosis: Mycosis fungoides, possibly with a granulomatous slack skin phenotype
data.description: A cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterized by persistent patches and plaques and epidermotropic malignant lymphocytes. A rare granulomatous slack skin variant causes loose, wrinkled skin in flexural areas, although its characteristic granulomatous histology is not established by these images.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic diffuse pruritic patches and plaques
Inguinal lymphadenopathy and weight loss, which can occur with advanced disease
Epidermotropic lymphocytes and Pautrier-like intraepidermal collections in the biopsy images
symptoms_not_in_common: HTLV-1 positivity favors consideration of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma rather than conventional mycosis fungoides
Palmoplantar collarette scale is not a classic presentation
Aortic aneurysms and dialysis-dependent renal disease are not characteristic manifestations

data.description: A leukemic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma typically characterized by widespread erythroderma, severe itching, lymphadenopathy, and circulating malignant T cells. Blood studies are required to establish this diagnosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Discrete brown macules and thin plaques rather than documented generalized erythroderma
Wrinkled axillary plaques are not a defining feature
Palmoplantar collarette scale is not characteristic
HTLV-1 positivity more specifically raises concern for adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma

data.diagnosis: Secondary syphilis due to reinfection or treatment failure
data.description: Disseminated infection with Treponema pallidum can cause a generalized rash involving the palms and soles and lymphadenopathy. Previous treatment does not exclude reinfection, but the biopsy appearance is more suggestive of a lymphoproliferative disorder.
symptoms_in_common: Brown macules and patches on the palms and soles
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent pruritus is less typical of secondary syphilis
Wrinkled axillary plaques are not characteristic
Prominent intraepidermal lymphocyte collections are not the usual histologic pattern
HTLV-1 positivity is not explained by syphilis

data.diagnosis: Scabies, including an atypical or crusted presentation
data.description: A contagious infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei causing intense itching and lesions in areas such as the wrists, axillae, and groin. HTLV-1 infection can predispose to severe or atypical infestation.
symptoms_in_common: Wrist and extremity lesions visible in the clinical photographs
HTLV-1 positivity, a risk factor for severe scabies
symptoms_not_in_common: Substantial weight loss over two years is not typical of uncomplicated scabies
Wrinkled axillary plaques and thin brown patches with collarette scale are not characteristic
The biopsy images show lymphocytic epidermotropism rather than identifiable mites, eggs, or burrows
Inguinal lymphadenopathy is not a primary defining feature

data.description: Mature CD4+ CD25+ T-cell neoplasm caused by HTLV-1, endemic in the Caribbean, often with skin involvement showing epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes and Pautrier-like microabscesses, lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: diffuse pruritic scaly papules and plaques
biopsy with large intraepidermal collections of atypical lymphocytes (Pautrier-like microabscesses)
immunostains showing a T-cell infiltrate with one strongly positive marker pattern compatible with CD4+/CD25+ cells and loss of other markers
chronic course compatible with smoldering or chronic subtype
symptoms_not_in_common: palmoplantar macules with collarette of scale are more typical of secondary syphilis
wrinkled axillary plaques are unusual
no reported hypercalcemia, lymphocytosis or hepatosplenomegaly

data.description: Most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, an indolent epidermotropic CD4+ T-cell proliferation presenting with patches, plaques and sometimes lymphadenopathy; a granulomatous slack skin variant causes lax folds in the axillae and groin.
symptoms_in_common: chronic pruritic scaly patches and plaques
epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes with Pautrier microabscesses on biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: HTLV-1 positivity points toward adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma instead
marked weight loss is uncommon in early disease
palmoplantar collarette-scaled macules are atypical

data.description: Disseminated stage of Treponema pallidum infection with generalized papulosquamous rash that classically involves palms and soles, lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: brown macules with collarette of scale on palms and soles
aortic root and ascending aortic aneurysm could reflect syphilitic aortitis
symptoms_not_in_common: rash is usually not markedly pruritic
previously treated with penicillin
2-year course is too long
biopsy shows intraepidermal atypical lymphocyte collections rather than a plasma cell-rich lichenoid or psoriasiform infiltrate
aneurysm is also explained by bicuspid aortic valve

data.description: Hyperinfestation with Sarcoptes scabiei in immunocompromised hosts, strongly associated with HTLV-1 infection and seen in dialysis patients, producing widespread hyperkeratotic scaly plaques.
symptoms_in_common: involvement of axillae, palms and soles
symptoms_not_in_common: weight loss not explained
biopsy shows no mites and instead shows atypical lymphocyte microabscesses
no burrows or thick crusts described

data.diagnosis: HTLV-1-associated infective dermatitis / chronic eczematous dermatitis (including uremic pruritus)
data.description: Chronic relapsing eczematous eruption linked to HTLV-1 infection, or chronic eczema and pruritus related to renal failure, affecting flexures with scaling and reactive (dermatopathic) lymphadenopathy.
symptoms_in_common: end-stage renal disease predisposes to pruritus and xerosis
symptoms_not_in_common: infective dermatitis mainly affects children and the scalp, ears and face
12 kg weight loss
palmoplantar macules
histology with atypical lymphocytes and Pautrier-like microabscesses rather than spongiosis

data.description: 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension and prior laminectomy, never smoker, with family history of prostate cancer in his father. Presented for evaluation; PSA and digital rectal examination were normal. Urine dipstick showed trace blood, with otherwise negative findings.

Noncancerous enlargement of the prostate, common in older men, that can occasionally cause urinary bleeding. Trace blood on dipstick alone does not confirm microscopic hematuria; urine microscopy is needed.
symptoms_in_common: Trace blood on urine dipstick, which could reflect prostatic bleeding
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal digital rectal examination, which provides no evidence of prostate enlargement

data.description: Stones in the kidneys, ureters, or bladder can irritate the urinary tract and cause blood in the urine, sometimes without pain.
symptoms_in_common: Otherwise negative urine dipstick, which can occur with uncomplicated stones

data.description: Cancer of the bladder lining can present with painless urinary bleeding. It is an important consideration in an older man if microscopic hematuria is confirmed, although this finding alone does not establish cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Trace blood on urine dipstick, potentially representing urinary bleeding

data.description: A malignancy arising in the kidney that may be asymptomatic or cause blood in the urine. Isolated trace dipstick blood is nonspecific and does not establish this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Trace blood on urine dipstick, potentially representing urinary bleeding

data.description: Disorders of the kidney's filtering units, such as IgA nephropathy, can cause microscopic hematuria and may be associated with hypertension.
symptoms_not_in_common: Otherwise negative urine dipstick, with no detected protein; proteinuria often accompanies clinically significant glomerular disease

data.description: Malignant tumor of the renal parenchyma, often found incidentally or through microscopic hematuria in older men; hypertension is a recognized risk factor.
symptoms_not_in_common: Never smoker (smoking is a major risk factor)
No flank pain or palpable mass reported
No weight loss or constitutional symptoms reported
Only trace rather than gross hematuria

data.description: Malignancy of the urothelial lining of the bladder or upper urinary tract, classically presenting with painless microscopic or gross hematuria in older men.
symptoms_not_in_common: Never smoker (smoking is the dominant risk factor)
No gross hematuria
No irritative voiding symptoms reported
No occupational chemical exposure reported

data.description: Non-malignant enlargement of the prostate, common in older men; friable prostatic vessels can cause microscopic hematuria.
symptoms_in_common: Normal PSA is compatible with benign disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal digital rectal examination (no enlargement noted)
No lower urinary tract symptoms reported (hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia)

data.description: Adenocarcinoma of the prostate, often asymptomatic in early stages; risk increases with age and with a first-degree relative affected.
symptoms_in_common: Family history of prostate cancer in father
Trace blood on urine dipstick (uncommon, but possible)
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal PSA
Normal digital rectal examination
No obstructive urinary symptoms or bone pain reported

data.description: Calculi within the kidney or urinary tract that may be clinically silent and cause isolated microscopic hematuria through mucosal irritation.
symptoms_in_common: Otherwise negative urinalysis (no signs of infection)
History of hypertension (associated with stone disease)
symptoms_not_in_common: No flank or colicky pain reported
No history of prior stones reported
No dysuria, nausea or vomiting reported

data.description: 66-year-old man with a 2-day history of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. Past history: hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; started azathioprine 75 mg 10 days earlier. On exam, temperature 38°C with bilateral tender knees and patellar tap. Labs showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated CRP and ESR, mildly elevated rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP, ANA/ENA, dsDNA, and ASO. Renal function and urinalysis were normal; chest radiograph was normal. Synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

An idiosyncratic reaction that commonly develops within the first few weeks of azathioprine treatment, causing fever, rash, arthralgias, and systemic inflammation. This is the leading possibility given the medication timeline.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms beginning approximately 8 days after starting azathioprine
Neutrophilic leukocytosis and elevated CRP and ESR
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral knee effusions with noninflammatory synovial fluid are not a defining feature

data.description: An acute neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by fever and tender red papules, nodules, or plaques. Azathioprine can trigger it; skin biopsy is needed to establish the characteristic neutrophilic infiltrate.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous plaques or nodules suggested by the photographs
Recent initiation of a potential triggering medication
symptoms_not_in_common: Noninflammatory knee effusions are not a characteristic diagnostic feature

data.description: An inflammatory panniculitis causing tender red subcutaneous nodules, usually on the shins, sometimes triggered by medications, infections, or systemic inflammatory disease.
symptoms_in_common: Painful red nodular-appearing lesions on the lower extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Apparent upper-extremity involvement is less typical than predominantly pretibial lesions
Broad plaque-like lesions are less characteristic than discrete subcutaneous nodules

data.description: A medication-associated inflammatory reaction producing fever, rash, and joint pain, typically within one to three weeks of exposure. Unlike classic serum sickness, renal involvement is generally absent.
symptoms_not_in_common: Painful nodular or plaque-like lesions are less typical than an itchy urticarial or morbilliform eruption
Prominent neutrophilic leukocytosis is less characteristic than in a neutrophilic dermatosis

data.description: Inflammation of small dermal blood vessels, sometimes triggered by medication, typically causing palpable purpura on dependent areas. Skin biopsy can distinguish it from other drug-related eruptions.
symptoms_in_common: Recent exposure to a new medication
symptoms_not_in_common: The photographed lesions appear more plaque-like or nodular than classic palpable purpura
Bilateral knee effusions with noninflammatory synovial fluid are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Azathioprine hypersensitivity syndrome (drug-induced Sweet-like neutrophilic dermatosis)
data.description: Idiosyncratic, dose-independent reaction typically occurring within 1-4 weeks of starting azathioprine, with fever, malaise, arthralgias, neutrophilia and tender erythematous papules/plaques or nodules that often resemble Sweet syndrome or erythema nodosum; resolves on drug withdrawal.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous papules and plaques on the limbs
symptoms_not_in_common: Mildly elevated rheumatoid factor (nonspecific)
No gastrointestinal symptoms, hypotension or liver/renal dysfunction, which often accompany the reaction

data.diagnosis: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, idiopathic or associated with autoimmune disease)
data.description: Neutrophilic dermatosis with abrupt onset of tender erythematous plaques or nodules, fever, neutrophilia and raised inflammatory markers; may be idiopathic, drug-induced, or associated with malignancy, infection or autoimmune disease.
symptoms_in_common: Abrupt painful erythematous plaques and papules
symptoms_not_in_common: Close temporal link to a new drug suggests a drug-induced rather than idiopathic form
No preceding upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection reported
No evidence of haematological malignancy
Face, neck and upper trunk involvement not described

data.description: Septal panniculitis presenting as tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules, classically on the shins, often with fever and arthralgia; triggered by infections (especially streptococcal), sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease or drugs.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous lesions on the lower limbs
Recent new medication as a possible trigger
symptoms_not_in_common: Lesions around the knee and on the arm rather than classic pretibial nodules
Papules and plaques rather than deep nodules
Negative ASO
Normal chest radiograph (no sarcoidosis)
Marked neutrophilia is less typical

data.diagnosis: Septic arthritis or disseminated infection (e.g. bacteraemia, disseminated gonococcal infection) in an immunosuppressed diabetic patient
data.description: Bacterial infection of joints or bloodstream, with higher risk in poorly controlled diabetes and immunosuppression; can cause fever, polyarthralgia or arthritis and skin lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Risk factors: poorly controlled diabetes and recent immunosuppression
symptoms_not_in_common: Noninflammatory synovial fluid
No bacteria on synovial fluid analysis
Bilateral symmetric joint involvement
Rash morphology is not pustular or typical of cellulitis
Onset timed to starting azathioprine

data.diagnosis: Small-vessel (leukocytoclastic/hypersensitivity) vasculitis or serum sickness-like drug reaction
data.description: Immune complex-mediated reaction, often triggered by drugs or infection, causing fever, arthralgias and a rash (palpable purpura or urticarial lesions) 1-2 weeks after exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Onset 10 days after a new drug
symptoms_not_in_common: Rash is painful erythematous plaques and papules rather than palpable purpura or urticaria
Normal urinalysis and renal function
Prominent neutrophilia rather than eosinophilia or low complement picture
Negative ANA/ENA

data.description: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. He performed poorly in the right hand alternating movement test. Physical examination revealed a blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg and heart rate of 116 beats per minute. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. Laboratory findings showed normal troponin T, creatine kinase (CK), and CK-myoglobin (CK-MB) levels, but elevated N-terminal-pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) levels at 3277 pg/ml. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Electrocardiography revealed sinus tachycardia without evidence of ischemia.

data.diagnosis: Group A streptococcal infective endocarditis of the mitral valve
data.description: The leading diagnosis: bacterial infection of the mitral valve causing vegetation, valve dysfunction, and possible systemic septic emboli. The echocardiographic valve-associated mass and positive blood culture strongly support this possibility.
symptoms_in_common: Blood culture positive for group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus
Neutrophilia and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Echocardiographic mass suspicious for mitral valve vegetation
Acute focal neurological deficits suggesting an embolic complication
Respiratory distress and elevated NT-pro-BNP suggesting associated heart failure

data.diagnosis: Cerebral septic embolism with ischemic stroke
data.description: An infected cardiac vegetation can embolize to a cerebral artery and cause acute neurological deficits. The focal brain imaging abnormality may represent embolic injury, although the supplied image alone cannot establish infarction or exclude an infectious lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Impaired rapid alternating movements of the right hand
Suspected cardiac vegetation providing an embolic source
Concurrent bacteremia and fever supporting a potentially septic embolus
symptoms_not_in_common: Loud apical systolic murmur is not explained by the cerebral lesion itself
Displaced apex beat is not a typical direct stroke finding
Markedly elevated NT-pro-BNP and respiratory distress suggest additional cardiac disease

data.diagnosis: Severe mitral regurgitation secondary to infective endocarditis
data.description: Infection can damage mitral valve leaflets or supporting structures, allowing blood to flow backward into the left atrium. The murmur and color Doppler findings suggest substantial regurgitation, but formal echocardiographic measurements are needed to establish severity.
symptoms_in_common: Grade 4/6 systolic murmur maximal at the apex
Color Doppler appearance suggestive of mitral regurgitation
symptoms_not_in_common: Fever and positive blood cultures indicate an infectious cause rather than isolated valve regurgitation
Acute dysarthria and right-hand coordination impairment require an associated neurological complication
Focal brain lesion is not a direct manifestation of regurgitation

data.diagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure due to valvular dysfunction
data.description: Mitral valve dysfunction can elevate pulmonary venous pressure and cause acute respiratory distress. The elevated NT-pro-BNP and cardiac examination support heart failure as a possible complication of the underlying infection.
symptoms_in_common: Prominent apical systolic murmur suggesting a valvular cause
symptoms_not_in_common: Group A streptococcal bacteremia is not explained by heart failure alone
Fever and elevated inflammatory markers suggest an underlying infection
Acute focal neurological deficits and the brain lesion require a separate embolic or infectious explanation
A valve-associated mass is not typical of uncomplicated heart failure

data.diagnosis: Splenic abscess secondary to septic embolization
data.description: Septic emboli from left-sided endocarditis can infect the spleen and form abscesses. The abdominal ultrasound shows hypoechoic lesions that could represent abscesses, although their organ location and nature require confirmation with a complete imaging study.
symptoms_in_common: Neutrophilia and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Suspected left-sided cardiac vegetation capable of systemic embolization
Hypoechoic abdominal lesions potentially compatible with abscesses
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute dysarthria and impaired right-hand coordination are not explained by a splenic abscess
Loud apical systolic murmur and displaced apex beat indicate associated cardiac disease
Respiratory distress and elevated NT-pro-BNP are not typical direct manifestations

data.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (group A streptococcus) of the mitral valve with septic embolization
data.description: Bacterial infection of the cardiac valve endocardium forming vegetations that destroy the valve, cause regurgitation and heart failure, and embolize to the brain and visceral organs (embolic stroke, splenic/hepatic abscesses or infarcts).
symptoms_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus
Echogenic mass (vegetation) on valve on transesophageal echo
Severe regurgitant jet on color Doppler
Acute dysarthria and right-hand dysdiadochokinesia with acute cerebral infarct on MRI
Hypoechoic visceral lesions on abdominal ultrasound consistent with septic emboli/abscesses
Elevated NT-pro-BNP, respiratory distress, displaced apex beat (heart failure)
symptoms_not_in_common: Group A streptococcus is an uncommon causative organism
No known predisposing valve disease, IV drug use or prosthetic valve
No described peripheral stigmata (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages)

data.description: Autoimmune inflammatory sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis causing pancarditis and valvulitis (commonly mitral regurgitation), arthritis, chorea, and elevated inflammatory markers.
symptoms_in_common: New apical systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation
Heart failure signs (elevated NT-pro-BNP, respiratory distress)
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 50 (typically children/adolescents)
Positive blood culture (rheumatic fever is non-bacteremic)
Large valvular mass on echo
Embolic cerebral infarct with dysarthria
Visceral hypoechoic lesions
No arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum or subcutaneous nodules

data.description: Benign primary cardiac tumor, usually in the left atrium, that can obstruct or damage the mitral valve, cause constitutional symptoms (fever, elevated ESR), and embolize systemically, causing stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Intracardiac echogenic mass near the mitral valve
Embolic stroke with dysarthria and limb incoordination
Heart failure symptoms and elevated NT-pro-BNP
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A streptococcus
Neutrophilia
Loud holosystolic regurgitant murmur with severe regurgitation (myxoma more often gives a diastolic murmur/tumor plop)
Abscess-like visceral lesions
Mass attached to valve leaflet rather than interatrial septum

data.description: Sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations on cardiac valves associated with malignancy, antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus, with a high tendency for systemic embolization and stroke.
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A streptococcus
Fever with neutrophilia
Severe valve destruction with loud regurgitant murmur and heart failure (usually small vegetations with little valve dysfunction)
No known malignancy or autoimmune disease

data.diagnosis: Streptococcal sepsis with primary visceral (hepatic/splenic) abscesses and coincident cardioembolic stroke from pre-existing degenerative mitral regurgitation
data.description: Invasive group A streptococcal bacteremia originating from a deep-seated abscess causing systemic sepsis, in a patient with underlying chronic mitral valve disease (e.g., prolapse or chordal rupture) predisposing to heart failure and stroke.
symptoms_in_common: Positive blood culture for group A streptococcus
Apical systolic murmur with displaced apex beat suggesting chronic mitral regurgitation
symptoms_not_in_common: Discrete echogenic valvular mass on TEE typical of vegetation
Acute embolic cerebral infarct best explained by septic embolus
Previously healthy with no known valve disease
Multiple visceral lesions favor embolic rather than primary source

data.description: 33-year-old bisexual Brazilian man with 4 months of painful bowel movements and rectal bleeding, with bright red blood on toilet paper and one daily stool. He denied abdominal pain and weight loss. He reported a sexual encounter with a man 6 weeks before initial presentation. Initial exam showed a tender external hemorrhoid and normal vital signs. Follow-up 10 weeks later noted bleeding hemorrhoids around the anus. Surgical examination found large superficial anal fissures at the anterior and posterior midline anal verge with small-to-moderate sentinel skin tags; digital rectal exam was moderately tender. Anoscopy showed fissures and small internal hemorrhoids. Flexible sigmoidoscopy showed mild-to-moderate inflammation of the distal 10 cm of rectum with edema and patchy erythema.

Rectal infection caused by Treponema pallidum. The biopsy shows prominent chronic inflammation, and the brown-stained slender organisms in panel D strongly suggest spirochetes. Confirmation requires the stain identification and syphilis serology.
symptoms_in_common: Painful bowel movements and rectal tenderness
Distal rectal edema and patchy erythema
Anal lesions that can resemble fissures
Sexual contact that could provide an exposure route, depending on the practices involved
Biopsy findings suggestive of spirochetal infection
symptoms_not_in_common: Anterior and posterior midline fissures with sentinel tags are more characteristic of chronic mechanical fissures
Coexisting hemorrhoids are not specifically explained by syphilis

data.description: Rectal infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis; lymphogranuloma venereum strains can produce particularly inflammatory or ulcerative proctitis.
symptoms_in_common: Inflammation confined to the distal rectum
Sexual contact that could provide an exposure route
symptoms_not_in_common: Midline fissures with sentinel tags are not a characteristic manifestation
One daily stool without reported diarrhea, discharge, or tenesmus is less typical of symptomatic lymphogranuloma venereum
The apparent spirochetes in panel D favor syphilis rather than chlamydial infection

data.description: An inflammatory bowel disease that can cause patchy intestinal inflammation and perianal fissures, skin tags, fistulas, or abscesses.
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain, diarrhea, or weight loss
Fissures confined to the anterior and posterior midline are more typical of mechanical fissures
Apparent tissue spirochetes are not explained by Crohn disease

data.description: A form of ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum, causing chronic mucosal inflammation and bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Inflammation involving the distal 10 cm of rectum
Inflammatory changes in the rectal biopsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Large anal fissures and sentinel tags are not characteristic primary findings
No reported urgency, tenesmus, or increased stool frequency
Patchy erythema is less typical than continuous inflammation in untreated disease
Apparent spirochetes in the biopsy favor an infectious cause

data.diagnosis: Chronic anal fissures with concomitant hemorrhoidal disease
data.description: Persistent tears in the anal lining cause pain during defecation and bright red bleeding; associated hemorrhoids can contribute additional bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Bright red blood on toilet paper
Tender external hemorrhoid and small internal hemorrhoids
Normal vital signs and absence of abdominal pain or weight loss
symptoms_not_in_common: Inflammation extending through the distal 10 cm of rectum is not explained by uncomplicated fissures or hemorrhoids
Prominent rectal mucosal inflammation and apparent tissue spirochetes suggest an additional process

data.description: Sexually transmitted infection of the rectum and anus caused by Treponema pallidum, producing anal ulcers or fissures and distal proctitis. Biopsy typically shows dense lymphoplasmacytic and histiocytic infiltrate with little crypt distortion, and spirochetes on immunohistochemistry.
symptoms_in_common: Man who has sex with men, with a recent sexual encounter with a man
Anal fissures at the anterior and posterior midline (possible chancres)
Distal proctitis limited to the last 10 cm with edema and patchy erythema
Biopsy showing dense plasma-cell-rich infiltrate with preserved crypt architecture
Immunostain showing numerous spiral organisms in the lamina propria
No abdominal pain or weight loss
symptoms_not_in_common: Primary chancres are classically painless
Symptoms began about 4 months ago, before the reported encounter 6 weeks prior to presentation
No rash, lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms reported
Hemorrhoids are not explained by syphilis

data.description: Invasive chlamydial infection causing proctitis or proctocolitis in men who have sex with men. It can closely mimic inflammatory bowel disease clinically and histologically, with a lymphohistiocytic and plasma cell infiltrate.
symptoms_in_common: Man who has sex with men, with a recent sexual encounter
symptoms_not_in_common: No mucopurulent discharge or tenesmus reported
No inguinal lymphadenopathy
No fever or systemic symptoms
Spirochetes on immunostain are not explained by chlamydia
One formed stool daily

data.description: Chronic idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease with patchy transmural inflammation that can involve the rectum and perianal area, causing fissures, skin tags and fistulas.
symptoms_in_common: Large anal fissures, including an atypical anterior one
Patchy erythema and edema of the rectum
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain
No weight loss
No diarrhea (one stool daily)
Midline fissures rather than the lateral or eccentric fissures typical of Crohn's
No granulomas or marked crypt architectural distortion
Spirochetes on immunostain
Recent sexual exposure points to infection

data.diagnosis: Ulcerative proctitis (ulcerative colitis limited to the rectum)
data.description: Idiopathic chronic mucosal inflammation confined to the rectum, presenting with rectal bleeding, urgency and tenesmus. Histology shows crypt distortion, basal plasmacytosis and crypt abscesses.
symptoms_in_common: Bright red rectal bleeding for months
Inflammation confined to the distal rectum
No abdominal pain or weight loss
symptoms_not_in_common: Patchy rather than continuous inflammation
Large anal fissures and skin tags are not typical
No urgency, tenesmus, diarrhea or mucus
Preserved crypt architecture
Spirochetes on immunostain
Marked anal pain

data.diagnosis: Gonococcal or herpes simplex virus proctitis
data.description: Common sexually transmitted causes of acute proctitis in men who have receptive anal intercourse. Gonorrhea causes mucopurulent proctitis; HSV causes very painful perianal and rectal ulcers.
symptoms_in_common: Man who has sex with men, with a recent sexual encounter
Distal proctitis with erythema and edema
symptoms_not_in_common: 4-month chronic course rather than an acute illness
No purulent discharge or tenesmus
No vesicles, fever, sacral paresthesias or urinary retention
No viral cytopathic changes or neutrophil-predominant inflammation on biopsy
Spirochetes on immunostain
Plasma-cell-rich infiltrate is not typical

data.description: 60-year-old woman with a 4-year history of progressively worsening gait and sensory disturbance with urinary urgency and nocturia. She also reported slowly progressive visual decline since age 50. Examination showed a spastic gait, increased lower-limb tone, sustained ankle clonus, brisk reflexes with flexor plantar responses, mild reduction in visual acuity, and dyschromatopsia, without visual field defect and with preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF showed oligoclonal bands. Blood tests, including folate and vitamin B12, were normal, and serum anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative. Family history was notable for a mother with blindness, Parkinson’s disease, and dementia.

data.diagnosis: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome
data.description: An inherited mitochondrial disorder causing progressive optic atrophy, sometimes accompanied by spastic paraplegia, peripheral neuropathy, ataxia, or other neurological manifestations. Genetic testing is needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive visual decline with dyschromatopsia
Bilateral optic disc pallor and retinal nerve fiber layer thinning on the supplied ocular images
Progressive spastic gait, increased lower-limb tone, brisk reflexes, and ankle clonus
Maternal history of blindness and neurological disease
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands are not a characteristic finding
Visual symptoms beginning at age 50 are later than the usual onset
Urinary urgency and nocturia are not defining features, although they may accompany spinal tract involvement

data.description: A demyelinating disease characterized by progressive neurological disability from onset, commonly involving spinal motor, sensory, and bladder pathways. Diagnosis requires appropriate MRI and clinical criteria; oligoclonal bands alone are insufficient.
symptoms_in_common: Four years of progressively worsening gait
Spasticity, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Optic atrophy and retinal nerve fiber layer thinning can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: A decade of slowly progressive visual decline without a reported optic neuritis attack is less typical
Maternal blindness with Parkinson’s disease and dementia suggests a possible inherited alternative
Preserved visual fields despite longstanding visual symptoms are less typical of substantial demyelinating optic neuropathy

data.diagnosis: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with an MS-like illness (Harding syndrome)
data.description: A mitochondrial optic neuropathy associated with central nervous system demyelination resembling multiple sclerosis, particularly in women. Mitochondrial DNA testing can distinguish it from other inherited optic neuropathies.
symptoms_in_common: Visual decline, dyschromatopsia, and bilateral optic atrophy
Progressive pyramidal signs and sensory disturbance
CSF oligoclonal bands can occur with the associated demyelinating illness
Maternal history of blindness is compatible with mitochondrial inheritance
symptoms_not_in_common: Visual loss progressing slowly over a decade rather than subacutely
Only mild reduction in visual acuity
No reported central or centrocecal visual field defect
Visual onset at age 50 is later than usual

data.diagnosis: Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia, including SPG7-related disease
data.description: A genetically heterogeneous group of disorders causing progressive lower-limb spasticity; complicated forms may also cause optic neuropathy, sensory abnormalities, and other neurological deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Increased lower-limb tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Optic atrophy with visual decline and dyschromatopsia
Family history suggesting inherited neurological disease
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands are not characteristic
The mother's blindness, Parkinson’s disease, and dementia do not establish a typical hereditary spastic paraplegia phenotype
Flexor plantar responses are less typical than extensor responses, although they do not exclude the diagnosis

data.description: An inflammatory disorder primarily causing optic neuritis and myelitis. A negative aquaporin-4 antibody test does not completely exclude it, but seronegative diagnosis requires stringent clinical and MRI criteria.
symptoms_in_common: Urinary urgency and nocturia consistent with spinal cord dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Slow continuous progression without distinct optic neuritis or myelitis attacks
Mild visual impairment with preserved visual fields rather than the often severe loss associated with attacks
CSF oligoclonal bands are less characteristic than in multiple sclerosis
Negative serum aquaporin-4 antibodies reduce support for this diagnosis
Maternal blindness and neurodegenerative disease suggest an inherited alternative

data.diagnosis: OPA1-related autosomal dominant optic atrophy plus with a multiple sclerosis-like disorder
data.description: Mitochondrial optic neuropathy caused by OPA1 mutations, producing slowly progressive bilateral visual loss with temporal disc pallor and dyschromatopsia. 'Plus' forms add spastic paraparesis, neuropathy, or an MS-like demyelinating illness, and families may show parkinsonism and dementia.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive bilateral visual decline since age 50
Dyschromatopsia with only mild reduction in visual acuity
Preserved pupillary light reflexes (typical of mitochondrial optic neuropathies)
Bilateral optic disc pallor with RNFL thinning on OCT
Progressive spastic gait with increased tone, clonus and brisk reflexes
CSF oligoclonal bands and white matter/spinal cord lesions described in OPA1 MS-like phenotype
Mother with blindness, Parkinson's disease and dementia (dominant inheritance, OPA1 linked to parkinsonism-dementia)
symptoms_not_in_common: Visual onset at age 50 is later than the usual childhood or early-adult onset
No visual field defect (central or centrocecal scotoma is usual)
Flexor plantar responses despite pyramidal signs
No reported hearing loss, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia often seen in plus forms

data.description: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system with gradual accumulation of disability from onset, most often presenting as a progressive spastic paraparesis in middle age.
symptoms_in_common: Increased lower-limb tone, sustained clonus and brisk reflexes
White matter and spinal cord lesions on MRI
Optic nerve involvement with dyschromatopsia and RNFL thinning
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset at around 56 years is late
Insidious, painless, symmetric visual decline over 10 years rather than acute optic neuritis
Preserved pupillary light reflexes with bilateral symmetric optic atrophy
Family history of blindness, Parkinson's disease and dementia
Flexor plantar responses

data.diagnosis: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with multiple sclerosis-like illness (Harding disease)
data.description: Maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA optic neuropathy which, particularly in women, may coexist with a demyelinating disorder indistinguishable from multiple sclerosis.
symptoms_in_common: Maternal history of blindness (compatible with maternal inheritance)
Spastic paraparesis, sensory and bladder symptoms
CSF oligoclonal bands and MS-like MRI lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Slow visual decline over a decade rather than subacute sequential severe loss
Only mild reduction in acuity (usually severe)
No visual field defect (dense central scotoma expected)
Onset at age 50 is late
Maternal Parkinson's disease and dementia are not typical

data.diagnosis: Complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy (e.g., SPG7)
data.description: Genetic degeneration of the corticospinal tracts causing slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity, with complicated forms adding optic atrophy, ataxia, or neuropathy. SPG7 often presents in adulthood and involves mitochondrial dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive spastic gait in adulthood
Increased lower-limb tone, clonus and brisk reflexes
Optic atrophy with mild visual loss and dyschromatopsia
Positive family history of neurological disease
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands
Inflammatory-appearing brain and spinal cord lesions on MRI
Visual symptoms preceding gait disorder by 6 years
Maternal Parkinson's disease and dementia
No cerebellar ataxia reported (common in SPG7)
Flexor plantar responses

data.diagnosis: Seronegative neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder / MOG antibody-associated disease
data.description: Antibody-mediated inflammatory disorders of the central nervous system that preferentially affect the optic nerves and spinal cord, usually in relapsing attacks.
symptoms_in_common: Combination of optic nerve and spinal cord involvement
Bilateral optic atrophy with RNFL thinning
Spinal cord signal abnormality on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Slowly progressive course without acute attacks
Mild visual impairment (attacks usually cause severe loss)
Negative anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies
CSF oligoclonal bands are uncommon
Preserved pupillary light reflexes and no field defect
Family history of blindness, Parkinson's disease and dementia

data.description: 59-year-old woman with a longstanding history of epilepsy with complex partial seizures, treated with phenytoin for more than 20 years, presented with a 3-year history of progressive muscle weakness and generalized bone and muscle pain causing marked limitation in daily activities. Symptoms worsened over time with increasing proximal muscle pain and weakness and more severe bone pain. Physical examination showed normal renal and liver function. Radiographs revealed bilateral Looser’s zones in the femoral neck.
Long-term phenytoin use can accelerate vitamin D breakdown, impairing bone mineralization and causing osteomalacia. This is a leading possibility given the medication history and Looser’s zones.
symptoms_in_common: Phenytoin treatment for more than 20 years
Progressive generalized bone and muscle pain
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent focal abnormality near the left proximal femur on the cross-sectional images is not specifically explained by medication-induced osteomalacia

data.description: A usually small phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor can produce excess FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting and defective bone mineralization despite otherwise normal renal function. The apparent focal lesion near the left hip warrants consideration, although imaging alone cannot establish this diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive bone pain over several years
Severe proximal muscle weakness and pain
Apparent focal abnormality near the left proximal femur on the supplied images
symptoms_not_in_common: Longstanding epilepsy is not a typical manifestation
Long-term phenytoin exposure provides an alternative explanation for osteomalacia

data.description: Inadequate vitamin D intake, limited sunlight exposure, or malabsorption can impair calcium absorption and bone mineralization. Confirmation requires biochemical testing and assessment of nutritional and absorption risks.
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent focal abnormality near the left hip is not typical of uncomplicated nutritional deficiency
Longstanding epilepsy is not a typical manifestation

data.description: Excess parathyroid hormone can increase bone turnover and cause bone pain, weakness, and fragility fractures. Calcium and parathyroid hormone measurements would help distinguish this from osteomalacia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral Looser’s zones are more characteristic of osteomalacia than isolated primary hyperparathyroidism
Long-term phenytoin exposure is not a typical cause of primary hyperparathyroidism
The apparent focal soft-tissue abnormality near the left hip is not a typical finding

data.description: Reduced bone mass after menopause can cause fragility or insufficiency fractures, including at the femoral neck. It may coexist with osteomalacia but does not adequately explain the full presentation alone.
symptoms_in_common: Age compatible with postmenopausal bone loss
Long-term antiseizure medication exposure, which can increase fracture risk
symptoms_not_in_common: Looser’s zones indicate impaired mineralization rather than uncomplicated osteoporosis
Prominent progressive proximal muscle weakness is not typical of osteoporosis alone
Diffuse muscle and bone pain without discrete fractures is not typical
The apparent focal abnormality near the left hip is not explained by osteoporosis

data.description: Paraneoplastic syndrome in which a usually small, benign phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor secretes FGF23, causing renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemia, low calcitriol and osteomalacia. Tumors are often located by somatostatin receptor imaging (octreotide scan/SPECT-CT) and MRI.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive proximal muscle weakness over years
Generalized bone and muscle pain with marked functional limitation
Bilateral Looser's zones in the femoral necks
Bone scan with multiple foci of uptake (ribs, pelvis, ankles) consistent with pseudofractures
Focal somatostatin-receptor-avid lesion near the left hip/obturator region on SPECT-CT
T2-hyperintense soft tissue mass on MRI at the same site
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-term phenytoin use offers an alternative explanation for osteomalacia
Phosphate and FGF23 levels not provided to confirm

data.description: Chronic use of enzyme-inducing antiepileptic drugs such as phenytoin accelerates hepatic catabolism of vitamin D, leading to vitamin D deficiency, hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism and defective bone mineralization.
symptoms_in_common: Phenytoin treatment for more than 20 years
Multiple foci of uptake on bone scan
symptoms_not_in_common: Somatostatin-receptor-avid focal lesion near the left hip
T2-hyperintense soft tissue mass on MRI
Onset and progression only after many years of stable therapy

data.diagnosis: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia (including malabsorption)
data.description: Defective bone mineralization from inadequate vitamin D intake, sun exposure or intestinal malabsorption (e.g., celiac disease), producing bone pain, proximal myopathy and pseudofractures.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral Looser's zones in the femoral necks
Multiple foci of uptake on bone scan
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of malabsorption, dietary deficiency or lack of sun exposure
Focal somatostatin-receptor-avid soft tissue mass on imaging
Long-term phenytoin use points to a drug-related rather than nutritional cause

data.diagnosis: Adult-onset hereditary or renal hypophosphatemic osteomalacia (e.g., autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets, Fanconi syndrome)
data.description: Disorders of renal phosphate wasting due to genetic FGF23 excess or proximal tubular dysfunction, causing chronic hypophosphatemia and osteomalacia with bone pain, weakness and pseudofractures.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple pseudofracture-like foci on bone scan
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset in the late 50s without family history or childhood rickets/short stature
Focal octreotide-avid soft tissue mass
No reported glycosuria, aminoaciduria or acidosis suggesting Fanconi syndrome
Long-term phenytoin use is not related to these conditions

data.diagnosis: Skeletal metastatic disease or multiple myeloma
data.description: Malignant involvement of bone causing diffuse bone pain, pathological fractures and multifocal uptake on bone scintigraphy (myeloma often being scan-negative).
symptoms_in_common: Multiple foci of increased uptake on bone scan
Soft tissue mass near the left hip on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral symmetrical Looser's zones are characteristic of osteomalacia, not malignancy
Prominent proximal muscle weakness
Slow 3-year course without weight loss or known primary tumor
Symmetric rib and pseudofracture pattern of uptake rather than random lesions
Normal renal function (against myeloma)

data.description: 20-year-old male with 3 years of bilateral breast enlargement without nipple discharge. Over the prior 4 years he had polydipsia and polyuria, recently improved. He also reported blurred vision corrected with glasses, occasional post-exertion headaches, decreased facial hair growth, recent constipation, and a history of nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic and focal right leg seizures between ages 6 and 13, treated with carbamazepine until age 14. Physical examination showed minimal facial hair, low blood pressure, bilateral breast enlargement without retraction, masses, or discharge, small testes, and a small posterior anal fissure with a coccygeal lump with central punctum.

data.diagnosis: Intracranial germinoma involving the suprasellar and pineal regions
data.description: A germ-cell tumor occurring predominantly in young people, particularly males. Combined suprasellar and pineal involvement is characteristic and can cause diabetes insipidus, pituitary hormone deficiencies, and visual impairment. This is a leading consideration given the apparent enhancing lesions in these regions and along the ventricular midline.
symptoms_in_common: Polyuria and polydipsia suggesting central diabetes insipidus
Small testes and minimal facial hair suggesting hypogonadism
Bilateral breast enlargement associated with hormonal imbalance
Low blood pressure potentially reflecting pituitary hormone deficiency
Apparent suprasellar, pineal-region, and ventricular enhancing lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Remote childhood seizures are not a typical presenting feature and may be unrelated
Blurred vision corrected with glasses is less characteristic than persistent visual-field loss
Posterior anal fissure and coccygeal lump with a central punctum are not characteristic

data.description: A usually benign epithelial tumor near the pituitary and hypothalamus that can impair vision and disrupt multiple pituitary hormones. It commonly has cystic components and may contain calcification.
symptoms_in_common: Polyuria and polydipsia from possible central diabetes insipidus
Small testes and reduced facial hair from gonadotropin deficiency
Breast enlargement potentially secondary to hypogonadism
Low blood pressure and constipation potentially reflecting pituitary dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Separate pineal-region and ventricular enhancing lesions are atypical
Remote childhood seizures are not a usual presentation
Posterior anal fissure and coccygeal lump are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypothalamic-pituitary involvement
data.description: A clonal inflammatory disorder that can infiltrate the pituitary stalk and hypothalamus, causing central diabetes insipidus and anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. Other organs, including bone and skin, may also be involved.
symptoms_in_common: Small testes and minimal facial hair suggesting gonadotropin deficiency
Breast enlargement potentially related to hypogonadism
Low blood pressure and constipation potentially related to additional pituitary deficiencies
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent pineal-region and ventricular masses are less typical than pituitary-stalk thickening
Visual-field loss is less common unless there is substantial mass effect
Remote childhood seizures are not a typical initial manifestation
The described anal fissure and punctum-bearing coccygeal lump are not characteristic manifestations

data.description: Granulomatous inflammation of the nervous system that can affect the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, meninges, and ventricular surfaces, producing endocrine abnormalities and enhancing intracranial lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Polyuria and polydipsia from possible central diabetes insipidus
Small testes and sparse facial hair suggesting pituitary dysfunction
Breast enlargement potentially secondary to hormonal imbalance
Low blood pressure and constipation potentially reflecting additional hormone deficiencies
Seizures can occur with central nervous system involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Combined discrete pineal and suprasellar masses in a young male favor germinoma over neurosarcoidosis
Blurred vision corrected with glasses is not typical of inflammatory optic involvement
Posterior anal fissure and coccygeal lump with a central punctum are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Pituitary macroadenoma with hypopituitarism, including possible prolactinoma
