data.description: 36-year-old Chinese man with 1 month of persistent fever. Previously healthy, with no history of tuberculosis, chronic illness, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, immune disease, regular medications, or recent travel. On admission, he was acutely ill with tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, and hypoxemia; exam showed bilateral pulmonary rales. He had persistent fever with pancytopenia, marked hyperferritinemia, low fibrinogen, and clinical deterioration to acute respiratory failure. Initial labs: WBC 1.25 ×10^9/L, hemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 41 ×10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.79 g/L, ferritin 375,554 ng/mL.

A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled immune activation, often triggered by infection or malignancy. This is the leading syndromic diagnosis, although additional testing is needed to establish formal diagnostic criteria and identify the trigger.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia affecting all three blood cell lines
Bone marrow images suggestive of hemophagocytosis
Hypotension and progressive acute respiratory failure

data.description: Tuberculosis involving multiple organs can trigger HLH and cause pulmonary failure and marrow dysfunction. The tissue images appear to show granulomatous inflammation with possible necrosis, but tuberculosis requires microbiological or molecular confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Tissue images suggestive of granulomatous inflammation
Extreme hyperferritinemia and reduced fibrinogen compatible with associated HLH
symptoms_not_in_common: Extreme hyperferritinemia is unusual in tuberculosis without associated HLH
Profound pancytopenia and reduced fibrinogen are not typical of uncomplicated pulmonary tuberculosis
Shock is uncommon in uncomplicated tuberculosis

data.description: Epstein-Barr virus infection can provoke severe immune activation and HLH, including in previously healthy adults. Confirmation requires viral testing and assessment for an associated lymphoproliferative disorder.
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomatous-appearing tissue inflammation is not characteristic of Epstein-Barr virus-associated HLH
Extensive pulmonary consolidation is less typical than systemic or hepatic manifestations

data.description: An underlying lymphoma, particularly a T-cell or NK-cell lymphoma, can first present as HLH with fever, cytopenias, extreme ferritin elevation, and rapid organ failure. No malignant diagnosis is established by the supplied images.
symptoms_in_common: Rapid clinical deterioration with respiratory failure
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomatous-appearing inflammation is not a typical diagnostic finding of lymphoma
Diffuse pulmonary consolidation is not a usual initial manifestation of most lymphomas

data.diagnosis: Severe pneumonia with septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and acute respiratory distress syndrome
data.description: A severe pulmonary infection can cause systemic shock, coagulation abnormalities, and inflammatory lung injury. This may coexist with HLH, but alone is a less complete explanation for the extreme ferritin elevation and apparent hemophagocytosis.
symptoms_in_common: Tachypnea, hypoxemia, and bilateral pulmonary rales
symptoms_not_in_common: Ferritin of 375,554 ng/mL is exceptionally unusual for uncomplicated bacterial sepsis
Profound pancytopenia is less typical than isolated thrombocytopenia
One month of persistent fever is less typical of acute bacterial pneumonia
Apparent marrow hemophagocytosis and granulomatous tissue inflammation suggest an additional underlying process

data.diagnosis: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) secondary to pyogenic liver abscess/bacterial sepsis
data.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome of uncontrolled macrophage and T-cell activation, here triggered by severe bacterial infection (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess with septic pulmonary spread), causing cytopenias, extreme hyperferritinemia and multiorgan failure.
symptoms_in_common: Hypodense liver lesions on CT consistent with abscess
Liver biopsy with inflammatory infiltrate and necrosis
Bilateral pulmonary consolidations with acute respiratory failure
symptoms_not_in_common: No diabetes, biliary disease or other predisposing condition for liver abscess
Leukopenia rather than the leukocytosis usual in pyogenic abscess
Fibrinogen only mildly reduced (above the HLH-2004 cutoff of 1.5 g/L)

data.diagnosis: Lymphoma-associated hemophagocytic syndrome (e.g., NK/T-cell or other aggressive lymphoma)
data.description: HLH triggered by an underlying malignant lymphoma, a common cause of adult secondary HLH in Asian populations, often with liver, spleen, marrow and lung involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported lymphadenopathy
No history of malignancy
Liver biopsy shows inflammatory/necrotic tissue rather than an evident atypical lymphoid infiltrate
Liver lesions look abscess-like on CT

data.description: The most common infection-triggered HLH in East Asian adults, in which Epstein-Barr virus infection of T/NK cells drives a cytokine storm and macrophage activation.
symptoms_in_common: Chinese ethnicity (higher incidence in East Asia)
symptoms_not_in_common: Focal hypodense liver lesions suggesting abscess
Dense multifocal lung consolidations are not typical of EBV alone
Necrotizing inflammatory infiltrate on liver biopsy
No reported pharyngitis or lymphadenopathy

data.description: Hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to lungs, liver and bone marrow, which can cause prolonged fever and cytopenias and is a recognized HLH trigger in endemic regions.
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of or known exposure to tuberculosis
No known immunosuppression
Liver biopsy without evident caseating granulomas
Mass-like consolidations rather than miliary nodules or cavities
Ferritin level far higher than usually seen with TB alone

data.diagnosis: Adult-onset Still's disease with macrophage activation syndrome
data.description: A systemic autoinflammatory disorder of young adults with high fevers and very high ferritin, which can be complicated by macrophage activation syndrome, a form of secondary HLH.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported rash, arthritis/arthralgia or sore throat
Focal liver lesions with necrotizing inflammation
Extensive bilateral lung consolidations
No history of immune disease
Shock picture more suggestive of sepsis

data.description: 45-year-old female with 13-year history of papular spiny eruptions on trunk and limbs with severe pruritus. Patient was otherwise in good health. Family history positive for psoriasis in sister. Treatment history included topical steroids and oral antihistamines without relief. Papular lesions on body presented before the alopecia of scalp and pubis, while axillae had been involved for 6 years.

A rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by scarring scalp alopecia, nonscarring axillary and pubic hair loss, and spiny follicular papules. This is the strongest diagnostic consideration; examination and biopsy correlation are needed for confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Longstanding spiny follicular papules on the trunk and limbs
Scalp, pubic, and axillary hair loss
Images showing follicular keratin plugs and an inflammatory infiltrate around follicles

data.diagnosis: Lichen planopilaris with disseminated follicular lichen planus
data.description: An inflammatory disorder in which lymphocytes damage hair follicles, producing perifollicular scale and permanent scalp hair loss; follicular papules can occur elsewhere.
symptoms_in_common: Perifollicular inflammation in the supplied histology
symptoms_not_in_common: The combined pattern of scalp, axillary, and pubic alopecia is more characteristic of Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome than conventional lichen planopilaris
Extensive spiny papules on the trunk and limbs are less typical of scalp-limited disease

data.description: A form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma involving hair follicles that may cause persistent itchy follicular papules and alopecia. Diagnosis requires assessment for atypical lymphocytes and appropriate ancillary testing.
symptoms_in_common: Long course with poor response to topical steroids and antihistamines
Follicular lymphocytic inflammation in the supplied images
symptoms_not_in_common: The specific combination of spiny body papules and scalp, axillary, and pubic hair loss favors Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome
The supplied histology does not clearly establish atypical lymphocytes or follicular mucinosis

data.description: A rare, usually inherited follicular keratinization disorder causing spiny papules and progressive scarring alopecia, generally beginning in childhood.
symptoms_in_common: Spiny follicular papules on the body
symptoms_not_in_common: Adult onset rather than the usual childhood onset
Severe pruritus is less characteristic
Axillary and pubic alopecia accompanying the eruption is less typical
The prominent follicular inflammatory infiltrate favors a lichenoid inflammatory disorder

data.description: A benign follicular keratinization disorder producing patches of small, rough papules with central keratin spines, usually on the trunk and extremities.
symptoms_not_in_common: Marked scalp alopecia
Pubic and axillary hair loss
Severe persistent pruritus
Follicular inflammation associated with apparent follicular destruction

data.description: Rare variant of lichen planopilaris characterized by the triad of progressive cicatricial alopecia of the scalp, non-scarring loss of axillary and pubic hair, and widespread follicular keratotic (spinous) papules on trunk and limbs; mostly affects middle-aged women.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic spiny follicular papules on trunk and limbs
Scalp alopecia with patchy scarring appearance and loss of follicular openings
Dermoscopy showing follicular keratotic plugs and perifollicular scaling
Histology with follicular hyperkeratotic plugging and perifollicular/lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate
Poor response to topical steroids and antihistamines
symptoms_not_in_common: Papules preceded scalp alopecia (alopecia usually comes first)
Family history of psoriasis is unrelated
No oral or nail lichen planus findings reported

data.description: Lymphocyte-mediated primary cicatricial alopecia targeting the hair follicle bulge, causing perifollicular erythema, scaling and patchy scarring hair loss, mainly of the scalp.
symptoms_not_in_common: Widespread spiny follicular papules on trunk and limbs
Axillary and pubic hair loss
Body lesions preceding scalp involvement by years

data.description: Rare genetic (often X-linked, MBTPS2) follicular keratinization disorder with widespread keratosis pilaris-like spiny papules and progressive scarring alopecia of scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes, often with photophobia and keratoderma.
symptoms_in_common: Spiny follicular keratotic papules on trunk and limbs
Follicular hyperkeratotic plugs on dermoscopy and histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Adult onset (usually begins in infancy or childhood)
Female sex (males predominantly affected)
No photophobia, corneal changes or palmoplantar keratoderma reported
Axillary and pubic hair loss
Severe pruritus
No family history of similar disease

data.description: Chronic papulosquamous disorder with follicular hyperkeratotic papules coalescing into orange-red plaques with islands of sparing, palmoplantar keratoderma and scalp scaling.
symptoms_in_common: Follicular keratotic papules on trunk and limbs
Chronic course with resistance to topical steroids
Family history of psoriasis may prompt consideration of a papulosquamous disorder
symptoms_not_in_common: Scarring scalp alopecia
Axillary and pubic hair loss
No orange-red confluent plaques with islands of sparing
No palmoplantar keratoderma
Lichenoid perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate rather than alternating ortho/parakeratosis

data.description: Follicle-centred disorder, idiopathic or associated with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with mucin deposition and/or atypical T-cell infiltration of follicles, producing follicular papules, plaques and alopecia with marked itch.
symptoms_in_common: Severe pruritus refractory to topical steroids and antihistamines
symptoms_not_in_common: No indurated plaques, tumours or head-and-neck predominant lesions
No follicular mucin or atypical folliculotropic lymphocytes described
Symmetric triad pattern involving axillary and pubic hair loss
Stable good general health over 13 years

data.description: 47-year-old woman admitted with left lumbar pain and macroscopic hematuria. Medical history was unremarkable. On examination, she had pale skin without peripheral edema, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, and diuresis of 1000 mL/day. She had moderate normocytic anemia. Autoimmune, antiphospholipid, vasculitis, anti-GBM, cryoglobulin, hepatitis B/C, HIV, and serum protein electrophoresis studies were negative.

An immune-mediated glomerular disease caused by mesangial IgA deposition, often presenting with visible hematuria. The apparent glomerular fluorescence could support this diagnosis if the stain represents IgA; the stain labels are not provided.
symptoms_in_common: Left lumbar pain, which can accompany episodes of gross hematuria
Normal blood pressure and absence of peripheral edema
Negative systemic autoimmune and infectious studies
symptoms_not_in_common: Moderate normocytic anemia is not typical of uncomplicated IgA nephropathy
The prominent concentric vascular changes in the biopsy suggest an additional vascular process

data.description: Renal microvascular endothelial injury that can produce vascular narrowing, glomerular ischemia, and hematuria. The biopsy appears to show concentric vascular remodeling and endothelial abnormalities, although confirmation requires the complete pathology report and laboratory findings.
symptoms_in_common: Concentric narrowing of small vessels in the biopsy
Possible endothelial injury on electron microscopy
Negative autoimmune and antiphospholipid studies do not exclude this diagnosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg is less typical of hypertension-associated thrombotic microangiopathy
Unilateral lumbar pain is not a characteristic presentation
Prominent glomerular immune staining, if confirmed, would suggest a coexisting glomerular disease

data.description: A complement-mediated glomerular disease characterized by dominant C3 deposition. It is a consideration if the positive fluorescence panel represents C3, but identification of the stains and electron-dense deposits is necessary.
symptoms_in_common: Negative autoimmune, viral, and serum protein electrophoresis studies
symptoms_not_in_common: Unilateral lumbar pain is not characteristic
Absence of edema and normal blood pressure are less typical of substantial nephritic disease
The supplied electron micrographs do not clearly demonstrate the deposits needed to support this diagnosis

data.description: An immune-complex glomerulonephritis associated with a preceding or ongoing infection, often producing hematuria and granular complement staining.
symptoms_not_in_common: No preceding or active infection is reported
Normal blood pressure and absence of peripheral edema are less typical of an acute nephritic presentation
Concentric vascular remodeling is not a defining feature
The supplied electron micrographs do not clearly show characteristic subepithelial humps

data.description: A renal inflammatory disease that can cause necrotizing or crescentic glomerular injury despite negative ANCA testing. Typically, kidney biopsy shows little or no immune deposition.
symptoms_in_common: Negative vasculitis serology does not completely exclude renal-limited disease
symptoms_not_in_common: The visibly positive glomerular fluorescence argues against a purely pauci-immune process
The supplied biopsy images do not clearly demonstrate necrosis or cellular crescents
Unilateral lumbar pain is not characteristic

data.description: Glomerulonephritis driven by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, defined by dominant C3 staining on immunofluorescence with little or no immunoglobulin; can present with hematuria and crescentic or membranoproliferative patterns.
symptoms_in_common: Immunofluorescence positive in one panel (presumed C3) and negative in the other (presumed immunoglobulin)
Glomeruli with circumferential crescents on semithin sections
Electron microscopy without large classic immune-complex deposits
Negative autoimmune, ANCA, anti-GBM, cryoglobulin, viral and paraprotein work-up
Normocytic anemia possibly reflecting renal impairment
No edema (nephritic rather than nephrotic picture)
symptoms_not_in_common: Unilateral lumbar pain
Normal blood pressure
Preserved diuresis
No clear sausage-shaped dense deposits on electron microscopy

data.description: Most common primary glomerulonephritis, caused by mesangial IgA immune-complex deposition; classically presents with episodic gross hematuria, sometimes with loin pain, and may rarely show crescents.
symptoms_in_common: Mesangial-type glomerular fluorescence in one panel
symptoms_not_in_common: One immunofluorescence panel is negative (IgA would be expected to be dominant)
No obvious mesangial electron-dense deposits
Moderate anemia
Normal blood pressure despite advanced lesions
No preceding mucosal infection reported

data.description: Necrotizing and crescentic small-vessel glomerulonephritis with scant immune deposits; about 10% of cases are ANCA-negative and renal-limited.
symptoms_in_common: No electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative vasculitis (ANCA) serology
Appreciable glomerular fluorescence in one panel
No extrarenal vasculitic signs
Preserved diuresis and normal blood pressure
Unilateral lumbar pain

data.description: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis following bacterial infection, with C3-dominant deposition and subepithelial humps; may present with gross hematuria and occasionally crescents.
symptoms_in_common: C3-dominant pattern of fluorescence with little immunoglobulin
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of recent infection
No edema or hypertension
No subepithelial humps on electron microscopy
Chronic-appearing fibrous crescents
Moderate anemia
Lumbar pain

data.diagnosis: Complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy (atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome)
data.description: Endothelial injury from complement dysregulation causing glomerular and arteriolar thrombosis, with anemia and renal injury; electron microscopy shows subendothelial widening with electron-lucent material.
symptoms_in_common: Possible subendothelial widening/lucency of capillary walls without deposits on electron microscopy
Negative antiphospholipid and autoimmune serologies (excluding secondary causes)
symptoms_not_in_common: Normocytic anemia without reported hemolysis, schistocytes or thrombocytopenia
Normal blood pressure
Prominent crescents
Macroscopic rather than microscopic hematuria
Unilateral lumbar pain

data.description: 36-year-old female with no past medical history developed progressive lower-limb and paraspinal muscle spasms over 3 months, worsening to wheelchair dependence by 6 months. She required regular IVIG, diazepam 30 mg/day, and morphine up to 60 mg/day for pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus. The spasms were severe enough to impair breathing, requiring intermittent oxygen.

An autoimmune disorder of impaired inhibitory neurotransmission causing axial and limb stiffness with painful spasms. The supplied electrophysiological recordings appear to show exaggerated muscle responses and reduced reflex inhibition, supporting this diagnostic category without establishing it definitively.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive paraspinal and lower-limb muscle spasms
Loss of mobility progressing to wheelchair dependence
Treatment with diazepam and IVIG is consistent with management of this disorder
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe clonus is less characteristic of classic stiff-person syndrome and raises consideration of a broader syndrome or spinal cord disease
Rapid progression to profound disability is less typical of an uncomplicated classic presentation

data.diagnosis: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
data.description: A severe stiff-person spectrum disorder, often associated with glycine-receptor antibodies, that causes rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms, myoclonus, and sometimes brainstem or autonomic dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive severe axial and lower-limb spasms
Use of IVIG and high-dose diazepam is compatible with treatment of this condition
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly lower-limb and paraspinal involvement is narrower than the often generalized presentation

data.description: A focal stiff-person spectrum disorder characterized by persistent stiffness and painful spasms predominantly affecting one or more limbs, often the legs.
symptoms_in_common: Treatment with diazepam and IVIG is compatible with this diagnosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Substantial paraspinal involvement suggests a more extensive stiff-person spectrum disorder
Spasms severe enough to impair breathing are unusual for a strictly focal limb syndrome
Severe clonus is not a defining feature

data.description: A peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder causing continuous muscle activity, stiffness, cramps, and delayed muscle relaxation; some cases are autoimmune.
symptoms_in_common: IVIG use is compatible with treatment of an autoimmune form
symptoms_not_in_common: Brisk reflexes with severe clonus suggest central rather than peripheral hyperexcitability
Prominent paraspinal and lower-limb spasms with respiratory compromise are less characteristic
The apparent exaggerated reflex responses in the supplied recordings favor a central inhibitory disorder over classic neuromyotonia

data.description: Inflammation of the spinal cord can disrupt descending motor pathways, producing spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and progressive gait impairment. Spinal MRI and a directed neurological examination are needed to assess this possibility.
symptoms_not_in_common: Dominant paraspinal spasms are less characteristic than limb spasticity
Breathing impairment specifically caused by spasms is less typical
The apparent abnormal reflex inhibition in the supplied electrophysiological recordings is more suggestive of a stiff-person spectrum disorder

data.description: Autoimmune disorder of impaired GABAergic inhibition causing progressive axial and lower-limb rigidity with superimposed painful, stimulus-sensitive spasms; neurophysiology shows exaggerated startle/exteroceptive reflexes and loss of blink reflex R2 recovery inhibition.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive paraspinal and lower-limb muscle spasms
Stimulus-induced generalized EMG bursts with short latency on polymyography
Enhanced blink reflex R2 recovery (2nd R2 larger than 1st) indicating brainstem hyperexcitability
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe clonus (pyramidal sign less typical of classic SPS)
Rapid progression to wheelchair within 6 months
Respiratory compromise from spasms is uncommon in classic form

data.diagnosis: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM, glycine receptor antibody-associated)
data.description: Severe stiff-person spectrum disorder, often with anti-GlyR antibodies, featuring rigidity, painful spasms, stimulus-sensitive myoclonus/hyperekplexia, brainstem and pyramidal signs, autonomic dysfunction and respiratory compromise; often immunotherapy responsive.
symptoms_in_common: Severe painful spasms of trunk and legs
Brisk reflexes and severe clonus (pyramidal signs)
Exaggerated stimulus-evoked generalized muscle response involving cranial muscles (orbicularis, masseter, sternocleidomastoid) on recording
Brainstem hyperexcitability on blink reflex recovery
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported cranial nerve/oculomotor abnormalities
No reported encephalopathy, seizures or autonomic disturbance
No explicit myoclonus described clinically

data.description: Paraneoplastic variant of stiff-person spectrum, typically in women with breast cancer or small-cell lung cancer, with rapidly progressive rigidity and painful spasms; often less responsive to benzodiazepines.
symptoms_in_common: High-dose diazepam requirement with incomplete control
symptoms_not_in_common: No known malignancy or constitutional symptoms
Predominantly lower-limb/paraspinal distribution (amphiphysin form often involves neck and arms)
Relatively young age

data.diagnosis: Acquired hyperekplexia / brainstem reticular reflex myoclonus (e.g., autoimmune or structural brainstem lesion)
data.description: Pathologically exaggerated startle response from brainstem disinhibition, producing generalized stimulus-induced jerks and tonic spasms, sometimes with apnea.
symptoms_in_common: Stimulus-evoked generalized muscle activation with early cranial muscle recruitment on polymyography
symptoms_not_in_common: Continuous progressive paraspinal and leg spasms/rigidity
Severe persistent pain
Wheelchair dependence from stiffness
No falls from startle described

data.diagnosis: Inflammatory or structural myelopathy with spasticity and tonic spasms (e.g., neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, primary progressive MS)
data.description: Spinal cord disease causing upper motor neuron signs, spasticity and painful tonic spasms of the limbs and trunk, potentially progressive to paraplegia.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive lower-limb involvement to wheelchair dependence
symptoms_not_in_common: No sensory level, weakness or sphincter dysfunction reported
Prominent paraspinal spasms
Generalized startle-like responses involving cranial muscles
Brainstem hyperexcitability on blink reflex recovery is not explained by cord disease
Respiratory compromise from spasms

data.description: 67-year-old female patient presented with chief complaint of swelling in right cheek. History of unhealed tooth extraction sockets from right upper posterior tooth extraction performed approximately one month previously. Past medical history significant for colorectal cancer treatment. Intraoral examination revealed localized, well-defined swelling measuring 4 cm × 5 cm obliterating buccal and palatal vestibules in region of unhealed extraction sockets of teeth 14, 15, and 16. Laboratory examination showed abnormal GTP level and slightly elevated serum CRP level.

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the right maxilla
data.description: An aggressive lymphoma of large B lymphocytes that can present as a destructive extranodal oral mass. The large atypical lymphoid-appearing cells and apparent CD10-negative, BCL6-positive, MUM1-positive pattern favor this diagnosis, potentially a non-germinal-center phenotype; confirmation requires additional immunophenotyping.
symptoms_in_common: Large right cheek and maxillary vestibular swelling
Apparent destructive right maxillary lesion with a soft-tissue mass on CT
Large atypical cells in the supplied cytology and histology images
symptoms_not_in_common: Abnormal GTP level is nonspecific and not a characteristic diagnostic feature

data.diagnosis: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the maxilla
data.description: Spread of colorectal cancer to maxillary bone or oral soft tissue, an uncommon metastatic site. Prior colorectal cancer makes this an important alternative, although the illustrated cell morphology appears more lymphoid than glandular.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent maxillary bone destruction on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Large dispersed lymphoid-appearing cells rather than recognizable malignant glands in the supplied images
Apparent BCL6 and MUM1 expression is not a typical colorectal adenocarcinoma profile

data.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary gingiva or alveolar ridge
data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor that can invade maxillary bone and resemble a dental infection or a nonhealing extraction site. Tissue biopsy with epithelial markers is needed to distinguish it from lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Bulky swelling of the upper gingival and vestibular region
symptoms_not_in_common: The supplied histology appears dominated by dispersed atypical cells rather than cohesive squamous nests or keratinization
Apparent BCL6 and MUM1 staining favors a hematolymphoid process rather than conventional squamous carcinoma

data.diagnosis: Plasmablastic lymphoma of the oral cavity
data.description: An aggressive lymphoma with plasma-cell differentiation that often involves the oral cavity. It can resemble other large-cell lymphomas and requires plasma-cell markers, B-cell markers, and Epstein-Barr virus testing for classification.
symptoms_in_common: Large atypical cells with prominent nuclei
Apparent MUM1 positivity and lack of substantial CD10 staining
symptoms_not_in_common: Apparent BCL6 positivity is less typical of plasmablastic lymphoma
Abnormal GTP level is not a characteristic diagnostic feature

data.diagnosis: Chronic odontogenic osteomyelitis of the right maxilla
data.description: Persistent infection and inflammation of maxillary bone, potentially following dental infection or extraction. It can cause swelling, bone destruction, and delayed socket healing, but does not adequately explain the illustrated atypical-cell population.
symptoms_in_common: Recent extraction of right upper posterior teeth
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent large atypical cells in the supplied cytology and histology images
Apparent BCL6-positive and MUM1-positive atypical-cell population suggests neoplasia rather than uncomplicated infection
A bulky localized mass obliterating both buccal and palatal vestibules is less typical of uncomplicated post-extraction infection

diagnoses.name: Primary oral diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
diagnoses.title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphomas

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (non-germinal center B-cell type) of the maxilla/maxillary sinus
data.description: Aggressive extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma of large atypical B cells; in the oral cavity it often presents as a swelling and non-healing extraction socket. A CD10-negative, BCL6-positive, MUM1-positive profile indicates the non-GCB subtype by the Hans algorithm.
symptoms_in_common: Unhealed extraction sockets one month after extraction
Well-defined 4 x 5 cm mass obliterating buccal and palatal vestibules
CT showing soft tissue mass with destruction of right maxillary alveolar bone and extension into the maxillary sinus
Cytology showing discohesive large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular/lobulated nuclei and basophilic cytoplasm
Immunohistochemistry CD10 negative, BCL6 positive, MUM1 positive
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)
No reported cervical lymphadenopathy
Abnormal GTP level is nonspecific

data.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the maxillary gingiva/maxillary sinus
data.description: Most common malignancy of the oral cavity and maxillary sinus; it invades and destroys bone and may present as a non-healing socket after extraction.
symptoms_in_common: Bone destruction of the maxilla with sinus involvement on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Cytology shows discohesive lymphoid-type cells rather than cohesive keratinizing epithelial cells
BCL6 and MUM1 positivity indicates lymphoid lineage
Smooth, well-defined swelling rather than an ulcerated indurated lesion

data.diagnosis: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma to the maxilla
data.description: Haematogenous spread of colorectal cancer to the jaw bones; rare, but can present as a rapidly growing mass in a recent extraction site.
symptoms_in_common: Rapidly growing mass at extraction site
Abnormal GTP level (could suggest hepatic involvement)
symptoms_not_in_common: Cytology shows discohesive round cells without glandular or mucin-producing features
Lymphoid immunophenotype (BCL6+, MUM1+) is not consistent with adenocarcinoma
Jaw metastases favour the posterior mandible over the maxilla

data.diagnosis: Plasmablastic lymphoma / plasma cell neoplasm (extramedullary plasmacytoma)
data.description: Neoplasms with plasmacytic differentiation that have a predilection for the oral cavity and jaws, typically MUM1 positive, and often arising in immunocompromised patients.
symptoms_in_common: Large atypical cells with basophilic cytoplasm and eccentric nuclei
symptoms_not_in_common: BCL6 positivity is unusual for plasmablastic or plasma cell neoplasms
No known HIV infection
No reported monoclonal protein, anaemia, renal impairment or hypercalcaemia

data.diagnosis: Chronic osteomyelitis / medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw with odontogenic infection
data.description: Infective or drug-related necrosis of jaw bone after tooth extraction, causing non-healing sockets, swelling and sinus involvement; a risk in cancer patients treated with antiresorptive or antiangiogenic agents.
symptoms_in_common: Unhealed extraction sockets one month after extraction
symptoms_not_in_common: Large well-defined solid 4 x 5 cm mass rather than exposed necrotic bone or pus discharge
CRP only slightly elevated
Cytology shows a monotonous population of large atypical lymphoid cells rather than mixed inflammatory cells
BCL6 and MUM1 positive neoplastic cells
No reported pain, fever or sequestrum

data.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.

data.diagnosis: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II)
data.description: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, resulting in lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle. This is overwhelmingly supported by the enzyme deficiency and two GAA variants in trans. CRIM status cannot be reliably assigned from the supplied blot without identifying the patient's lane.
symptoms_in_common: Profoundly reduced GAA activity on newborn screening and confirmatory lymphocyte testing
Compound heterozygous GAA variants c.2024_2026del and c.2040+1G>T
Elevated CK and ALT, consistent with muscle involvement
Markedly elevated pro-BNP, suggesting cardiac stress
Apparent enlargement of the cardiac silhouette on the chest radiograph
Slightly decreased facial folds, potentially reflecting subtle facial muscle involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal muscle power and reflexes, although these can be preserved very early in the disease
No poor feeding, reduced activity, or weak cry
No macroglossia, which is not required for diagnosis

data.description: An X-linked lysosomal disorder caused by LAMP2 deficiency that can produce severe cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy. It is a distant differential because it does not explain the confirmed GAA deficiency and GAA genotype.
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation during the first week of life in a female is highly unusual
Profound GAA deficiency is not characteristic
Two GAA variants in trans support Pompe disease rather than Danon disease
Normal muscle power and absence of overt skeletal myopathy

data.diagnosis: Glycogen storage disease type IIIa (Cori disease)
data.description: An autosomal recessive glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency affecting liver and muscle, sometimes causing cardiomyopathy. It is much less likely than Pompe disease in this case.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cardiac enlargement and elevated pro-BNP
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound GAA deficiency is not expected
The GAA variants in trans are not explained by this disorder
Clinically significant cardiac disease in the first week of life is unusual
No reported hepatomegaly or feeding difficulties

data.diagnosis: Glycogen storage disease type IV, congenital neuromuscular form
data.description: An autosomal recessive glycogen branching enzyme deficiency that can cause neonatal muscle disease and cardiomyopathy. Severe congenital forms generally produce substantial weakness or respiratory compromise.
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal muscle power and reflexes
No weak cry, poor feeding, or reduced activity
Profound GAA deficiency is not characteristic
The compound heterozygous GAA genotype instead supports Pompe disease

data.diagnosis: Transient neonatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy associated with maternal diabetes
data.description: Fetal hyperinsulinemia associated with maternal diabetes can cause macrosomia and transient myocardial hypertrophy. Maternal diabetes is not documented here, and echocardiography would be required to establish hypertrophy.
symptoms_in_common: High birth weight of 4,380 g at full term
Preserved feeding, activity, and muscle strength can occur in mildly symptomatic cases
symptoms_not_in_common: Profound GAA deficiency is not explained
Two GAA variants in trans are not explained
Elevated CK and ALT are not typical defining findings
Slightly decreased facial folds are not characteristic

data.diagnosis: Infantile-onset Pompe disease (Glycogen storage disease type II), classic form
data.description: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by biallelic GAA variants leading to acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, with lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypotonia and elevated muscle enzymes in early infancy.
symptoms_in_common: Positive newborn screening with very low GAA activity (0.18 uM/h)
Deficient lymphocyte GAA activity on confirmatory testing
Compound heterozygous GAA variants in trans (p.N675del and c.2040+1G>T)
Slightly decreased facial folds (mild facial weakness)
Western blot showing absent or reduced mature GAA protein
Onset in the first week of life
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal muscle power and reflexes
No macroglossia
No poor feeding, poor activity or weak cry
Absence of the common Taiwanese p.D645E variant

data.diagnosis: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of the infant of a diabetic mother
data.description: Transient septal or ventricular hypertrophy caused by fetal hyperinsulinism in response to maternal hyperglycemia, usually with macrosomia, and resolving over the first months of life.
symptoms_in_common: Otherwise well-appearing newborn with normal feeding and activity
symptoms_not_in_common: Deficient GAA enzyme activity
Pathogenic GAA variants in trans
Elevated CK
Elevated ALT
Decreased facial folds
No maternal diabetes reported

data.description: X-linked lysosomal glycogen storage disease with normal acid maltase activity, causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy and elevated CK and transaminases; usually presents in childhood or adolescence, later and milder in females.
symptoms_not_in_common: Deficient GAA activity (normal in Danon disease)
Biallelic GAA variants
Neonatal presentation
Female sex with early onset
Macrosomia

data.diagnosis: Glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease)
data.description: Autosomal recessive debranching enzyme (AGL) deficiency causing hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, elevated transaminases and CK, with myopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in some patients; usually presents in infancy or childhood.
symptoms_not_in_common: Deficient GAA activity
Pathogenic GAA variants
No hypoglycemia reported
No hepatomegaly reported
Presentation in the first week of life
Decreased facial folds
Macrosomia

data.diagnosis: GAA pseudodeficiency or late-onset Pompe disease detected by newborn screening
data.description: Low measured GAA activity on screening due to pseudodeficiency alleles (common in East Asian populations, clinically benign) or milder GAA variants that cause later-onset disease, typically without cardiomyopathy in infancy.
symptoms_in_common: Low GAA activity on newborn screening
No feeding difficulty, poor activity or weak cry
symptoms_not_in_common: Cardiomegaly on chest radiograph
Markedly elevated pro-BNP
Elevated CK
Elevated ALT
Severely deficient lymphocyte GAA activity
Two pathogenic variants in trans including a splice-site variant
GAA activity and ratio in the critical range
Decreased facial folds

data.description: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

data.diagnosis: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
data.description: A mosquito-transmitted nematode infection associated with canine reservoirs and endemic in parts of the Mediterranean, including Croatia. The supplied microscopy appears to show a nematode with a thick, externally ridged cuticle, strongly favoring Dirofilaria repens; definitive identification requires pathological or molecular confirmation.
symptoms_in_common: Normal blood counts and inflammatory markers, which are common in localized infection
Outdoor exposure in an endemic region
Dog ownership, indicating proximity to a potential reservoir rather than direct transmission
Microscopic appearance compatible with a cuticular-ridged filarial nematode

data.description: A tissue-invasive nematode infection usually acquired by eating raw or undercooked infected freshwater animals, causing intermittent migrating subcutaneous swellings.
symptoms_not_in_common: A discrete, painless nodule is less typical than itchy, painful, or edematous migrating swellings
Normal blood counts without reported eosinophilia
No travel outside Croatia makes the usual geographic exposure less likely
The apparent ridged filarial cuticle is more consistent with Dirofilaria than Gnathostoma

data.description: Infection by a larval Spirometra tapeworm, typically acquired through contaminated water or raw infected animal tissue, which can produce migrating subcutaneous masses.
symptoms_in_common: Normal inflammatory markers can occur in localized infection
symptoms_not_in_common: The supplied microscopy appears to show a cylindrical nematode rather than a tapeworm larva
A thick, ridged cuticle and internal nematode structures are not characteristic of sparganosis

data.description: Tissue infection with larval Taenia solium following ingestion of tapeworm eggs, sometimes presenting as small, painless subcutaneous nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Normal blood counts and inflammatory markers can occur with isolated lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Migrating nodules are not typical
Negative cysticercosis serology lowers suspicion, although it does not exclude an isolated lesion
The microscopy appears to show a nematode rather than a cysticercus

data.description: A benign tumor of mature fat that commonly presents as a painless, circumscribed subcutaneous mass; it is a clinical alternative before tissue examination.
symptoms_in_common: Normal blood counts and inflammatory markers
symptoms_not_in_common: Firm consistency is less typical than the soft or rubbery texture of a lipoma
True migration of nodules is not characteristic
The supplied microscopy shows an apparent parasitic structure rather than mature adipose tissue

data.description: Mosquito-borne zoonotic filarial infection whose natural hosts are dogs; endemic in Mediterranean Europe including Croatia. In humans it usually produces a single subcutaneous, sometimes migrating nodule containing an immature worm.
symptoms_in_common: Firm, migrating subcutaneous nodule in the upper arm
Residence in Istria (endemic Mediterranean area) with no travel abroad
Dog ownership and outdoor recreation in forests and islands (mosquito exposure)
Normal blood counts without eosinophilia, normal ESR and CRP
Negative serology for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis
Histology showing a nematode cross-section with thick multilayered cuticle bearing external longitudinal ridges and a well-developed muscle layer
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal ultrasonographic appearance of the nodule (a cystic lesion with a linear, sometimes mobile, echogenic structure is often seen)

data.description: Dog heartworm transmitted by mosquitoes; in humans it typically causes solitary pulmonary coin lesions and only rarely subcutaneous nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Mosquito exposure in an area where canine dirofilariasis occurs
Nodule containing a nematode on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Subcutaneous migrating nodule rather than a pulmonary lesion
No respiratory symptoms
Cuticle with external longitudinal ridges on histology (D. immitis cuticle is smooth)

data.description: Filarial infection transmitted by blackflies that forms subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas) containing adult worms; O. volvulus is endemic to Africa and Latin America, while rare zoonotic cases from animal Onchocerca species occur in Europe.
symptoms_in_common: Nematode seen within the nodule on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel to areas endemic for O. volvulus
Migrating nature of the nodule (onchocercomas are fixed)
No pruritus, dermatitis or eye involvement
No eosinophilia
Cuticular morphology with longitudinal ridges rather than the annular ridges of Onchocerca

data.description: Food-borne nematode infection (Gnathostoma spinigerum) acquired from raw fish or other undercooked intermediate hosts, mostly in Asia and Latin America, causing intermittent migratory subcutaneous swellings.
symptoms_in_common: Nematode parasite present in the tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel outside Croatia
Painless, non-pruritic, non-inflamed nodule (gnathostomiasis swellings are usually itchy, painful and erythematous)
No eosinophilia
Histology lacks the cuticular spines typical of Gnathostoma larvae

data.description: Tissue infection with larval cysts of the pork tapeworm after ingestion of eggs, producing firm, painless subcutaneous or muscular nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Normal inflammatory markers and blood counts
symptoms_not_in_common: Negative cysticercosis serology
Migrating nodule (cysticerci do not migrate)
Normal ultrasound without a cyst containing a scolex
Histology shows a nematode with cuticle and musculature rather than a cestode larva
Usually multiple nodules rather than a single one

data.description: 26-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks’ gestation with monochorionic diamniotic twins; history of childhood asthma, obesity, anxiety, depression, gestational diabetes, polyhydramnios in one fetus, and two prior uncomplicated pregnancies. Three weeks before presentation, after sick contacts in her children, she developed conjunctival erythema with greenish discharge, followed by nonproductive cough, sore throat, ear pain, and new leg edema. One week before admission, progressive right leg pain developed, later becoming bilateral leg tenderness with worsening edema, severe coughing episodes, and expiratory wheezes. Initial vitals included fever absent, tachycardia, and hypotension; legs were edematous without erythema or warmth. She then developed sudden severe crushing chest pain, became unresponsive and pulseless, and had cardiac arrest with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Acute inflammation of the heart muscle, potentially following a viral infection, that can cause heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and malignant ventricular arrhythmias. The preceding conjunctivitis and respiratory illness make a viral trigger plausible, but do not establish a specific virus.
symptoms_in_common: Conjunctivitis and respiratory illness preceding cardiac deterioration
Cough and wheezing potentially caused by pulmonary congestion
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and cardiac arrest
Chest imaging suggestive of pulmonary edema with small bilateral pleural effusions
symptoms_not_in_common: Initially unilateral leg pain is not a typical manifestation
Greenish conjunctival discharge and ear pain are not direct manifestations of myocardial inflammation

data.description: Pregnancy-associated systolic heart failure without another identifiable cause, usually developing near the end of pregnancy or after delivery. Twin gestation increases risk; presentation at 32 weeks is earlier than the classic timing.
symptoms_in_common: Cough and expiratory wheezing consistent with pulmonary congestion
Chest imaging suggestive of pulmonary edema and pleural effusions
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctivitis, sore throat, and ear pain are not characteristic
Initially unilateral leg pain is not typical
Sudden crushing chest pain is less typical than progressive heart-failure symptoms

data.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism arising from deep vein thrombosis
data.description: A venous clot traveling to the pulmonary arteries can cause acute right-heart strain, obstructive shock, and cardiac arrest. Pregnancy and obesity increase thromboembolic risk.
symptoms_in_common: Right leg pain preceding bilateral leg tenderness and edema
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctivitis, sore throat, and ear pain are not characteristic
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia is less typical than pulseless electrical activity in massive pulmonary embolism
Diffuse pulmonary edema is less characteristic than findings of acute right-heart strain

data.description: Spontaneous separation of layers of a coronary artery can obstruct coronary blood flow and cause myocardial infarction, ventricular arrhythmias, and shock. Pregnancy-associated cases often occur postpartum but can occur during pregnancy.
symptoms_in_common: Pulmonary congestion potentially resulting from acute ischemic heart failure
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctivitis and upper respiratory symptoms are not characteristic
Leg pain and edema developing before the acute chest pain are not a typical initial presentation
The supplied coronary angiographic image does not show an obvious dissection, although a single image cannot exclude it

data.description: Acute, often reversible ventricular dysfunction triggered by physical or emotional stress that can mimic myocardial infarction despite the absence of an obstructive coronary lesion.
symptoms_in_common: Significant physical stress from respiratory illness and twin pregnancy
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age is less typical than the usual postmenopausal presentation
Conjunctivitis, sore throat, and ear pain are not direct manifestations
Initially unilateral leg pain is not typical
Several weeks of progressive peripheral edema is less typical than an abrupt presentation

data.description: Viral infection of the myocardium causing inflammation, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock; adenovirus classically causes conjunctivitis, pharyngitis and otitis before cardiac involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Sore throat, ear pain and cough preceding cardiac symptoms
Wheezing and cough possibly from pulmonary edema (cardiac asthma)
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and cardiac arrest
Pleural effusions and pulmonary opacities on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of fever
Leg pain and tenderness
Sudden crushing nature of the chest pain is more typical of ischemia or embolism
Greenish purulent discharge suggests bacterial rather than viral conjunctivitis

data.description: Idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy with systolic dysfunction arising late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery; risk factors include multiple gestation and obesity.
symptoms_in_common: Cough and wheeze from pulmonary congestion
symptoms_not_in_common: Preceding infectious prodrome (conjunctivitis, sore throat, ear pain)
Sudden crushing chest pain
Leg pain and tenderness
Slightly earlier onset than typical (usually last month of pregnancy or postpartum)

data.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism with deep vein thrombosis
data.description: Venous thrombus, usually from the legs, embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and causing right heart strain, obstructive shock and arrest; pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state.
symptoms_in_common: Pregnancy and obesity as risk factors
Leg pain beginning unilaterally (right) with edema and tenderness
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctivitis, sore throat and ear pain
Bilateral symmetric edema without warmth or erythema
Arrest rhythm of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia rather than pulseless electrical activity
Expiratory wheezes
Bilateral pleural effusions and pulmonary edema pattern
No evident pulmonary artery filling defect on the CT images

data.diagnosis: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection / acute myocardial infarction
data.description: Tear or intramural hematoma in a coronary artery wall causing myocardial ischemia; the leading cause of pregnancy-associated myocardial infarction in young women.
symptoms_in_common: Young pregnant woman in the third trimester
Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and cardiac arrest
symptoms_not_in_common: Three-week infectious prodrome
Progressive leg edema, cough and wheeze before the chest pain
Leg pain and tenderness
Coronary angiogram appears free of dissection or occlusion

data.diagnosis: Preeclampsia with pulmonary edema / mirror (Ballantyne) syndrome
data.description: Pregnancy-related endothelial dysfunction causing maternal edema and pulmonary edema; mirror syndrome is maternal fluid overload mirroring fetal hydrops, as can occur with complicated monochorionic twins such as twin-twin transfusion.
symptoms_in_common: Monochorionic twin pregnancy with polyhydramnios in one fetus
Obesity and gestational diabetes as risk factors
Cough and wheezing from pulmonary edema
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypotension rather than hypertension
Infectious prodrome with conjunctivitis, sore throat and ear pain
Crushing chest pain
Ventricular tachycardia and cardiac arrest
Leg pain and tenderness

data.description: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

An eruption of crater-shaped, keratin-producing squamous tumors that can recur after trauma. The supplied timeline reports 15 histologically diagnosed keratoacanthomas, making this the leading diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple papules and nodules on sun-exposed forearms and dorsal hands
Central keratin plugs and crusted, crater-like lesions
New lesions following excision, described as an isomorphic response
Histology showing crateriform squamous proliferation with keratinization
symptoms_not_in_common: Sleep-disrupting pruritus is less typical of isolated keratoacanthomas
Persistent progression over many months is less typical of a solitary keratoacanthoma, which may spontaneously regress

data.description: A malignant keratinocyte tumor that may resemble keratoacanthoma clinically and histologically. Prior transplantation increases risk, and individual suspicious lesions require assessment for invasive carcinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Keratinizing, crusted nodules on sun-exposed skin
Squamous proliferation with prominent keratinization on the supplied histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Numerous similarly appearing eruptive papules are less typical of conventional squamous cell carcinoma
Severe widespread pruritus is not a characteristic presenting feature
The supplied timeline reports keratoacanthomas rather than invasive squamous cell carcinoma

data.description: A disorder associated with advanced kidney disease in which dermal material is eliminated through the epidermis, producing intensely itchy papules with central plugs.
symptoms_in_common: Papules on the extremities with central crusts or plugs
Lesions occurring at sites of trauma or scratching
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominantly sun-exposed distribution is not characteristic
The supplied histology shows keratinizing squamous tumors rather than demonstrated transepidermal elimination
Multiple lesions were reported histologically as keratoacanthomas

data.description: A chronic itch-associated disorder producing firm, excoriated papules and nodules through an itch-scratch cycle; chronic kidney disease can contribute to the underlying itch.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple crusted or excoriated papules and nodules on accessible extremities
Advanced kidney disease, which can cause chronic pruritus
symptoms_not_in_common: Discrete crateriform lesions with central keratin plugs are less typical
Restriction to sun-exposed skin is not characteristic
Histologically documented keratoacanthomas are not explained by prurigo nodularis

data.description: Human papillomavirus-associated common warts causing hyperkeratotic papules, frequently on the hands. The supplied timeline reports three histologically confirmed warts, suggesting coexistence with the predominant keratoacanthoma eruption.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple papules on the hands and forearms
History of transplantation, a risk factor for persistent warts
Three excised lesions reported histologically as verrucae vulgares
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe sleep-disrupting pruritus is unusual for ordinary warts
Large crateriform, centrally crusted nodules are not typical
Most sampled lesions were reported as keratoacanthomas rather than warts

data.description: Rare sporadic adult-onset disorder with eruption of numerous keratoacanthomas, typically intensely pruritic, with a chronic progressive course, koebnerization and poor response to treatment.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple papules and crateriform nodules with central keratin plugs
Onset in fifth to sixth decade
Histology of multiple lesions showing keratoacanthoma (crateriform, glassy keratinocytes, keratin-filled crater)
Partial response to topical imiquimod and 5-fluorouracil
symptoms_not_in_common: Distribution limited to sun-exposed extremities rather than generalized with facial and mucosal involvement
Lesions larger than the typical 1-5 mm follicular papules
No reported ectropion or masked facies
Setting of terminal kidney disease and prior transplant immunosuppression is not typical

data.diagnosis: Multiple cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas (keratoacanthoma type) in an immunosuppressed transplant/dialysis patient
data.description: Organ transplant recipients and patients with long-term immunosuppression or uremia develop multiple well-differentiated squamous cell carcinomas and keratoacanthomas on sun-exposed skin, often together with viral warts.
symptoms_in_common: History of two kidney transplants with immunosuppression
Multiple crateriform keratotic nodules on sun-exposed forearms and hands
Histology showing keratoacanthomas alongside verrucae vulgares
Recurrence and new lesions after excisions
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe pruritus is unusual
Rapid eruptive onset of dozens of lesions within months
Marked isomorphic response at surgical scars
No habitual UV or carcinogen exposure
No metastases and well-differentiated crateriform architecture without frank invasion
Grafts rejected years earlier so immunosuppression presumably stopped

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis (Kyrle disease / reactive perforating collagenosis)
data.description: Pruritic papulonodular eruption with central keratotic plugs seen in patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis or diabetes, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material and koebnerization.
symptoms_in_common: Severely pruritic papules and nodules with central keratotic plugs
symptoms_not_in_common: Histology shows keratoacanthoma rather than transepidermal elimination of collagen or elastic fibres
Large crateriform tumours and confluent plaques
Restriction to sun-exposed areas
No diabetes

data.diagnosis: Hypertrophic lichen planus with eruptive keratoacanthoma-like lesions
data.description: Chronic variant of lichen planus with very itchy hyperkeratotic plaques and nodules, showing koebnerization, in which keratoacanthomas or squamous cell carcinomas can arise; it may also be drug-induced.
symptoms_in_common: Hyperkeratotic papules and nodules on extremities
Multiple potentially lichenoid-inducing drugs (beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, allopurinol)
symptoms_not_in_common: Typically affects shins rather than sun-exposed forearms and hands
No lichenoid band-like infiltrate or interface dermatitis described
No violaceous flat-topped papules, Wickham striae or mucosal lesions
Crateriform architecture with central keratin plug in most lesions

data.description: Chronic dermatosis of intensely itchy, excoriated hyperkeratotic nodules on extensor limbs caused by repeated scratching, frequently associated with chronic kidney disease and uremic pruritus.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple excoriated, crusted papules and nodules on extensor extremities
symptoms_not_in_common: Histology diagnostic of keratoacanthoma with keratin-filled crater and glassy keratinocytes
Crateriform nodules with central horn plugs
Rapid eruption with new lesions in surgical scars
Response to imiquimod and 5-fluorouracil
Limitation to sun-exposed areas

data.description: A 34-year-old woman presented with acute abdominal and back pain 3 years before evaluation at the oncology clinic. She had been well until this onset. Her medical history was notable for migraines. She did not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. She worked full time as a social worker and lived in New Jersey with her husband and child. Family history included breast cancer in maternal grandmother (70s), uterine cancer in paternal aunt (40s), and colon cancer in two paternal cousins (30s and 50s). On physical examination: temperature 36.5°C, blood pressure 108/78 mm Hg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, body-mass index 27.7. The abdomen had well-healed surgical scars; remainder of physical examination was normal. Laboratory results showed elevated tumor marker CA 19-9 at 110 IU per milliliter (reference <35), while alpha-fetoprotein and carcinoembryonic antigen levels were normal.
A malignant tumor of the intrahepatic bile ducts. This is the leading possibility given the liver mass, elevated CA 19-9, and apparent gland-forming carcinoma within dense fibrous stroma.
symptoms_in_common: Hepatic mass with heterogeneous enhancement and apparent diffusion restriction
Histology showing irregular glandular structures in desmoplastic stroma
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 34 is younger than the usual age at presentation
Abrupt onset of pain is less typical than an insidious presentation

data.diagnosis: Colorectal adenocarcinoma metastatic to the liver
data.description: Colorectal cancer can spread to the liver and produce gland-forming tumors with a fibrous stromal response. Identifying an intestinal primary and performing immunohistochemistry would help distinguish it from a primary biliary cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Family history of colon cancer, including an affected relative in their 30s
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age is less typical for sporadic colorectal cancer
Normal carcinoembryonic antigen is less supportive, although it does not exclude the diagnosis
Back pain is not a characteristic initial symptom

data.diagnosis: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma metastatic to the liver
data.description: An adenocarcinoma arising from pancreatic ducts that commonly spreads to the liver and can resemble cholangiocarcinoma histologically.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal pain radiating to the back
Hepatic mass compatible with a metastatic deposit
Glandular tumor morphology with desmoplastic stroma
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 34 is unusually young for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
An apparently localized hepatic lesion is less typical than multiple liver metastases
Abrupt onset of pain is less typical than progressive pain

data.description: A primary liver malignancy containing both hepatocellular and biliary differentiation. A limited tissue sample may show only its gland-forming biliary component.
symptoms_in_common: Normal alpha-fetoprotein does not exclude this diagnosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age is less typical
The supplied histology does not clearly demonstrate a hepatocellular component
Abrupt abdominal and back pain is not a characteristic presentation

data.description: A rare primary liver cancer that often affects young adults without cirrhosis and usually has normal alpha-fetoprotein. Its characteristic histology consists of large hepatocellular tumor cells separated by lamellar fibrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Previously well patient without reported chronic liver disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated CA 19-9 is not characteristic
The apparent gland-forming histology is more consistent with adenocarcinoma than fibrolamellar carcinoma
Abrupt onset of abdominal and back pain is less typical

data.description: Primary adenocarcinoma arising from the intrahepatic bile duct epithelium, typically a mass-forming lesion with desmoplastic stroma, peripheral biliary dilatation and elevated CA 19-9; a subset carries targetable alterations such as FGFR2 fusions or IDH1 mutations.
symptoms_in_common: Lobulated liver mass on MRI with restricted diffusion
Heterogeneous, hypoenhancing mass with peripheral bile duct dilatation
Histology showing glands and nests of malignant cells in dense desmoplastic stroma
Previously well with no underlying liver disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age (34 years)
No known risk factors such as primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver fluke infection or cirrhosis
No jaundice or weight loss reported

data.diagnosis: Metastatic adenocarcinoma to the liver (pancreatobiliary or upper gastrointestinal primary)
data.description: Spread of an adenocarcinoma from the pancreas, gallbladder, stomach or other site to the liver; histologically it can be indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Hypoenhancing liver mass with restricted diffusion
Adenocarcinoma with desmoplastic stroma on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Solitary dominant liver lesion rather than multiple lesions
No primary tumor described elsewhere
Young age
Normal carcinoembryonic antigen
Peripheral bile duct dilatation favors a primary biliary tumor

data.diagnosis: Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma associated with Lynch syndrome
data.description: Hereditary mismatch-repair deficiency predisposes to early-onset colorectal, endometrial and other cancers (including biliary tract cancers); colorectal cancer commonly metastasizes to the liver.
symptoms_in_common: Family history of colon cancer in two paternal cousins, one in the 30s
Family history of uterine cancer in a paternal aunt in her 40s
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal carcinoembryonic antigen
No bowel symptoms, bleeding or anemia reported
No colonic primary identified
Isolated elevation of CA 19-9
Bile duct dilatation and desmoplastic small-gland morphology favor a biliary origin

data.description: Primary malignant tumor of hepatocytes; the fibrolamellar variant occurs in young adults without cirrhosis, with normal alpha-fetoprotein and fibrous bands within the tumor.
symptoms_in_common: Young adult without underlying liver disease
Normal alpha-fetoprotein (typical of the fibrolamellar variant)
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated CA 19-9
No arterial hyperenhancement with washout on imaging
Peripheral bile duct dilatation
Glandular rather than hepatocytic histology with no large eosinophilic cells or lamellar fibrosis
No central scar

data.description: Rare primary liver cancer with both hepatocytic and biliary differentiation, with imaging and marker features that overlap both tumor types.
symptoms_in_common: Glandular component with desmoplastic stroma on histology
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal alpha-fetoprotein
No hepatocellular component evident on histology
No chronic liver disease or cirrhosis
Young age
No arterial hyperenhancing component on imaging

data.description: A 47-year-old woman presented with intermittent cough, shortness of breath, fever (body temperature up to 38.5°C), accompanied by right eyelid swelling around June 17, 2017, which worsened day by day. Weight loss was about 9 kg. Physical examination included high body temperature of 39°C, right eyelid swelling, and a painless enlarged lymph node about 2 cm × 2 cm in size in the left axilla. Auscultation of lungs revealed coarse respiratory sounds with moist rale. No hepatosplenomegaly and edema in lower limbs.

A rare cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma involving subcutaneous fat. The apparent lymphocytic infiltration around adipocytes in the supplied biopsy makes this an important possibility, although confirmation requires immunophenotyping and molecular studies.
symptoms_in_common: Eyelid swelling potentially caused by subcutaneous infiltration
Apparent inflammatory or infiltrative changes in subcutaneous tissue
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent cough and shortness of breath with multiple pulmonary nodules are unusual
Enlarged axillary lymph node is less typical because this lymphoma usually remains predominantly in subcutaneous fat

data.description: An aggressive, usually Epstein–Barr virus-associated lymphoma that can involve upper airway structures, skin, orbital tissues, and lungs. Tissue immunophenotyping and Epstein–Barr virus testing are required for diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules and surrounding opacities on the supplied CT
symptoms_not_in_common: Painless axillary lymphadenopathy is less characteristic than extranodal disease
An adipocyte-rimming infiltrate is more suggestive of a panniculitic lymphoma than the classic destructive pattern of this disease

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with extranodal involvement
data.description: An aggressive B-cell malignancy that can cause constitutional symptoms, painless lymphadenopathy, and involvement of the lungs, orbit, or soft tissues.
symptoms_in_common: Eyelid swelling potentially reflecting orbital or eyelid involvement
Cough, shortness of breath, and multiple pulmonary nodules
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent adipocyte-rimming lymphocytic pattern in the biopsy is not the usual morphology
Diffuse panniculitis-like soft-tissue involvement is uncommon

data.description: A systemic small-vessel vasculitis that commonly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys and can produce pulmonary nodules and orbital inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Unilateral eyelid swelling potentially related to orbital inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Painless axillary lymphadenopathy is not characteristic
The supplied biopsy appears predominantly lymphocytic and panniculitic rather than showing characteristic necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection involving pulmonary and extrapulmonary sites, potentially including lymph nodes and, rarely, ocular or soft tissues. Confirmation requires microbiologic testing or compatible tissue findings.
symptoms_not_in_common: Progressive unilateral eyelid swelling is an uncommon manifestation
The apparent lymphocytic adipocyte-rimming biopsy pattern is not typical of tuberculous granulomatous inflammation

data.diagnosis: Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (with pulmonary involvement)
data.description: Rare cytotoxic T-cell lymphoma infiltrating subcutaneous fat, with neoplastic lymphocytes rimming individual adipocytes; often presents with fever, weight loss, subcutaneous swelling or nodules, and may be complicated by hemophagocytic syndrome. Extracutaneous (e.g., lung) spread is uncommon.
symptoms_in_common: Diffuse subcutaneous swelling of the limb with abnormal fat on surgical exploration
Histology showing lymphoid infiltrate of fat lobules with rimming of adipocytes by immunostain-positive cells
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules and consolidations (lung involvement is rare)
Cough, shortness of breath and moist rales
Lymphadenopathy is uncommon
No hepatosplenomegaly

data.description: Aggressive EBV-associated lymphoma that typically involves the nasal cavity/midface but can affect skin, subcutaneous tissue, orbit and lung, with angiodestructive growth and necrosis.
symptoms_in_common: Subcutaneous soft tissue infiltration with panniculitis-like histology
symptoms_not_in_common: No nasal obstruction, epistaxis or midfacial destructive lesion reported
No skin ulceration or obvious necrosis
Adipocyte rimming pattern is more typical of subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma

data.description: ANCA-associated necrotizing granulomatous small-vessel vasculitis affecting the upper airway, lungs and kidneys; may cause orbital inflammatory masses and multiple lung nodules.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules with surrounding ground-glass opacity
symptoms_not_in_common: Painless axillary lymphadenopathy
Subcutaneous fat infiltration by atypical lymphocytes rimming adipocytes rather than granulomatous vasculitis
No sinonasal symptoms or renal involvement reported
No cavitation of the nodules

data.diagnosis: Lupus erythematosus panniculitis (lupus profundus) / systemic lupus erythematosus
data.description: Autoimmune lobular panniculitis associated with lupus, causing subcutaneous nodules or plaques, sometimes periorbital edema, with lymphoplasmacytic infiltration of fat; a key histologic mimic of panniculitic lymphoma.
symptoms_in_common: Subcutaneous swelling with lymphocytic lobular panniculitis
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple nodular pulmonary masses are atypical
No malar rash, arthritis, photosensitivity or serositis reported
Adipocyte rimming by cytotoxic lymphocytes favours lymphoma
Severity of weight loss and persistent high fever

data.diagnosis: Disseminated infection (tuberculosis or invasive fungal infection such as cryptococcosis/aspergillosis)
data.description: Hematogenously or bronchogenically spread infection producing multiple lung nodules and consolidations with systemic symptoms, occasionally with soft tissue and lymph node involvement, including infectious panniculitis.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules with halo-like ground-glass opacity and consolidation
symptoms_not_in_common: Eyelid swelling
Diffuse subcutaneous fat infiltration by lymphoid cells without granulomas, caseation or organisms
Adipocyte rimming on immunohistochemistry suggests a neoplastic process
No known immunosuppression reported
