Does not explain the abnormal mobility of the costal cartilages on ultrasound

data.diagnosis: Costal cartilage fracture or stress fracture of a lower rib
data.description: Exercise-induced stress injury or fracture of the rib or costal cartilage from repetitive muscular pull, seen in athletes such as rowers, golfers and weightlifters.
symptoms_in_common: Sharp, localized lower anterior chest wall pain
Onset after starting a new strenuous training regime
Atraumatic onset is possible with stress injuries
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain would usually be constant or present with deep breathing, coughing and daily movements, whereas the patient is asymptomatic outside training
Ultrasound shows no cortical or cartilage discontinuity, step-off, callus or haematoma
Costal cartilages appear intact with a homogeneous hypoechoic appearance
Focal persistent point tenderness would be expected

data.diagnosis: Anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES) or intercostal neuralgia
data.description: Entrapment or irritation of the terminal branches of the lower intercostal nerves as they pass through the rectus abdominis or along the costal margin, causing sharp, localized abdominal or chest wall pain aggravated by abdominal muscle contraction.
symptoms_in_common: Pain worsened by abdominal muscle contraction such as crunches (Carnett-type aggravation)
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is usually located in the abdominal wall at the lateral border of the rectus muscle rather than over the lower thoracic wall
No reported sensory changes such as hypoaesthesia, allodynia or burning pain
Usually also symptomatic in daily activities and positions
Does not explain the abnormal mobility of the 8th and 9th costal cartilages on ultrasound

data.description: A multitrauma patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to an intrahepatic hematoma. On the 7th day of ICU hospitalization, he presented fever. Laboratory blood tests showed leucocytosis and elevated liver function values.

Inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, often occurring after major trauma or during critical illness. The ultrasound appears to show a thick-walled gallbladder-like structure with internal debris, which may support this diagnosis but is not definitive.
symptoms_in_common: Possible gallbladder wall thickening and internal debris on ultrasound
symptoms_not_in_common: The traumatic intrahepatic hematoma is a separate injury rather than a typical manifestation

data.description: Secondary bacterial infection of a traumatic blood collection within the liver, potentially causing systemic inflammation and liver injury.
symptoms_in_common: Delayed onset of fever after injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Possible gallbladder-centered ultrasound abnormalities would not be directly explained

data.description: A bacterial pus collection within the liver that can develop following trauma or infection of damaged hepatic tissue.
symptoms_in_common: Recent hepatic trauma as a possible predisposing factor
symptoms_not_in_common: A traumatic hematoma alone does not establish an abscess
Possible gallbladder wall thickening is not a defining feature

data.description: An infected collection of leaked bile caused by traumatic injury to intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile ducts.
symptoms_in_common: Recent major trauma involving the liver
symptoms_not_in_common: The documented collection is described as a hematoma rather than a bile collection
Possible gallbladder wall thickening is not typical of an isolated biloma

data.description: Infection of the bile ducts, usually associated with impaired biliary drainage; traumatic biliary injury or blood entering the ducts could provide a mechanism in this setting.
symptoms_not_in_common: An intrahepatic hematoma is not a usual manifestation
Possible gallbladder-centered ultrasound findings favor gallbladder inflammation rather than isolated bile duct infection

data.description: Inflammation of the gallbladder without gallstones, typically occurring in critically ill, trauma, or ICU patients due to bile stasis, ischemia and gallbladder wall injury. Ultrasound shows wall thickening (>3 mm), distension, pericholecystic fluid and sludge.
symptoms_in_common: Fever arising on day 7 of ICU stay
Ultrasound appearing to show a gallbladder with a thickened wall (calipers on the wall) and no obvious stones
symptoms_not_in_common: Intrahepatic hematoma is not itself a feature, though it could explain the liver test abnormalities independently
No documented right upper quadrant pain or Murphy sign (often unassessable in ICU patients)

data.diagnosis: Infected intrahepatic hematoma / pyogenic liver abscess
data.description: Secondary bacterial infection of a post-traumatic liver hematoma leading to abscess formation, presenting with fever, leucocytosis and abnormal liver tests days after injury.
symptoms_not_in_common: Ultrasound appears to show gallbladder wall thickening rather than a complex intrahepatic collection with gas or debris
No described enlargement or change of the hematoma

data.description: Bleeding into the biliary tree after liver trauma, with clots filling the gallbladder and obstructing the cystic duct, causing gallbladder inflammation and biliary obstruction.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported gastrointestinal bleeding (melena or hematemesis)
No reported jaundice or biliary colic
No drop in hemoglobin mentioned
No clear echogenic clot seen in the gallbladder lumen

data.description: Bacterial infection of the biliary tree usually due to obstruction (stones, clots, strictures), presenting with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain, with cholestatic liver tests.
symptoms_in_common: Possible biliary obstruction from clots or compression by the hematoma
symptoms_not_in_common: No bile duct dilatation described on imaging
No reported jaundice
Imaging appears centred on the gallbladder wall rather than the bile ducts

data.diagnosis: Post-traumatic biloma / bile leak with secondary infection
data.description: Bile duct injury after liver trauma leading to an intra- or perihepatic bile collection that can become infected, causing fever and abnormal liver tests.
symptoms_not_in_common: No well-defined anechoic perihepatic or intrahepatic collection described
Ultrasound appears to show gallbladder wall thickening instead
No signs of bile peritonitis reported

data.description: A patient with known Crohn's disease presented with difficulties to pass stool, a sensation of a foreign body in the rectum and limited rectal bleeding. An endoscopy was performed as the first examination. A gallstone was found in the rectum and it was removed without complications.

A gallstone that has entered the intestinal tract becomes lodged in the rectum, causing mechanical difficulty with defecation and local mucosal irritation. This is the best-supported diagnosis because a gallstone was identified and removed endoscopically.
symptoms_in_common: Sensation of a foreign body in the rectum
Gallstone found in the rectum during endoscopy

data.description: An abnormal connection between the gallbladder and colon can allow a gallstone to pass directly into the colon and reach the rectum. The arrowed gallbladder–bowel interface appears suspicious for a biliary-enteric communication, although these images alone do not establish its precise anatomy.
symptoms_in_common: Gallstone found in the rectum, consistent with passage through a biliary-enteric fistula
Difficulty passing stool caused by a migrated stone
Rectal foreign-body sensation caused by a migrated stone
symptoms_not_in_common: Limited rectal bleeding is not a typical direct manifestation of the fistula itself

data.description: An abnormal connection between the gallbladder and duodenum allows gallstones to enter the intestine. A stone may traverse the bowel and become impacted distally; this is an alternative route to a cholecystocolonic fistula.
symptoms_in_common: Gallstone found in the rectum, compatible with migration through the intestinal tract
Difficulty passing stool if the migrated stone becomes impacted
Rectal foreign-body sensation from distal stone impaction
symptoms_not_in_common: Limited rectal bleeding is not typical of the fistula itself

data.description: Chronic inflammation and fibrosis from Crohn's disease can narrow the anus or rectum, obstructing defecation and potentially promoting stone impaction. This is a possible contributing condition, not established by the supplied findings.
symptoms_not_in_common: A gallstone in the rectum is not explained by an anorectal stricture alone

data.description: Crohn's-related rectal inflammation can cause bleeding, tenesmus, and difficulty evacuating. It is a possible coexisting condition but is less compelling than the directly observed rectal gallstone as the explanation for this presentation.
symptoms_in_common: Rectal foreign-body sensation compatible with tenesmus
symptoms_not_in_common: A gallstone found in the rectum is not a typical manifestation of proctitis

data.diagnosis: Cholecystocolonic fistula with gallstone passage into the colon/rectum
data.description: An abnormal communication between the gallbladder and the colon (usually the hepatic flexure), most often caused by chronic cholecystitis with stone erosion. It allows gallstones to pass directly into the colon, where they may lodge in the rectosigmoid.
symptoms_in_common: Foreign body sensation in the rectum
Limited rectal bleeding from mucosal irritation
MRI showing a tract and inflammatory enhancement between the gallbladder region and adjacent colon at the hepatic flexure
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported diarrhoea or bile acid malabsorption
No reported cholangitis, fever or right upper quadrant pain
No pneumobilia described

data.diagnosis: Cholecystoduodenal fistula with gallstone passage through the bowel (gallstone ileus spectrum)
data.description: The most common type of biliary-enteric fistula, between the gallbladder and the duodenum. Stones enter the small bowel and typically impact at the terminal ileum, but smaller stones can travel through to the colon and rectum.
symptoms_in_common: Gallstone found in the intestinal lumen (rectum)
Obstructive symptoms with difficulty passing stool
Fistulous tract in the gallbladder region on MRI
Crohn's disease, in which strictures could alter stone transit
symptoms_not_in_common: No small bowel obstruction, vomiting or abdominal distension
Stone passed the ileocaecal valve, which is unusual for a large stone
Imaging suggests the tract involves the colon rather than the duodenum

data.diagnosis: Crohn's disease-related enterobiliary fistula (fistulizing Crohn's disease)
data.description: Transmural inflammation in Crohn's disease can produce fistulas between the bowel and adjacent organs, rarely including the gallbladder. Crohn's disease also predisposes to gallstones through ileal bile salt malabsorption.
symptoms_in_common: Fistulous communication between gallbladder and bowel on MRI
Bowel wall enhancement or thickening near the hepatic flexure
symptoms_not_in_common: Crohn's fistulas to the gallbladder are extremely rare
No reported active flare symptoms such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain or weight loss
A gallstone-driven fistula from chronic cholecystitis is the more usual mechanism

data.diagnosis: Gallbladder carcinoma with fistulization to the colon
data.description: A malignant gallbladder tumour, often associated with gallstones, can invade adjacent structures such as the hepatic flexure and create a malignant cholecystoenteric fistula.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal enhancing tissue in the gallbladder region on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No discrete gallbladder mass or liver invasion described
No weight loss, jaundice or constitutional symptoms
No lymphadenopathy or metastases evident
Bleeding is explained by the rectal stone

data.diagnosis: Rectal faecalith/enterolith or faecal impaction mimicking a gallstone
data.description: Hardened stool or a concretion formed within the bowel (for example proximal to a Crohn's stricture) can lodge in the rectum and cause obstructive symptoms and bleeding. Anorectal Crohn's stricture can contribute.
symptoms_in_common: Foreign body sensation in the rectum
Crohn's disease, which predisposes to strictures and enteroliths
symptoms_not_in_common: The object was identified as a gallstone at endoscopy
MRI shows a gallbladder-to-bowel abnormality that explains a biliary origin
No rectal stricture described

data.description: A 31-year-old female, G3P2, came in with 5-day history of severe menorrhagia. She was treated medically and discharged. She was readmitted 2 days later with menorrhagia and anaemia (haemoglobin of 77). The patient had suffered a spontaneous miscarriage a few months earlier.

Abnormal connections between uterine arteries and veins that can develop after pregnancy loss and cause recurrent, potentially life-threatening bleeding. The supplied image is not interpretable; confirmation requires vascular imaging, typically Doppler ultrasound.
symptoms_in_common: Marked anaemia with haemoglobin reported as 77
Bleeding recurring shortly after medical treatment

data.description: Pregnancy tissue remaining in the uterus after miscarriage, sometimes forming a vascular placental polyp and causing persistent or delayed bleeding.
symptoms_not_in_common: Presentation several months after miscarriage is less typical, although delayed bleeding can occur

data.description: A contained injury to a uterine arterial wall that can intermittently rupture and cause severe delayed bleeding after pregnancy or uterine procedures.
symptoms_in_common: Bleeding following a recent pregnancy loss
Rapid recurrence after initial medical treatment

data.description: Persistent or malignant pregnancy-derived trophoblastic tissue, including choriocarcinoma, that may develop after miscarriage and cause uterine bleeding. Evaluation requires serum beta-hCG and appropriate imaging.
A benign uterine smooth-muscle tumour projecting into the endometrial cavity that can cause heavy menstrual bleeding, anaemia, and pregnancy loss.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent bleeding despite initial medical treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt severe bleeding in the months after miscarriage is less characteristic than a longstanding pattern of heavy menstrual bleeding

data.description: Abnormal direct communication between uterine arteries and veins, often acquired after miscarriage, curettage or other uterine trauma, causing intermittent, torrential bleeding that responds poorly to medical therapy. Note: the supplied image is entirely black and could not be interpreted, so this ranking is based on the clinical history alone.
symptoms_in_common: Spontaneous miscarriage a few months earlier
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented instrumentation or curettage after the miscarriage
No imaging confirmation available (image not interpretable)

data.description: Persistent placental or fetal tissue in the uterus after miscarriage or delivery, causing prolonged or heavy bleeding, sometimes with infection; may be highly vascular and mimic an arteriovenous malformation.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrence of bleeding after medical treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Miscarriage occurred a few months earlier, whereas bleeding usually presents within days to weeks
No reported fever, pelvic pain or offensive discharge

data.diagnosis: Gestational trophoblastic disease (invasive mole or choriocarcinoma)
data.description: Abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue that can follow any pregnancy, including miscarriage, producing hypervascular uterine lesions, heavy bleeding and elevated beta-hCG.
symptoms_not_in_common: No beta-hCG elevation reported
No uterine enlargement, hyperemesis or metastatic symptoms described

data.description: Contained rupture of a uterine artery wall, usually after uterine trauma, surgery, curettage or delivery, causing delayed and potentially life-threatening haemorrhage.
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented surgical procedure, curettage or caesarean section
Bleeding described as menorrhagia rather than sudden haemorrhage

data.description: Benign smooth muscle tumour of the uterus projecting into the endometrial cavity; a common cause of heavy menstrual bleeding and iron-deficiency anaemia in reproductive-age women, and associated with miscarriage.
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute 5-day onset rather than chronic, progressively heavy periods
No pelvic pressure symptoms or palpable mass reported
Temporal link to the recent miscarriage is not explained by a fibroid

data.description: At the age of 30 months, the patient began presenting an evolving framework of severe cognitive and neurological impairment, with tetraparesis and mixed spastic-dystonic features, language delay and deafness. Moreover, she has coarse facial features, presenting a high forehead and hypertelorism; her tongue is protruding due to macroglossia.

An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-L-fucosidase deficiency, producing progressive neurodegeneration and coarse facial features. The apparent low T2 and relatively high T1 thalamic signal on the supplied images supports this possibility but is not diagnostic.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive severe cognitive and neurological impairment beginning in early childhood
Coarse facial features with a prominent forehead
Apparent thalamic signal abnormalities and periventricular white-matter changes on MRI

data.description: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by beta-galactosidase deficiency, resulting in lysosomal accumulation of GM1 ganglioside and progressive neurological deterioration.
symptoms_in_common: Severe cognitive impairment and language delay
Possible thalamic and white-matter MRI abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Deafness is less characteristic
Marked facial coarsening and macroglossia are less typical of the late-infantile form than of the infantile form

data.diagnosis: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I, severe form (Hurler syndrome)
data.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, leading to glycosaminoglycan accumulation and progressive multisystem disease.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent dystonia is not typical
Severe tetraparesis early in childhood is less typical unless spinal cord compression or advanced neurological disease is present

data.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency, commonly producing intellectual disability, hearing impairment, coarse facial features, and motor dysfunction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Rapid progression to severe spastic tetraparesis is less typical
Prominent dystonia is less characteristic than ataxia
The apparent thalamic MRI signal pattern is not a hallmark

data.description: An autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder caused by neuraminidase deficiency, with childhood forms producing coarse facial features, developmental impairment, and progressive neurological disease.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive motor impairment with possible spasticity
symptoms_not_in_common: Deafness is not a defining feature
A predominantly spastic-dystonic tetraparesis is less characteristic
The apparent thalamic MRI signal pattern is not typical

data.description: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease due to alpha-L-fucosidase (FUCA1) deficiency, causing progressive neurodegeneration, coarse facies, spasticity and dystonia, hearing loss, and characteristic MRI with hypomyelination and T2-hypointense globus pallidus.
symptoms_in_common: onset in early childhood with progressive cognitive and neurological deterioration
periventricular white matter T2 hyperintensity with T2-hypointense pallidi/thalami on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: no angiokeratoma reported
no dysostosis multiplex or recurrent infections reported
hypertelorism and high forehead are nonspecific

data.description: Lysosomal storage disorder from alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency with glycosaminoglycan accumulation, causing coarse facies, macroglossia, developmental regression, hearing loss, skeletal dysplasia and organomegaly.
symptoms_in_common: white matter signal changes on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: prominent spastic-dystonic tetraparesis
no corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly or skeletal changes reported
no enlarged perivascular spaces on MRI
basal ganglia T2 hypointensity is not typical

data.description: Beta-galactosidase deficiency leading to ganglioside accumulation in neurons, with progressive neurodegeneration, dystonia, spasticity, variable coarse facies and skeletal changes; MRI shows hypomyelination and basal ganglia abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: white matter abnormalities with pallidal T2 hypointensity
symptoms_not_in_common: deafness is not a prominent feature
no cherry-red spot, seizures or skeletal dysplasia reported
coarse facies are usually mild in the late infantile/juvenile form

data.description: Lysosomal storage disease caused by alpha-mannosidase deficiency, characterised by intellectual disability, sensorineural hearing loss, coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, immune deficiency and ataxia.
symptoms_not_in_common: severe spastic-dystonic tetraparesis (ataxia is more typical)
relatively rapid severe neurological deterioration
no recurrent infections or skeletal anomalies reported
pallidal T2 hypointensity is not typical

data.diagnosis: Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (Hunter syndrome, severe form)
data.description: X-linked lysosomal storage disorder due to iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, causing coarse facies, macroglossia, hearing loss, progressive cognitive decline, organomegaly and skeletal involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: patient is female (X-linked disease, almost exclusively in males)
spastic-dystonic tetraparesis is not typical
no hepatosplenomegaly, joint contractures or skin lesions reported
pallidal T2 hypointensity is not typical

data.description: A 23-year-old female presented with a complaint of intermittent dyspnea (New York Heart Association NYHA grade, II), which aggravates on exertion and mild chest pain. No past significant medical and surgical history was given by the patient. On clinical examination, bruit was heard on auscultation in the left mid-zone.

An abnormal direct connection between pulmonary arteries and veins that bypasses the capillary bed and can cause a right-to-left shunt. This is the leading possibility: the images appear to show a lobulated peripheral left-lung vascular sac with enlarged connecting vessels.
symptoms_in_common: Localized bruit over the left mid-zone
Apparent peripheral vascular sac with enlarged feeding and draining vessels

data.description: Focal dilation of a pulmonary artery, potentially congenital or associated with pulmonary hypertension, infection, or vasculitis. It can resemble an arteriovenous malformation, but should not have a direct enlarged draining vein.
symptoms_in_common: Focal contrast-enhancing vascular lesion in the left lung
symptoms_not_in_common: Localized chest bruit is less typical
Apparent paired enlarged vessels connecting to the lesion favor an arteriovenous malformation

data.description: A focal aneurysmal dilation of a pulmonary vein, either congenital or acquired. It may appear as a lobulated vascular opacity but lacks an arterial feeder and an arteriovenous shunt.
symptoms_in_common: Lobulated vascular opacity in the left lung
Dyspnea, if the venous abnormality is hemodynamically significant
symptoms_not_in_common: Localized left mid-zone bruit
Mild chest pain is not a usual presentation
Apparent enlarged arterial feeder is not expected

data.description: A rare abnormal connection between a systemic artery, such as a bronchial or intercostal artery, and a pulmonary vein. It can produce a thoracic bruit and a peripheral vascular mass; identifying the arterial origin distinguishes it from a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation.
symptoms_in_common: Peripheral vascular lesion with enlarged connecting vessels
symptoms_not_in_common: The apparent connection to the pulmonary arterial circulation favors a pulmonary rather than systemic arterial feeder

data.description: A congenital region of abnormal lung tissue lacking normal airway communication and supplied by a systemic artery. It can present as a peripheral lung lesion with an anomalous vessel, although the supplied images favor a vascular malformation rather than sequestered lung.
symptoms_in_common: A focal lung lesion associated with enlarged vessels
symptoms_not_in_common: Localized bruit is uncommon
A strongly enhancing vascular sac without an obvious abnormal lung segment is atypical
Apparent pulmonary arterial supply rather than systemic arterial supply

data.description: Abnormal direct communication between a pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein without an intervening capillary bed, causing a right-to-left shunt. It may be congenital and sporadic or associated with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.
symptoms_in_common: CT angiography showing a dilated feeding artery and draining vein with a peripheral aneurysmal sac in the left lung
Opacity in the left mid-zone on chest X-ray
symptoms_not_in_common: No cyanosis, clubbing or polycythemia reported
No history of stroke, brain abscess or other paradoxical embolism
No hemoptysis

data.diagnosis: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome) with pulmonary AVM
data.description: Autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia characterised by mucocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis and visceral arteriovenous malformations in the lung, liver and brain.
symptoms_not_in_common: No recurrent epistaxis
No mucocutaneous telangiectasias described
No family history reported
Single lesion rather than multiple AVMs
No significant past medical history

data.description: Focal dilatation of a pulmonary artery branch, caused by infection, vasculitis such as Behçet disease, trauma, pulmonary hypertension or a congenital defect.
symptoms_in_common: Aneurysmal enhancing vascular sac in the left lung
symptoms_not_in_common: Enlarged draining vein to the left atrium indicates an arteriovenous communication rather than an isolated aneurysm
No hemoptysis
No history of infection, trauma or vasculitis
No oral or genital ulcers
No evidence of pulmonary hypertension

data.description: Localised aneurysmal dilatation of a pulmonary vein, either congenital or acquired through raised left atrial pressure such as in mitral valve disease. It is usually asymptomatic.
symptoms_in_common: Dilated tubular vascular structure draining toward the left atrium
Nodular vascular opacity on chest X-ray
symptoms_not_in_common: Enlarged feeding pulmonary artery would not be expected
Bruit is not typical
Exertional dyspnea is uncommon because a varix is usually asymptomatic
No mitral valve disease reported
Peripheral aneurysmal nidus suggests an arteriovenous connection

data.diagnosis: Pulmonary sequestration or systemic arterial supply to the lung (systemic artery-to-pulmonary fistula)
data.description: Congenital anomaly in which a segment of lung, or a vascular malformation within it, receives arterial supply from the systemic circulation such as the aorta, intercostal or bronchial arteries. It can cause a left-to-right shunt and a continuous murmur.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal enlarged vessels in the left lung
symptoms_not_in_common: Feeding vessel appears to arise from the pulmonary artery, not the aorta or another systemic artery
No recurrent pneumonia or productive cough
Lesion is in the mid-zone rather than the typical lower-lobe posterobasal location
No abnormal lung parenchyma or cystic mass

data.description: Patient is a 2 month-old male, full-term infant, with severe malnutrition and failure to thrive, admitted to the intensive care unit, with long term feeding difficulties. The study was performed initially to rule out malrotation.

data.diagnosis: Congenital duodenal web with partial obstruction
data.description: A thin congenital membrane narrows the duodenal lumen, allowing some passage of food but potentially causing persistent feeding intolerance. This is a possible explanation for the apparent duodenal distention and limited downstream contrast passage.
symptoms_in_common: Apparent duodenal distention on the contrast study

data.diagnosis: Annular pancreas causing partial duodenal obstruction
data.description: Pancreatic tissue encircles the duodenum and can narrow it, producing complete or partial obstruction. The contrast images alone cannot establish the presence of annular pancreatic tissue.
symptoms_in_common: Possible proximal duodenal obstruction on imaging

data.diagnosis: Intestinal malrotation with obstructing Ladd bands
data.description: Abnormal embryologic intestinal rotation can leave congenital bands compressing the duodenum and predispose to volvulus. Diagnosis requires clear assessment of the duodenal course and duodenojejunal junction, which these selected images do not conclusively provide.
symptoms_in_common: Feeding difficulties beginning in early infancy

data.description: Compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta can cause partial obstruction. Severe loss of body fat may contribute, although this condition is very uncommon in a two-month-old infant.
symptoms_in_common: Possible duodenal distention with impaired downstream passage
symptoms_not_in_common: Long-standing feeding difficulties from early infancy are less typical and suggest a congenital cause

data.description: Thickening of the pyloric muscle obstructs gastric emptying, typically presenting during the first weeks of life. Ultrasound is the preferred diagnostic examination; the apparent duodenal abnormality here makes this a less likely explanation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Apparent duodenal distention is not the characteristic imaging pattern of isolated pyloric obstruction

data.description: Acquired hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causing gastric outlet obstruction in infants, typically presenting between 2 and 8 weeks of age, more often in males.
symptoms_in_common: upper GI study that could show delayed gastric emptying or a narrowed pyloric channel
symptoms_not_in_common: projectile non-bilious vomiting not explicitly reported
long-term feeding difficulties suggest a more chronic or congenital process
contrast appears to reach the duodenum and proximal small bowel
no palpable olive mass described

data.diagnosis: Intestinal malrotation (with or without intermittent midgut volvulus / Ladd bands)
data.description: Congenital anomaly of midgut rotation and fixation, with an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction; can cause chronic partial duodenal obstruction or acute volvulus.
symptoms_in_common: upper GI study performed specifically to evaluate for it
duodenal course on the images may be abnormal
symptoms_not_in_common: bilious vomiting not reported
no acute abdominal catastrophe described
chronic course without acute obstruction is less typical
study wording suggests an alternative or incidental finding

data.diagnosis: Congenital duodenal stenosis / duodenal web / annular pancreas
data.description: Congenital partial obstruction of the duodenum from an intrinsic web or stenosis, or from extrinsic encirclement by pancreatic tissue, causing chronic proximal dilation and poor feeding tolerance.
symptoms_in_common: long-term feeding difficulties from early life
contrast-filled, apparently prominent proximal duodenum on upper GI study
passage of some contrast distally consistent with partial obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: vomiting not explicitly reported
no mention of trisomy 21 or other associated anomalies
complete obstruction would usually present in the first days of life rather than at 2 months

data.diagnosis: Gastroesophageal reflux disease with or without hiatal hernia
data.description: Retrograde passage of gastric contents into the esophagus causing regurgitation, feeding aversion, and poor weight gain in infants; may be demonstrated on upper GI study.
symptoms_not_in_common: severe malnutrition requiring intensive care is unusual for simple reflux
no regurgitation, irritability, or respiratory symptoms described
images concentrate on the stomach and duodenum rather than showing reflux

data.diagnosis: Gastric volvulus / congenital microgastria (gastric anatomic anomaly)
data.description: Abnormal rotation of the stomach, or a congenitally small, tubular stomach, leading to poor reservoir function, feeding intolerance, reflux, and growth failure in infancy.
symptoms_in_common: possibly abnormal configuration or position of the contrast-filled stomach on upper GI images
symptoms_not_in_common: no megaesophagus described
no associated anomalies such as asplenia or limb/cardiac defects reported
no acute retching or epigastric distension reported
rare conditions

data.description: A 32 year-old male presented to his primary care provider with unremitting neck pain. He denied any history of trauma. The patient was unresponsive to conservative therapy and plain-film radiographic evaluation was negative. Patient was subsequently referred for a cervical spine MR for further evaluation.

A glial tumor involving the brainstem, potentially the medulla in this case. The apparent medullary enlargement and heterogeneous signal and enhancement make this a consideration, although the supplied images alone cannot establish the diagnosis.
symptoms_in_common: Normal cervical plain radiographs, which do not exclude a brainstem lesion

data.description: A tumor arising from ependymal cells near the fourth ventricle or central canal. It can involve the medulla and produce a heterogeneous, enhancing mass with local expansion.
symptoms_in_common: Negative plain radiographs despite persistent symptoms

data.description: A cluster of abnormal small blood vessels that can cause recurrent bleeding within the brainstem. Mixed internal signal can resemble the apparent heterogeneous medullary lesion; susceptibility-sensitive MRI would help evaluate this possibility.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent symptoms not explained by cervical radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: Unremitting pain without a reported abrupt onset or episodic neurological deterioration is less characteristic of symptomatic hemorrhage

data.description: A highly vascular, usually benign tumor that can occur in the medulla and typically enhances strongly. Dedicated contrast-enhanced imaging would help assess for a discrete enhancing nodule and associated vessels.
symptoms_in_common: Normal plain radiographs despite an intracranial cause of symptoms

data.diagnosis: Subependymoma of the fourth ventricle or medulla
data.description: A slow-growing, usually benign tumor near the ventricular lining that can produce symptoms through local mass effect. It is a less likely alternative because subependymomas typically show little enhancement.

Glial tumor arising from the ependymal lining of the fourth ventricle; characteristically a soft, 'plastic' tumor that extends through the foramen of Magendie and foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal, often presenting with neck pain or torticollis. Heterogeneous signal and heterogeneous enhancement are typical.
symptoms_in_common: Unremitting neck pain without trauma (tumor extension through foramen magnum)
Heterogeneous T2 hyperintense mass in the fourth ventricle
Inferior extension of the mass toward the foramen magnum/upper cervical canal
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 32 (posterior fossa ependymoma is more common in children)
No reported headache, nausea, vomiting or ataxia despite the mass and hydrocephalus

data.description: Benign, slow-growing WHO grade 1 intraventricular tumor, usually found in the inferior fourth ventricle of adults; often asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic and found incidentally.
symptoms_in_common: Fourth ventricular mass with T2 hyperintensity
Paucity of neurological symptoms despite a sizeable mass (indolent course)
symptoms_not_in_common: Typically occurs in middle-aged or older adults
Usually shows little or no enhancement, whereas this mass enhances heterogeneously
Extension through the foramen magnum is less characteristic
Prominent neck pain is uncommon

data.description: Malignant embryonal tumor of the cerebellum; in adults it accounts for a small proportion of posterior fossa tumors, may arise from the vermis or the cerebellar hemisphere, and can fill the fourth ventricle causing hydrocephalus.
symptoms_not_in_common: Most common in children; adult cases are often lateral in the cerebellar hemisphere
Does not typically extrude through the foramina into the cervical canal
Usually less T2 hyperintense due to high cellularity
Absence of headache, vomiting or ataxia
Isolated neck pain is an atypical presentation

data.description: Benign intraventricular neoplasm of choroid plexus epithelium; in adults it most commonly arises in the fourth ventricle and causes hydrocephalus from obstruction or CSF overproduction.
symptoms_in_common: Possible extension through the fourth ventricular outlet foramina
symptoms_not_in_common: Usually shows intense, homogeneous enhancement with a lobulated frond-like contour, rather than heterogeneous enhancement
Neck pain as the only symptom is unusual
No headache or other signs of raised intracranial pressure reported

data.description: Benign vascular tumor that is the most common primary posterior fossa parenchymal tumor in adults; may be sporadic or associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease, and usually appears as a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule, less often as a solid mass.
symptoms_in_common: Posterior fossa mass near the cervicomedullary junction
symptoms_not_in_common: Usually located in the cerebellar hemisphere rather than within the fourth ventricle
No classic cyst with avidly enhancing mural nodule
No prominent flow voids described
No known history or family history of von Hippel-Lindau disease
Isolated neck pain is not a typical presentation
